Sustained attention, also called vigilance, is the ability to keep focus on something over a long stretch of time, especially when little is happening, as a lifeguard watching a calm pool or a security guard watching screens must.

Research on vigilance shows a reliable decline in performance over time, called the vigilance decrement, where people miss more and more rare signals as the minutes drag on, which has serious practical consequences for jobs built around watchful waiting.

Keeping these three apart matters because a person can be strong in one and weak in another, and because the theories in later chapters are usually about one variety at a time.


12.1.2 Spatial, feature-based, and object-based attention

Whereas the previous sub-section sorted attention by its job, this one sorts it by what, exactly, gets selected, and the answer turns out to be more than just places.

Spatial attention is the selection of a region of space, so that whatever falls in the attended location is processed better, and it is often pictured as a spotlight that can be aimed around the visual field independently of the eyes.

The spotlight metaphor captures the finding that things near the centre of attention are seen faster and more accurately, while things outside it are handled poorly, as though lit or left in shadow.

Feature-based attention is the selection of a particular property, such as a colour or a direction of motion, applied across the whole scene at once rather than at one spot.

For instance, if you look for your friend in a red coat, you can boost red everywhere in the crowd at the same time, which is feature-based attention doing its work, and this global boosting of a chosen feature has been confirmed in both behaviour and brain activity.

Object-based attention is the selection of a whole object, so that once you attend to any part of a thing, its other parts and properties become easier to process too, because attention spreads across the object as a unit.

Evidence for this comes from studies where people are faster to judge two features when both belong to the same object than when they belong to two different objects, even with everything else held equal, showing that the object itself, not just a location, can be the thing selected.

The practical upshot is that attention is flexible about its target: depending on the task, the mind can spotlight a place, tune to a feature everywhere, or grab hold of a whole object, and a full theory of attention has to allow all three.


12.1.3 Overt and covert, exogenous and endogenous orienting

This sub-section adds two further cross-cutting distinctions about how attention is aimed, both of which are essential for reading the later research.

Orienting simply means directing attention toward something, and the first distinction concerns whether that directing is visible from the outside.

Overt orienting is shifting attention by moving the sense organ, most obviously by turning your eyes to look straight at something, so an observer could see where your attention has gone.

Covert orienting is shifting attention without moving the eyes, attending to something out of the corner of your vision while looking elsewhere, which you can prove to yourself right now by fixing your gaze ahead and yet attending to an object off to the side.

The demonstration that covert attention is real, largely due to Michael Posner in the late 1970s, was pivotal, because it showed attention can be decoupled from the eyes and studied as a mental spotlight in its own right.

The second distinction concerns what drives the shift, and it separates attention that is captured from attention that is chosen.

Exogenous orienting is attention grabbed automatically by something in the world, such as a sudden flash, a loud bang, or movement in the periphery, and it is fast, involuntary, and hard to resist, an evolutionary sensible reflex toward possible threats or opportunities.

Endogenous orienting is attention directed on purpose, from your own goals, such as deliberately watching a doorway because you are expecting someone, and it is slower to engage, voluntary, and under your control.

The two can pull in different directions, which is why an unexpected notification can yank your attention away from work no matter how firmly you had chosen to concentrate, and researchers have found they even rely on partly different brain networks.

These pairs, overt versus covert and exogenous versus endogenous, combine freely with the varieties of the earlier sub-sections, giving attention research its precise, sometimes intimidating, but ultimately clarifying vocabulary.


12.2 The founding question

Having named the varieties, this section steps back to ask why attention exists at all, which is the question that gave birth to the whole field.

The answer is deceptively simple and deeply important: attention exists because the mind cannot do everything at once.

Understanding this founding logic makes every later theory easier to grasp, because they are all, in the end, proposals about how a limited system copes.


12.2.1 Attention as selection under a capacity limit

The founding idea is that attention is fundamentally about selection forced upon us by a limit on how much we can process, called a capacity limit.

Capacity here means the total amount of information the mind can handle at one time, and the claim is that this amount is far smaller than the amount the senses deliver.

At every instant your eyes, ears, skin, and other senses pour in vastly more information than the brain can fully analyse, so something has to give, and attention is the mechanism that decides what gets the limited processing and what is left out.

This is why the earliest and most influential theories, which we meet in the next chapter, were framed as questions about a bottleneck, a narrow point in the flow of information where selection happens, much as a narrow neck limits how fast liquid leaves a bottle.

Selection under a capacity limit has two sides that are worth naming: enhancing the chosen information so it is processed more fully, and suppressing or ignoring the rest so it does not interfere, and attention does both.

Framing attention this way also tells you what a theory of attention owes you: it must say where in the stream of processing the selection happens, how much of the unattended material still gets analysed, and what sets the size of the limit, which are exactly the debates the following chapters take up.

So this small idea, that the mind must choose because it cannot do all, is the seed from which the entire science of attention grows.


12.2.2 Why a mind with unlimited capacity would need no attention

This closing sub-section drives the founding point home with a useful thought experiment, and it clarifies what attention is by imagining its absence.

Picture a mind with unlimited processing capacity, one that could fully analyse every sight, sound, and thought all at once, with no ceiling on how much it could handle.

Such a mind would have no need of attention at all, because attention is only useful when resources are scarce and must be rationed; with infinite resources there is nothing to ration and nothing to choose between.

This is a clarifying insight because it tells us that attention is not a thing added to the mind for its own sake but a direct consequence of limitation, the mind's strategy for being finite in a world that offers more than it can process.

It also explains why attention involves cost and effort and can fail, why focusing on one thing means missing others, because these are the unavoidable trade-offs of dividing a fixed and limited resource among competing demands.

The point connects attention to a broader theme that runs through the whole science of cognition, that many features of the mind are best understood as clever solutions to the problem of doing as well as possible with limited means.

Seen this way, attention is not a quirk or a weakness but a signature of any real, resource-bounded intelligence, which is precisely why a machine built to think in a humanlike way, as konnectome aims to, will need mechanisms of attention of its own, for it too cannot process everything at once.

CHAPTER 13. SELECTION: BOTTLENECK, LOAD, AND CAPACITY (PROCESS)

This chapter is about a simple fact of daily life: your mind cannot fully process everything that reaches your senses at once, so it must choose.

Selection is the name for that choosing, the way the mind lets some information through for full treatment while holding the rest back.

The big question in this chapter is not whether the mind selects, because clearly it does, but where in the stream of processing the selection happens, and what sets the limit that makes selection necessary.

Answering that question well matters for konnectome, because any machine that must act in a rich, noisy world faces the same problem of too much information and too little capacity to handle all of it.


13.1 The bottleneck theories

A bottleneck is the narrow neck of a bottle that lets only a little liquid through at a time, and here it is a metaphor for a narrow stage in mental processing that only a little information can pass through at once.

The first theories of attention argued about exactly where that narrow point sits, and this section lays out the three classic answers in the order they were proposed.


13.1.1 Early selection and the filter model

Early selection is the idea that the mind picks what to attend to very soon after information arrives, before it works out what the information actually means.

The idea grew out of a real-world puzzle that the psychologist Colin Cherry named in 1953, the cocktail party problem, which is the everyday ability to follow one voice in a room full of overlapping conversations.

To study this in the laboratory, researchers used a task called dichotic listening, in which a person wears headphones and hears one spoken message in the left ear and a different message in the right ear at the same time.

The listener is told to shadow one ear, meaning to repeat aloud what that ear hears, while ignoring the other ear.

Cherry found that people could do this, and that afterward they remembered almost nothing about the ignored ear, not even whether the language had changed to a foreign tongue, though they did notice crude physical facts such as whether the voice was male or female.

The British psychologist Donald Broadbent built these findings into the first full theory of attention in his 1958 book Perception and Communication, and it is called the filter model.

Broadbent proposed that all incoming signals first enter a very brief sensory store, then pass to a selective filter that lets only one channel through based on simple physical features such as which ear it came from or the pitch of the voice.

The rejected channel is blocked at this early gate, so its meaning is never analysed, which is why the ignored ear seemed to leave no trace.

Beyond the filter sits a limited-capacity channel, a narrow stage that can handle only one stream at a time, and this is the bottleneck.

The strength of the model is that it explained the shadowing results cleanly, and it introduced the flow diagram, a boxes-and-arrows picture of the mind, which became a standard tool of the field.

Its weakness is that it turned out to be too strict, because people sometimes do notice meaningful things in the supposedly blocked ear, which a truly early gate should not allow.


13.1.2 Attenuation

Attenuation means turning something down rather than shutting it off, the way you might lower the volume on a radio without switching it silent.

The attenuation model was proposed by Anne Treisman in the early 1960s to fix a specific problem with Broadbent's strict filter.

The problem was evidence that unattended information sometimes gets through, most famously the finding that many people hear their own name spoken in the ignored ear, which is a modern echo of the cocktail party effect.

If the filter truly blocked the unattended channel before its meaning was read, hearing your own name there should be impossible.

Treisman's fix was to say the filter does not block the unattended channel but weakens it, so the unattended signal is still analysed, just at reduced strength.

She added the idea that different words have different thresholds, a threshold being the level of evidence needed before a word is recognised.

Important or personally relevant words, such as your own name or the word fire, have permanently low thresholds, so even a weakened signal is enough to trip them into awareness.

This neatly explains why most unattended words are lost but a special few break through.

Treisman's model is often described as a middle position, softer than Broadbent's hard early gate but still placing selection relatively early, because most unattended material is attenuated and never fully processed.


13.1.3 Late selection

Late selection is the opposite bet from early selection, the claim that the mind fully analyses the meaning of everything that comes in and only then chooses what to keep for awareness and response.

This view was put forward by J. Anthony Deutsch and Diana Deutsch in 1963, and later developed by Donald Norman.

On this account there is no early filter at all, because all incoming signals, attended and unattended, are processed all the way to the level of meaning.

The selection happens near the end, at the gate to memory and response, where only the most relevant or important item is allowed through to guide behaviour and enter awareness.

This model easily explains cases where unattended meaning has an effect, since on this view meaning is always computed.

Its cost is that it seems wasteful, because it requires the brain to fully analyse a great deal of material that is then thrown away, and it struggles to explain why people remember so little of the ignored channel.

For decades the early and late camps argued back and forth, and the honest summary is that neither pure position won outright, which set the stage for a theory that made the location of selection flexible rather than fixed.


13.2 Load and capacity

This section moves from the question of where selection happens to the question of what governs it and how the mind shares out its limited processing power.

The key modern idea is that selection is not always early or always late, but shifts depending on how hard the current task is, and this reframes the old debate as being about load.


13.2.1 Perceptual load theory and the movable locus of selection

Perceptual load theory, proposed by Nilli Lavie in 1995, is the idea that whether selection is early or late depends on how demanding the task in front of you is right now.

Perceptual load simply means the amount of perceptual work a task requires, for example how many items you must scan or how finely you must discriminate them.

Locus of selection is a technical phrase that just means the place in processing where the choosing occurs, and the word movable signals that this place can shift.

Lavie's central claim is that we have a fixed and limited pool of perceptual capacity that is used up automatically and involuntarily.

When a task has high perceptual load, it consumes all of that capacity, leaving nothing to spill over onto irrelevant distractors, so distractors are effectively filtered out and selection looks early.

When a task has low perceptual load, spare capacity remains after the main task is served, and because perception runs automatically that leftover capacity flows onto the distractors, so they get processed and selection looks late.

A common demonstration uses a target letter to find among either few items, which is low load, or many crowded items, which is high load, while an irrelevant distractor sits to the side.

The distractor slows people down under low load but not under high load, which is the signature the theory predicts.

Lavie's proposal is powerful because it reconciles the old early-versus-late fight by saying both camps were partly right, and which one applies depends on load.

Later work has qualified the theory, noting that the effects depend on how load is defined and that some findings are harder to reproduce, so it is influential rather than settled.


13.2.2 Limited-capacity and multiple-resource models

This sub-section asks a deeper question: is attention one single pool of mental fuel, or several separate pools.

A limited-capacity model treats attention as one general reservoir of mental effort that any task can draw on, a view associated with Daniel Kahneman's 1973 book Attention and Effort.

On this single-pool view, two tasks interfere with each other whenever their combined demand exceeds the one shared supply, no matter what kind of tasks they are.

The multiple-resource model, developed chiefly by Christopher Wickens, challenges that by proposing several separate pools rather than one.

On this view resources are divided along dimensions such as the sense used, for instance vision versus hearing, the kind of code, for instance verbal versus spatial, and the stage, for instance perceiving versus responding.

The prediction that follows is concrete and useful: two tasks clash badly when they compete for the same pool but coexist far more easily when they draw on different pools.

This is why you can often drive while listening to speech, since driving is largely visual and spatial while listening is auditory and verbal, but you struggle to read a map and read a text message at once, since both are visual and verbal.

The multiple-resource idea is widely used in human-factors engineering, the practical science of designing tasks and machines to fit human limits, precisely because it predicts which combinations of tasks will overload a person.


13.2.3 Automaticity and controlled processing

This sub-section is about the difference between mental actions that run by themselves and mental actions that demand deliberate effort.

Controlled processing is slow, effortful, capacity-limited, and open to conscious guidance, the kind of thinking you use when doing unfamiliar arithmetic in your head.

Automatic processing is fast, effortless, hard to stop, and runs with little or no drain on capacity, the kind of processing that lets a fluent reader take in a word without trying.

The classic account comes from Richard Shiffrin and Walter Schneider in 1977, who showed that heavy, consistent practice can turn a controlled task into an automatic one.

In their studies people searched for target items among distractors, and when the targets and distractors kept swapping roles the task stayed slow and effortful, but when a fixed set of items was always the target, performance became fast and nearly automatic with practice.

A famous everyday illustration of automaticity is the Stroop effect, named after John Ridley Stroop, in which naming the ink colour of a colour word is slowed when the word spells a different colour, for example the word red printed in blue ink.

The Stroop effect shows that reading has become so automatic in a literate adult that it happens whether or not you want it to, and it then interferes with the colour-naming you are trying to do.

The practical lesson is that automaticity frees up limited capacity for other things, which is why skilled performance feels easy, but it also makes well-learned habits hard to suppress.


13.3 The central bottleneck in performance

Having examined selection among competing inputs, this section turns to a related limit that shows up when you try to do two response tasks at nearly the same moment.

The evidence here points to a single central stage that can only handle one decision at a time, a bottleneck not at the input but at the choosing of a response.


13.3.1 The psychological refractory period

The psychological refractory period (PRP) is the reliable delay in responding to a second task when it arrives hard on the heels of a first task.

The word refractory borrows from physiology, where it names a brief period after a nerve fires during which it cannot fire again, and here it names a stretch during which the mind seems unable to start a second decision.

The standard experiment presents two quick tasks, each needing its own speedy response, and varies the gap between them, a gap the field calls the stimulus onset asynchrony (SOA), meaning the time between the start of the first stimulus and the start of the second.

The finding is that the response to the first task stays about the same, but the response to the second task gets slower as the two are squeezed closer together.

The standard explanation, developed in detail by Harold Pashler, is a central bottleneck at the stage of response selection, the moment when you decide which action goes with the stimulus you just perceived.

On this account, perception of the two stimuli can proceed in parallel, but the choosing of a response can only serve one task at a time, so the second task must wait its turn, and that forced waiting is the delay.

This gives a clean picture of the mind as able to sense many things at once but able to decide only one thing at a time.


13.3.2 Dual-task cost and its interpretation

Dual-task cost is simply the drop in performance you pay for doing two things at once compared with doing each alone, measured as slower responses, more errors, or both.

The interesting part is not that the cost exists but what it tells us about the mind's architecture, and here researchers disagree.

One interpretation is the structural bottleneck view described above, which says the cost comes from a fixed stage that can process only one response decision at a time, forcing the tasks into a queue.

A rival interpretation is graded capacity sharing, which says there is no strict one-at-a-time gate but a limited pool that can be split between tasks, so each task runs slower because each gets only part of the supply.

Distinguishing these is hard, because both predict that two tasks will interfere, and the debate over the exact shape of the interference is still open in the research literature.

There is also evidence that some of the bottleneck reflects strategy rather than a hard wall, because when people are told to treat both tasks as equally urgent the pattern of interference can change.

A further important finding is that extensive practice can shrink dual-task costs dramatically, and in some cases two well-practised tasks can be run together with almost no cost, which fits the earlier point that practice breeds automaticity.

The balanced conclusion is that there really is a serious limit on doing two decision-heavy tasks at once, that the limit is partly structural and partly strategic, and that training can loosen it but rarely erases it.


CHAPTER 14. SPATIAL ATTENTION AND CONTROL NETWORKS (PROCESS)

This chapter is about attention in space, the way you can concentrate on one region of your visual world without moving your eyes, and about the brain systems that steer that concentration.

It matters because much of attention is fundamentally about location: choosing where to look, or where to prioritise, is one of the mind's most constant jobs.

The chapter moves from the behavioural metaphors that describe how spatial attention behaves, to the large-scale brain networks that control it, to the fine-grained neural theory of how selection changes the activity of single cells.


14.1 The mechanics of spatial attention

This section describes how spatial attention behaves as measured by experiments, using metaphors that capture its shape and its movement, and the laboratory methods that reveal it.


14.1.1 The spotlight and zoom-lens metaphors

The spotlight metaphor, associated with Michael Posner around 1980, pictures attention as a beam of light that you can move across a scene, so that whatever falls inside the beam is processed better and faster than whatever falls outside it.

A key point is that this beam can move independently of the eyes, so you can fix your gaze on one spot while secretly attending to another, which researchers call covert attention, meaning attention without an accompanying eye movement.

The zoom-lens metaphor, proposed by Charles Eriksen and colleagues in 1986, adds an important refinement, namely that the spotlight is not a fixed size but can widen or narrow like the zoom of a camera.

The trade-off built into the zoom lens is that a wide focus covers more area but processes each part less finely, while a narrow focus covers less area but processes it in sharp detail.

Together these metaphors capture two robust facts: attention gives a processing advantage to a chosen region, and the size of that region is adjustable at the cost of resolution.


14.1.2 Cueing, orienting, and inhibition of return

This sub-section describes the main laboratory tool for studying spatial attention and one of its most surprising discoveries.

Orienting means directing attention to a location, and the standard way to study it is the spatial cueing task devised by Michael Posner, often just called the Posner cueing task.

In this task a cue, such as a brief flash or an arrow, indicates a location, and then a target appears that the person must respond to as fast as possible.

When the target appears at the cued location the response is faster, a benefit, and when it appears elsewhere the response is slower, a cost, which shows that the cue pulled attention to its location.

There is an important distinction between two ways of being cued: exogenous orienting, which is attention grabbed automatically by a sudden event in the world such as a flash, and endogenous orienting, which is attention sent deliberately according to a meaningful signal such as an arrow you have learned to obey.

Exogenous cueing is fast and reflexive, giving a benefit within roughly a tenth of a second, while endogenous cueing is slower and voluntary.

The surprising discovery is inhibition of return (IOR), which is the finding that after attention has been drawn to a location and then moved away, responses to that same location become slower rather than faster.

This slowing appears when the delay between cue and target grows beyond about a fifth to a third of a second, reversing the earlier benefit.

Inhibition of return is thought to be useful because it biases attention toward new, unexplored locations and discourages it from returning to places already checked, which would help an animal searching its environment efficiently.


14.2 The attention networks

This section moves from behaviour to biology, describing the influential proposal that attention is not one thing in the brain but a set of cooperating networks with distinct jobs.


14.2.1 Alerting, orienting, and executive control

The framework of three attention networks was proposed by Michael Posner and Steven Petersen in 1990 and updated by them in later reviews.

The alerting network maintains a general state of readiness, the difference between being drowsy and being on your toes, and it can be briefly boosted by a warning signal that tells you something is about to happen.

The orienting network selects information from among the senses and directs attention to particular locations, which is the spatial steering described earlier in this chapter.

The executive control network handles the harder supervisory work, such as resolving conflict between competing responses, detecting errors, and keeping behaviour aligned with your goals.

Researchers built a single test called the Attention Network Test to measure all three in one sitting, by combining a warning cue, a spatial cue, and a conflict task, which lets them estimate each network's efficiency separately.

The value of this framework is that it treats attention as a team of specialised systems rather than a single faculty, which fits evidence that these functions can be disturbed independently by different brain conditions.


14.2.2 The frontoparietal control of attention

Frontoparietal refers to the partnership between the frontal lobes at the front of the brain and the parietal lobes toward the top and back, and these two regions working together form the core hardware of spatial attention.

An influential model by Maurizio Corbetta and Gordon Shulman, published in 2002, divides this machinery into two cooperating systems.

The dorsal attention network, which includes a region called the frontal eye fields and part of the parietal lobe near the intraparietal sulcus, carries out voluntary, goal-driven attention, the deliberate sending of focus according to your current purpose.

The word dorsal here just means toward the upper or back part of the brain.

The ventral attention network, which includes the temporoparietal junction and part of the ventral frontal cortex, acts as a kind of alarm, breaking in when something unexpected but potentially important appears outside the current focus.

The word ventral means toward the lower part.

A helpful way to picture the pair is that the dorsal system aims the flashlight where you intend, while the ventral system taps you on the shoulder when something surprising happens elsewhere and needs to be checked.

This division fits patterns of brain injury, since damage to the ventral system on the right side is linked to a striking condition called spatial neglect, in which patients fail to attend to one side of space.


14.3 The neural theory of selection

This section descends to the level of individual brain cells and asks what attention actually does to neural activity, giving a mechanism beneath the metaphors and networks.


14.3.1 Biased competition

Biased competition is a theory, proposed by Robert Desimone and John Duncan in 1995, that explains attention as the tipping of a contest between brain cells.

The starting idea is that when several objects fall within the region a neuron cares about, called its receptive field, the objects compete, because the neuron cannot fully represent all of them at once.

Left alone this competition is roughly balanced, and the neuron's response is a kind of compromise between the competing stimuli.

Attention enters as a bias, an extra push that favours the neurons representing the attended object, so that they win the competition and the attended object comes to dominate the neuron's response.

Single-cell recordings in monkeys supported this directly: when two stimuli sat in a cell's receptive field the response was intermediate, but when the animal attended to one of them the response shifted toward the value that stimulus would produce on its own.

The appeal of biased competition is that it explains selection without any separate spotlight mechanism, treating attention instead as a thumb on the scale of an ordinary neural contest.


14.3.2 Attentional modulation of neural gain

Gain is an engineering word for how strongly a system amplifies its input, like the volume knob that sets how loudly a faint signal comes through, and gain modulation means attention turning that knob.

The central finding is that attending to a stimulus increases the responses of the neurons that represent it, effectively amplifying the attended signal relative to the ignored background.

This shows up in several ways: attended stimuli produce larger neural responses, the baseline activity of relevant neurons can rise even before a stimulus appears, and the sharpness with which neurons distinguish stimuli can improve.

One useful way to summarise the effect is that attention improves the signal-to-noise ratio, meaning it makes the wanted signal stand out more clearly against random background activity.

Gain modulation and biased competition are not rivals so much as two descriptions of the same underlying process, since boosting the gain of the attended neurons is one natural way to bias the competition in their favour.

Together they give the field a mechanistic account of selection, connecting the everyday experience of concentrating on something to concrete, measurable changes in how brain cells fire.


CHAPTER 15. ATTENTION, BINDING, AND ITS FAILURES (PROCESS)

This chapter is about one of attention's least obvious but most important jobs: gluing separate features into whole objects, and about the striking ways attention fails.

When you see a red ball, your brain processes its colour and its shape in partly different places, yet you experience one unified red ball, and the puzzle of how that unity is achieved is called the binding problem.

This chapter explains the leading theory that attention is the glue, the evidence for a distinct binding step, and then the dramatic failures that reveal how much of the visual world we miss.


15.1 Attention and the binding of features

This section presents the theory that binding features into objects requires attention, and traces how that theory was tested and refined.


15.1.1 Feature integration theory and the preattentive to attentive transition

Feature integration theory (FIT), proposed by Anne Treisman and Garry Gelade in 1980, is the influential claim that separate features are combined into objects only where attention is directed.

The theory divides vision into two stages.

In the first, preattentive stage, meaning the stage before attention is applied, basic features such as colour, orientation, and motion are registered automatically, in parallel, across the whole scene at once and effortlessly.

In the second, attentive stage, attention moves to a location and binds together the features present there into a single object, and this stage is serial, meaning it handles one location at a time.

The evidence comes from visual search, the task of finding a target among distractors.

When the target differs from the distractors by a single basic feature, such as a red item among green ones, it seems to pop out instantly, and the time to find it barely changes as you add more distractors, which fits automatic parallel processing.

When the target is defined by a combination of features, such as a red vertical bar among red horizontal bars and green vertical bars, search becomes slow and the time rises steadily with each added distractor, as if attention must visit items one at a time to bind their features.

This contrast between flat and rising search times is the core support for the idea that binding needs attention.


15.1.2 Illusory conjunctions as evidence of a binding step

An illusory conjunction is a perceptual mistake in which features from different objects are wrongly combined, so that you might report seeing a red X when the display actually contained a red O and a green X.

Treisman and colleagues demonstrated these errors by showing people displays very briefly, or by loading their attention elsewhere, so that attention could not be properly directed to each item.

Under those conditions people reliably reported these wrong combinations, mixing up which colour went with which shape.

The importance of this finding is that it is exactly what feature integration theory predicts: if attention is the glue that binds features to the right object, then removing attention should let features float free and recombine incorrectly.

Illusory conjunctions therefore provide positive evidence that binding is a real, separable step in perception rather than something that happens automatically for free.

They also gently unsettle our confidence in perception, showing that without attention the visual system can assemble an object that was never actually there.


15.1.3 Guided search as a refinement

Guided search is a revision of feature integration theory, developed chiefly by Jeremy Wolfe from the late 1980s onward, that keeps the two-stage idea but makes the search smarter.

The problem with the original theory was that it implied combination searches were essentially blind, with attention wandering from item to item at random until it stumbled on the target.

Real search is more efficient than that, so guided search proposes that the fast preattentive stage does more than just register features: it also builds a rough map of where the promising items are and steers attention toward them.

For example, when looking for a red vertical bar, the preattentive stage can flag all the red things and all the vertical things, and attention is then guided to locations that score high on both, which are the likely targets.

This means attention is not random but biased toward candidates that share features with the target, which explains why combination search, though slower than pop-out, is far more efficient than pure item-by-item checking would be.

Guided search is now one of the most developed and well-tested models of visual search, and it is best seen as an extension that preserves the core of feature integration theory while making it realistic.


15.2 The failures of attention

This section turns to what happens when attention is absent or overloaded, and the results are surprising demonstrations of how much of the world goes unnoticed.


15.2.1 Inattentional and change blindness

Inattentional blindness is the failure to see a fully visible object simply because your attention was occupied elsewhere.

The most famous demonstration is the invisible gorilla study by Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris in 1999, which built on earlier work by Ulric Neisser.

Viewers watched a video and counted how many times players in white shirts passed a basketball, and while they were absorbed in counting, a person in a gorilla suit walked into the scene, faced the camera, thumped its chest, and walked off.

About half of the viewers, deeply focused on counting, never saw the gorilla at all.

Change blindness is a related failure: the difficulty people have noticing large changes to a scene when the change happens during some interruption such as a brief blank, a cut in a film, or a blink.

In striking demonstrations, people fail to notice that a conversation partner has been swapped for a different person during a momentary interruption.

Both phenomena carry the same lesson: we feel as though we take in the whole rich scene before us, but in truth we consciously register far less than we think, and attention is required to notice even obvious things.

This is humbling and practically important, for example in eyewitness reports and in the danger of distracted driving.


15.2.2 The attentional blink

The attentional blink is a brief lapse in attention that follows the successful detection of one target, during which a second target is likely to be missed.

It is studied with a method called rapid serial visual presentation, in which a stream of items, such as letters, is flashed one after another at the same spot very quickly, roughly ten per second.

The viewer must spot two targets embedded in the stream, for example two letters of a particular colour among other letters.

The finding is that if the second target appears very soon after the first, within about half a second, it is often missed entirely, as if attention had briefly blinked.

Curiously, if the second target comes immediately after the first, with no gap at all, it is usually caught, and if it comes after a longer delay it is also caught, so the failure is worst at an intermediate lag.

The blink is not a failure of the eyes, since they are open the whole time, but a limit of central processing: consolidating the first target into a form that can be reported ties up attention for a moment, leaving the second target vulnerable.

The attentional blink is valuable to researchers because it exposes the timing of the bottleneck between merely perceiving something and turning it into a reportable, conscious item.


15.3 The binding problem in general

This section widens the lens from perception to a problem that runs through all of cognition and through artificial intelligence: how a system represents which things go with which.


15.3.1 Feature binding and the unity of the percept

Feature binding is the specific problem of how the separately processed features of an object become tied together into a single unified perception.

The puzzle is real because the brain analyses different attributes in partly different regions, for instance colour and motion are handled by distinct areas, yet we never experience a scene as a loose soup of free-floating colours and motions.

Instead we see whole, coherent objects, each with its colour, shape, and motion correctly assigned, and something must be doing the assigning.

One leading proposal is temporal synchrony, an idea developed by Christoph von der Malsburg and others, that neurons representing features of the same object fire in time with one another, while neurons for different objects fire out of step, so that being in sync marks features as belonging together.

This idea is elegant and has some experimental support, but it remains debated, and there is no consensus that synchrony is the brain's actual solution.

The honest state of the science is that feature binding is a recognised, deep problem with several candidate answers, of which attention and neural synchrony are the most discussed, and none is settled.


15.3.2 The variable-binding problem for symbolic and connectionist systems

Variable binding is the more abstract cousin of feature binding, and it is the problem of temporarily tying a role to a filler, for instance binding the role agent to the filler John in the thought that John chased the dog.

The word variable here is borrowed from mathematics and computing, where a variable is a slot that can hold different values at different times.

Symbolic systems, meaning the classical approach to artificial intelligence that manipulates language-like symbols according to rules, handle variable binding naturally, because assigning a value to a named slot is exactly what such systems are built to do.

This is often cited as a strength of the symbolic approach, since it makes structured, compositional thought, such as understanding who did what to whom, straightforward.

Connectionist systems, meaning neural networks that represent information as patterns of activity spread across many simple units, find variable binding much harder, because there is no obvious built-in way to keep track of which pattern is currently filling which role.

This difficulty was a central point in a long-running debate, sparked by a 1988 critique from Jerry Fodor and Zenon Pylyshyn, over whether neural networks can support the systematic, structured character of human thought.

Researchers have proposed various fixes, including the temporal synchrony idea mentioned above and specialised network designs, and modern deep-learning systems address related challenges with mechanisms such as attention layers.

The broad lesson for konnectome is that binding, whether of visual features or of abstract roles, is one of the genuine hard problems that any complete architecture of mind, natural or artificial, must solve, and it is not yet fully solved by anyone.



================================================================================

PART FOUR. MEMORY: RETAINING AND RECONSTRUCTING

================================================================================

CHAPTER 16. SENSORY AND SHORT-TERM STORES (PROCESS)

This chapter begins the study of memory, and it starts at the front door, with the very brief and very short stores that hold information for moments rather than for a lifetime.

Memory is not a single thing but a set of systems that operate over different time scales, and this chapter covers the fastest of them.

Understanding these early stores matters because everything that ends up in lasting memory has to pass through them first, so they set the terms on which the rest of memory operates.


16.1 The modal model

This section describes the classic overall picture of memory as a flow of information through a series of stores, a picture so widely adopted that it earned the name modal, meaning the standard or most common model.


16.1.1 The sensory, short-term, and long-term stores

The modal model, laid out by Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin in 1968, pictures memory as three stores arranged in sequence, through which information passes.

The first is sensory memory, a very brief, high-capacity hold that keeps a faithful sensory copy of what just hit the senses for a fraction of a second.

The second is short-term memory, a limited store that holds a small amount of information for a matter of seconds, roughly what you are consciously thinking about right now.

The third is long-term memory, a vast and durable store that can hold information for years or a lifetime.

Information flows from sensory memory into short-term memory if it is attended to, and from short-term into long-term memory if it is processed enough, often through rehearsal, meaning the repeating or working-over of material to keep it alive and pass it along.

The model is called a structural account because it proposes distinct storage boxes, and it also describes control processes, the strategies such as rehearsal that the person uses to move information between the boxes.

This three-store framework has been revised heavily over the decades, but it remains the shared starting point for almost all later theories of memory, which is why it is worth learning first.


16.1.2 The transfer between stores and its controversies

This sub-section examines the arrows in the model, the claimed movement of information between stores, which turned out to be more contentious than the boxes themselves.

The original model leaned heavily on rehearsal as the engine of transfer, proposing that the longer an item sat in short-term memory being rehearsed, the more likely it was to enter long-term memory.

This simple idea ran into trouble.

Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart argued in 1972 that sheer repetition is a poor predictor of lasting memory, and that what matters instead is the depth of processing, meaning whether you engage with the meaning of material rather than just its surface.

Merely repeating a word over and over, which they called maintenance rehearsal, does surprisingly little to build long-term memory, while thinking about its meaning, called elaborative rehearsal, does far more.

A further controversy concerns whether short-term and long-term memory are genuinely separate stores at all, since some theorists argue that short-term memory is simply the currently activated portion of long-term memory rather than a separate box.

The evidence usually cited for a real separation includes patients whose long-term memory is devastated while their short-term memory is spared, and the opposite pattern in other patients, a double pattern that suggests two distinct systems.

The reasonable modern position is that the distinction between short-term and long-term memory is real and useful, but that the neat one-way flow of the original diagram is too simple, and the systems interact richly in both directions.


16.2 Sensory memory

This section zooms in on the first and briefest store, the fleeting sensory trace that holds a rich copy of the world for a moment before it fades.


16.2.1 Iconic memory and the partial-report advantage

Iconic memory is the visual form of sensory memory, a brief snapshot-like store that holds a large amount of visual detail for roughly a quarter to a half of a second.

The word icon here just means a visual image, and the store is named for that fleeting image.

The classic evidence comes from George Sperling's experiments in 1960, which cleverly measured a store that vanishes too fast to report in full.

Sperling flashed a grid of letters, for example three rows of four, for a fraction of a second, and when he asked people to report as many as they could, the whole-report condition, they managed only about four or five.

The trick was the partial-report condition, in which a tone sounded just after the grid disappeared, high, medium, or low, telling the person to report only the top, middle, or bottom row.

Because the tone came after the grid was gone, people could only succeed by reading the answer off a lingering mental image, and they did well on whichever row was cued, showing that nearly the whole grid was briefly available.

This gap, between the many letters momentarily available and the few that survive long enough to report, is called the partial-report advantage, and it proves that iconic memory briefly holds far more than we can report before it fades.

Sperling further showed that the advantage shrinks as the tone is delayed, disappearing after about a second, which measures how fast the icon decays.


16.2.2 Echoic memory

Echoic memory is the auditory form of sensory memory, the brief store that holds a trace of what you just heard, and it is the reason a sound seems to linger for a moment after it stops.

The word echoic comes from echo, capturing the way the sound seems to persist.

Echoic memory lasts noticeably longer than iconic memory, on the order of a few seconds rather than a fraction of a second, which makes sense because sound unfolds over time and must be held long enough to be interpreted.

A familiar everyday sign of echoic memory is the experience of not quite catching what someone said, asking what, and then finding you can suddenly replay and understand the words after all, because the trace was still available.

Laboratory studies use methods analogous to Sperling's partial-report technique but with sounds presented to different locations, and they find a similar brief, high-capacity auditory store that fades over a few seconds.

Echoic memory is especially important for understanding speech and music, because both require holding recent sounds in mind long enough to relate them to what comes next.


16.3 Short-term memory

This section covers the second store, the small workspace that holds the handful of items you are actively aware of, and the questions of how much it holds, how its contents are ordered, and why they are lost.


16.3.1 Capacity, the magical number, and chunking

This sub-section is about how much short-term memory can hold, one of the most famous questions in all of psychology.

In 1956 George Miller wrote a celebrated paper titled The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two, observing that people can typically hold about seven items in short-term memory, give or take a couple.

Miller himself treated the number partly with humour and did not mean it as an exact law, but it became one of the best-known figures in the field.

The crucial refinement is that the limit is measured not in raw items but in chunks, a chunk being a meaningful unit that groups several pieces of information into one.

For example, the string of letters F B I C I A can be held as six separate letters or, if you recognise them, as two familiar chunks, FBI and CIA, which is far easier.

Chunking is powerful because it lets long-term knowledge repackage information into fewer, denser units, which is a large part of why experts can seem to hold so much in mind within their field.

More recent work, especially by Nelson Cowan in 2001, argues that when chunking and rehearsal are prevented so that pure capacity is measured, the real limit is closer to about four chunks rather than seven.

The reasonable summary is that the honest number is smaller than Miller's famous seven, roughly three to five chunks under strict conditions, and that chunking is the trick by which people seem to exceed it.


16.3.2 Serial position, primacy, and recency

This sub-section is about a reliable pattern in how well we remember a list depending on where an item sat in it.

When people try to recall a list of items in any order, their success depends strongly on position, and plotting accuracy against position gives a U-shaped curve called the serial position curve.

The primacy effect is the better memory for items at the beginning of the list, thought to arise because those early items received more rehearsal and had a better chance of entering long-term memory.

The recency effect is the better memory for items at the end of the list, thought to arise because those last items are still sitting in short-term memory, freshly available, when recall begins.

A classic piece of evidence that these two effects have different causes is that delaying recall by a filled interval, such as counting backward for half a minute, wipes out the recency effect while leaving the primacy effect intact.

This makes sense because the delay lets the fragile short-term contents fade, removing recency, while the durably stored early items survive, preserving primacy.

The serial position curve is important because it offers behavioural support for the distinction between a short-term and a long-term store, since the two ends of the curve seem to draw on different systems.


16.3.3 Decay against interference as the cause of loss

This sub-section addresses a basic question: when something slips out of short-term memory, why does it go.

There are two classic answers, and they have competed for decades.

The decay account says that memory traces simply fade with the passage of time if they are not refreshed, so forgetting is caused by time itself, like a footprint smoothed away.

The interference account says that time as such is not the culprit, and that items are lost because other items crowd them out or overwrite them, so forgetting is caused by competition, not by the clock.

Interference comes in two directions: proactive interference, where older material disrupts memory for newer material, and retroactive interference, where newer material disrupts memory for older material.

Distinguishing decay from interference is genuinely hard, because in ordinary situations time and competing material go together, so a delay during which more items arrive could hurt memory for either reason.

The debate is not fully resolved, and honest reviews note that the evidence is mixed, but many researchers lean toward interference, and some influential accounts argue that pure time-based decay plays little or no role once interference is controlled.

For a builder of cognitive systems the practical point stands regardless of which side is right: a small, fast store loses its contents quickly unless they are actively maintained or protected from competing information.

CHAPTER 17. WORKING MEMORY (PROCESS)

This chapter is about the small mental workspace you use to hold and juggle information for the few seconds you are actually using it.

Working memory is the name for the system that keeps a phone number alive in your head while you dial it, or holds the first half of a sentence while you read the second half.

It matters because almost everything else the mind does, from understanding speech to solving a puzzle, depends on being able to keep a few things in mind and work on them at the same time.

The older term for this idea was short-term memory, which mostly meant simple storage, and working memory is the richer modern idea that adds the active manipulation of what is stored.


17.1 The multicomponent model

The most influential picture of working memory says it is not one thing but a team of parts that each do a different job.

This picture was proposed by Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch in 1974, and it is usually called the multicomponent model.

The following sub-sections walk through each member of that team in turn.


17.1.1 The central executive

The central executive is the boss of the working memory system, the part that decides what to pay attention to and how to coordinate the other parts.

In plain terms, it is the mental manager that directs your limited attention, chooses which task to work on, and switches between jobs.

Baddeley described it as a control system with limited attentional capacity, meaning it can only supervise so much at once before it becomes overloaded.

It does not store information itself in the original model; instead it steers the storage parts and shares out attention among them.

Because it was defined mostly by what it does rather than by a clear mechanism, critics complained that the central executive was a bit like a "homunculus", which means a little person inside the head doing all the clever work without being explained.

In response, later versions broke the executive down into more specific abilities, such as focusing attention, dividing attention between tasks, and switching between tasks.

Researchers today often link these executive abilities to what are called executive functions, a set of control skills covered in a later chapter, and this connection is one of the model's most fruitful legacies.


17.1.2 The phonological loop and its behavioural signatures

The phonological loop is the part of working memory that holds sound-based and speech-based information for a short time.

You can think of it as an inner voice combined with an inner ear that lets you silently repeat and briefly store words and numbers.

Baddeley proposed that it has two pieces, a store that holds speech sounds for a couple of seconds before they fade, and a rehearsal process that refreshes those sounds by silently repeating them, which is often called subvocal rehearsal.

A "behavioural signature" means a reliable pattern in people's performance that reveals a hidden mechanism at work, and the phonological loop has several famous ones.

The first is the word-length effect, which is the finding that people remember fewer long words than short words, because long words take longer to rehearse and so more of them fade before they can be refreshed.

The second is the phonological similarity effect, which is the finding that lists of words that sound alike, such as cat, cap, and mat, are harder to recall in order than words that sound different, because the sound-based store confuses similar sounds.

The third is articulatory suppression, which is what happens when you force a person to say something irrelevant out loud, such as repeating "the, the, the", and this blocks rehearsal and wipes out the other effects, showing that the inner voice really is doing the rehearsing.

The fourth is the irrelevant speech effect, where unattended background speech disrupts recall because it intrudes into the same sound-based store.

Together these findings are strong evidence that verbal short-term memory really does rely on a sound-based code kept alive by silent rehearsal.


17.1.3 The visuospatial sketchpad

The visuospatial sketchpad is the part of working memory that holds visual and spatial information, such as what things look like and where they are.

In everyday terms, it is the mental scratch pad you use to picture a route, imagine how furniture would fit in a room, or keep track of where a moving object is.

Baddeley and later colleagues suggested it can be divided into a visual part, which handles form and colour, and a spatial part, which handles location and movement, though the exact split is still debated.

The evidence that this system is separate from the phonological loop comes from the finding that a visual or spatial task and a verbal task interfere with each other far less than two visual tasks do, which suggests they draw on different stores.

For example, you can often repeat a string of numbers out loud while also tracking a moving dot, because each task uses a different subsystem, but tracking two moving dots at once is much harder.

This subsystem is important for navigation, for mechanical reasoning, and for mental imagery, which is the ability to picture things in the mind's eye.


17.1.4 The episodic buffer

The episodic buffer is a part that Baddeley added to the model much later, in the year 2000, to fix two gaps the original three parts could not fill.

The first gap was that the sound-based store and the picture-based store use different codes with no shared format, so nothing in the old model explained how a single united experience, such as remembering a person's face together with their name, could be held at once.

The second gap was that the old model did not explain how working memory talks to long-term memory, which is your vast permanent store of knowledge.

The episodic buffer is described as a limited store that binds information from the different subsystems, and from long-term memory, into single integrated chunks, called episodes, that you can be consciously aware of.

You can picture it as a mental meeting room where sounds, images, and stored knowledge are brought together into one combined scene.

It is thought to be controlled by the central executive and to be the workspace where conscious, unified experience in working memory is assembled.

Fifty years on, the multicomponent model remains one of the field's most cited frameworks, and its authors continue to refine it, though as the next section shows it is not the only way to think about working memory.


17.2 The alternative frameworks

The multicomponent model treats working memory as a set of dedicated boxes, but other researchers describe it quite differently, and it is honest to say there is no single agreed theory.

Several major alternatives see working memory not as separate stores but as a special state of attention or of long-term memory.

The following sub-sections lay out the main rivals so you can see where they agree and disagree.


17.2.1 Working memory as activated long-term memory and the focus of attention

One influential alternative says there is no separate short-term store at all, and that working memory is simply the currently activated portion of your long-term memory.

On this view, associated most closely with Nelson Cowan and with earlier ideas from theorists such as James Nairne and Anders Ericsson, remembering something for a moment is just a matter of that stored knowledge being switched on and made temporarily more active.

Cowan added an important refinement called the focus of attention, which is a very narrow spotlight that holds only a handful of items in a state of direct, immediate access.

Inside this framework, items in the broader activated store are quickly available, but only the few items inside the focus of attention are being directly used right now.

This picture is attractive because it explains neatly how working memory and long-term knowledge are connected, since they are, in effect, the same store seen in two states.

It also gives a natural home for the well-supported estimate, discussed later, that the focus of attention holds only about four items at once.


17.2.2 Working memory as executive attention and its link to fluid intelligence

A closely related framework, developed by Randall Engle, Michael Kane, and their colleagues, argues that the heart of working memory is executive attention, meaning the ability to control attention and keep a goal in mind despite distraction.

On this account, what really varies between people is not the size of a storage box but how well they can hold information in an active state while resisting interference and intrusion.

The striking finding that drove this view is that measures of working memory capacity correlate strongly with measures of fluid intelligence, which is the ability to reason and solve new problems that do not depend on prior knowledge.

In plain terms, people who are better at holding and protecting information in mind also tend to score higher on tests of on-the-spot reasoning.

The proposed explanation is that both abilities lean on the same underlying skill of controlling attention, especially the skill of keeping a relevant goal active while pushing away distractions and unwanted thoughts.

This is one of the most robust and important results in the study of individual differences, though researchers still debate exactly which ingredient of attention control does the work.


17.2.3 Time-based resource sharing and interference accounts

A third family of theories asks a more basic question, which is why the contents of working memory are lost at all, and the answers split into two camps.

The time-based resource sharing model, developed by Pierre Barrouillet and Valerie Camos, proposes that memory traces fade with time unless attention is used to refresh them, and that attention must be shared between refreshing old items and processing new ones.

On this view, the more of your time is taken up by other processing, the less time is left to refresh the fading memories, and so more is lost, which is why the pace and difficulty of a task matters so much.

The rival interference account argues that time itself is not the enemy, and that forgetting instead comes from items overwriting, blurring, or competing with one another.

In an interference account, a memory is lost not because it faded on the clock but because other similar items degraded it or crowded it out.

This debate between decay-with-time and interference is genuinely unsettled, and careful experiments have been used to support each side, so the current honest position is that both processes may contribute.


17.3 The nature of the capacity limit

Everyone agrees that working memory can hold only a little at once, but there is real disagreement about what form that limit takes.

This section looks at how much fits, and at whether the limit is best described as a fixed number of slots or a shared pool that can be spread thin.


17.3.1 The slots against continuous-resource debate

The oldest famous claim about capacity came from George Miller in 1956, who suggested the limit was about seven items, plus or minus two, a figure he half-jokingly called the magical number seven.

Later work by Nelson Cowan, published in 2001, argued that once you strip away tricks like rehearsal and grouping, the true limit is smaller, roughly four chunks of information, a figure sometimes called the magical number four.

Beyond the exact number lies a deeper argument about the very shape of the limit, and this is the slots against continuous-resource debate, most sharply studied in visual working memory.

The slot theory says working memory has a fixed, small number of discrete slots, so it can hold about three or four items with good detail, and anything beyond that is simply not stored and must be guessed.

The continuous-resource theory says instead that working memory is a shared pool of a limited resource that can be spread across any number of items, so that the more items you try to hold, the less precisely each one is remembered.

The practical difference is testable, because slot models predict some items are remembered sharply and the rest not at all, while resource models predict that everything gets fuzzier as the load grows.

Neither pure version fits all the data perfectly, and many current researchers favour hybrid models, in which there is both a limit on the number of items and a graded loss of precision, so this remains an active and unresolved question.


17.3.2 Compression, chunking, and expertise

If capacity is so small, the natural question is how anyone manages to hold complex material in mind, and the answer is that the mind repackages information to make each unit count for more.

Chunking is the process of grouping separate items into a single meaningful unit, so that a chunk, rather than a raw item, is what fills a slot.

For example, the letters F, B, and I are three items, but for someone who knows the agency, FBI is a single familiar chunk, and the long number 1, 7, 7, 6 can become one date for someone who recognises it.

Chunking works by drawing on long-term knowledge, which is why the same string is easier to hold for a person who finds meaning in it, and this directly links capacity to what you already know.

Compression is a broader term for any way the mind recodes information into a more efficient form, squeezing out redundancy so that more fits within the same limit.

This is why expertise matters so much, because an expert has a large store of learned patterns and can package incoming information into a few large, meaningful chunks that a novice would have to hold as many small ones.

The classic demonstration is that chess masters can glance at a real game position and reproduce it almost perfectly, far outperforming novices, but this advantage vanishes when the pieces are placed at random, showing that the skill is meaningful chunking rather than raw memory power.


17.4 The neural basis

Working memory is not just a psychological idea; it corresponds to real activity in the brain, and studying that activity has both confirmed and complicated the psychological picture.

This section looks at how the brain seems to hold information over short delays, and at a lively recent debate about the mechanism.


17.4.1 Persistent activity in prefrontal cortex

The classic neural account of working memory is that certain neurons keep firing steadily during the delay while information is being held, and this steady firing is called persistent activity.

The prefrontal cortex, which is the front part of the brain just behind the forehead and is heavily involved in control and planning, is the region where this was first and most famously observed.

In pioneering studies with monkeys, researchers such as Joaquin Fuster and Patricia Goldman-Rakic found neurons that fired continuously during the gap between seeing a cue and having to respond, as though the cell were holding the memory alive by its own ongoing activity.

The natural interpretation is that a memory is kept in mind by a self-sustaining loop of neural firing, sometimes described using the mathematics of attractor networks, which are stable patterns of activity that maintain themselves.

This view dominated for decades and fits nicely with the idea of an active, effortful workspace, since holding the activity going takes continuous energy and can be disrupted by distraction.


17.4.2 Activity-silent and synaptic accounts

More recent work has challenged the assumption that a memory must be held by continuous firing, and has proposed that information can be stored in a hidden, activity-silent form.

The activity-silent idea, developed prominently by Mark Stokes and colleagues from around 2013, is that during a delay the relevant neurons can fall quiet, yet the memory survives in temporary changes to the connections between neurons.

The proposed storage mechanism is short-term synaptic plasticity, which means rapid, brief changes in the strength of synapses, the junctions where neurons pass signals to one another.

In this account a memory can rest silently in briefly strengthened synapses, perhaps through leftover calcium building up at the connections, and can be read back out later by a pulse of activity, rather than needing to be held aloud the whole time.

Evidence for this comes from findings that the pattern of brain activity holding a memory is often dynamic and can even disappear and then be revived, which is hard to square with a simple steady loop.

The current consensus is not that one account is right and the other wrong, but that both persistent activity and activity-silent synaptic storage occur, and the brain may use whichever suits the moment, so the two mechanisms are best seen as complementary rather than rivals.


CHAPTER 18. LONG-TERM MEMORY SYSTEMS (PROCESS)

This chapter is about the mind's vast and lasting store, the memory that holds your knowledge, your past, and your skills for days, years, or a lifetime.

Long-term memory is not a single warehouse but a set of different systems that store different kinds of information in different ways.

Understanding that it comes in distinct kinds matters because damage or disease can knock out one kind while leaving another untouched, which tells us the systems are genuinely separate.

This chapter maps those systems, then looks at two special corners of memory, the memory of your own life and the memory for things you still intend to do, and finally at the surprising discovery that remembering the past and imagining the future share the same machinery.


18.1 The taxonomy of long-term memory

A taxonomy is simply an organised classification, a way of sorting things into named groups, and long-term memory has a well-developed one.

The main division separates memory you can consciously bring to mind and put into words from memory that shows up only in behaviour, and the sub-sections below unpack that scheme.


18.1.1 Declarative against non-declarative memory

The broadest split in long-term memory is between declarative memory and non-declarative memory, a distinction associated especially with Larry Squire.

Declarative memory is memory for facts and events that you can consciously recall and, as the name suggests, declare or state in words, such as knowing that Paris is a city or recalling what you ate this morning.

Non-declarative memory, also called implicit memory, is memory that shapes your behaviour without conscious recollection, such as knowing how to ride a bicycle or being unconsciously influenced by something you saw earlier.

The reason to believe these are truly different systems comes largely from patients with amnesia, which is severe memory loss usually from brain damage.

The most famous case is a patient known for decades by his initials H. M., later revealed as Henry Molaison, who after surgery to his medial temporal lobes could no longer form new declarative memories, yet could still learn new motor skills while having no conscious memory of the practice sessions.

This double pattern, a devastated declarative memory alongside a preserved skill-learning ability, is powerful evidence that the two kinds of memory rely on different brain systems.

Declarative memory depends heavily on the hippocampus and nearby structures in the medial temporal lobe, while various non-declarative forms depend on other regions such as the basal ganglia and cerebellum.


18.1.2 Episodic against semantic memory

Within declarative memory there is a further important split, proposed by Endel Tulving in 1972, between episodic memory and semantic memory.

Episodic memory is memory for specific personal experiences tied to a particular time and place, such as remembering your last birthday or where you left your keys.

Semantic memory is memory for general facts and knowledge about the world that is not tied to any particular occasion of learning, such as knowing that water is made of hydrogen and oxygen, or that a dog is an animal.

Tulving argued that episodic memory involves a special kind of conscious re-experiencing, a mental time travel back into the remembered event, which he called autonoetic awareness, meaning a self-knowing awareness that this happened to you.

Semantic memory, by contrast, feels more like simply knowing something, without any sense of reliving the moment you learned it.

The two are connected, since repeated episodes can feed into general knowledge, and much of what you know began as specific experiences whose individual details have faded.

Evidence for the split again comes from patients, since some people with brain damage lose the ability to recall personal events while keeping their general knowledge relatively intact, and the reverse pattern also occurs.


18.1.3 Procedural memory, priming, and conditioning

Non-declarative memory is not one thing either, and it includes at least three important kinds worth naming.

Procedural memory is the memory for skills and habits, the knowing-how that lets you perform actions such as typing, swimming, or reading fluently without consciously recalling the rules.

A hallmark of procedural memory is that it is hard to put into words, since a skilled cyclist cannot easily explain the fine adjustments that keep them upright, yet their body performs them reliably.

Priming is a subtler form, in which recent exposure to something makes you faster or more likely to recognise or produce it later, even when you have no conscious memory of the exposure.

For example, if you have just seen the word "doctor", you will complete the fragment "nur_e" as "nurse" more readily, without realising why, which is priming at work.

Conditioning is the third kind, and it refers to simple learned associations of the sort studied by Ivan Pavlov, in which a neutral signal that reliably precedes an important event comes to trigger a response on its own.

The classic example is a dog that learns to salivate at a bell that has repeatedly preceded food, an association that forms and operates without any need for conscious, declarative recollection.

These non-declarative forms are evolutionarily ancient and widely shared across animals, and they run quietly beneath awareness, which is exactly why they survive when conscious memory is destroyed.


18.2 Autobiographical and prospective memory

Beyond the basic taxonomy, two kinds of memory are especially close to daily life and deserve their own treatment.

One is the memory of your own life story, and the other is memory for the future, the ability to remember to carry out plans, and the sub-sections take each in turn.


18.2.1 The self across time in autobiographical memory

Autobiographical memory is the memory for the events and facts of your own life, and it is what gives you a continuous sense of who you are across time.

It is a blend of episodic and semantic memory, combining specific remembered episodes, such as a particular family holiday, with general personal facts, such as which town you grew up in.

Researchers describe it as organised in layers, from broad lifetime periods, such as your school years, down through general events, down to specific single episodes, and recall usually works top down through these layers.

One robust finding is the reminiscence bump, which is the tendency of older adults to recall a disproportionate number of memories from roughly their teens to their late twenties, perhaps because this is a formative period rich in novel, identity-defining experiences.

Another is that autobiographical memory is not a neutral record but is shaped by your current self, since your present beliefs, mood, and goals colour which events come to mind and how they are remembered.

Because it links memory to identity, damage to autobiographical memory can be deeply disorienting, robbing a person not just of facts but of the felt story of their own life.


18.2.2 Remembering to act in prospective memory

Prospective memory is the memory for actions you intend to carry out in the future, such as remembering to take medicine at night or to pass on a message when you see a friend.

It is different from ordinary memory because the challenge is not to recall a fact when asked, but to remember, at the right moment and without any prompt, that there was something you meant to do.

Researchers distinguish two types, event-based prospective memory, where a cue in the world reminds you, such as seeing the friend, and time-based prospective memory, where you must act at a certain time with no external cue, which is generally harder.

Prospective memory has two ingredients, a prospective part, which is remembering that there is an intention at all, and a retrospective part, which is remembering what the intended action actually was.

There is an ongoing debate about how the right moment is caught, between accounts that say it takes continuous effortful monitoring of the environment and accounts that say a suitable cue can trigger the intention more automatically, and the balance probably depends on the situation.
