Failures of prospective memory are among the most common and consequential everyday memory lapses, ranging from the harmless, such as forgetting to post a letter, to the tragic, such as forgetting a child in a car.


18.3 The convergence with imagination

One of the most striking discoveries in memory science is that memory is not only about the past, and this section explains why.

It turns out that recalling what happened and imagining what might happen draw on much the same mental and neural machinery.


18.3.1 The shared machinery of remembering the past and simulating the future

For a long time memory was pictured as a kind of recording of the past, but evidence now shows that the very same brain network is active whether you remember a past event or imagine a future one.

Brain imaging studies, along with observations of patients, revealed that a common core network, including the hippocampus and connected midline regions, lights up both when people recall autobiographical events and when they imagine plausible personal futures.

Tellingly, some amnesic patients who cannot recall their past also cannot construct vivid imagined future scenes, which suggests the two abilities depend on one shared system rather than two separate ones.

Daniel Schacter and Donna Rose Addis captured this in what they called the constructive episodic simulation hypothesis, proposed in 2007.

The core idea is that episodic memory is not a faithful playback but a flexible process of pulling apart and recombining stored details, and that this same recombining ability is exactly what is needed to build a novel imagined future.

In this view, remembering and imagining are two uses of a single constructive system, one aimed backward in time and one aimed forward.


18.3.2 Memory as a tool for prospection rather than a record

This convergence leads to a deeper rethinking of what memory is for, and the proposal is that memory evolved less to preserve the past than to help us prepare for the future.

Prospection is the general term for thinking about and mentally simulating the future, and the argument is that the adaptive payoff of memory lies here.

An animal that can recombine fragments of past experience into simulations of what might happen can rehearse plans, weigh options, and anticipate outcomes without having to try them out in the risky real world.

On this account the flexible, reconstructive nature of memory is not a design flaw but the very feature that makes future simulation possible, since a rigid, tape-like record could not be freely recombined into new scenarios.

The same flexibility, however, comes at a price, because a system that recombines details can also stitch them together wrongly, which is one root of the memory errors covered in Chapter 20.

So the honest summary is that memory's usefulness for imagining the future and its vulnerability to distortion are two sides of the same coin.


CHAPTER 19. ENCODING, CONSOLIDATION, AND RETRIEVAL (PROCESS)

This chapter follows a memory through its life, from the moment it is formed, through the slow process by which it is made durable, to the act of bringing it back.

These three stages have names, encoding for getting information in, consolidation for making it stable, and retrieval for getting it back out.

Understanding them matters because most memory successes and failures happen at one of these stages, and knowing which one is at fault points to how to remember better.

The chapter takes each stage in order and shows that memory is an active process at every step, not a passive recording.


19.1 Encoding

Encoding is the first stage, the process of taking in information and turning it into a memory trace that the brain can store.

How you encode something, and not just how long you stare at it, largely decides how well you will remember it, as the following sub-sections show.


19.1.1 Levels of processing and elaboration

The levels of processing idea, proposed by Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart in 1972, says that how deeply you think about something at the moment of learning determines how well it sticks.

Shallow processing means attending only to surface features, such as what a word looks like or sounds like, and it tends to produce weak, quickly fading memories.

Deep processing means attending to meaning, thinking about what something signifies and how it relates to what you already know, and it produces stronger, longer-lasting memories.

The classic demonstration asks people questions about words, some about appearance, such as is it in capital letters, and some about meaning, such as does it fit in this sentence, and later memory is far better for the meaning-based items even though people were not told to memorise anything.

Elaboration is the key to why depth helps, and it means enriching new information by connecting it to other knowledge, forming many links that later serve as routes back to the memory.

The more meaningful connections you build at encoding, the more handles you create for retrieval, which is why explaining an idea in your own words beats simply rereading it.

One caution is that the theory can be slightly circular, since deep processing is partly defined by producing good memory, but the practical lesson that meaningful engagement aids memory is very well supported.


19.1.2 Encoding specificity and transfer-appropriate processing

Memory does not depend on encoding alone but on the match between how you encoded something and how you later try to retrieve it.

The encoding specificity principle, formulated by Endel Tulving and Donald Thomson, states that retrieval works best when the cues present at recall match the conditions present when the memory was formed.

In plain terms, the way you first learned something, including the surrounding context, becomes part of the memory, and reinstating that context later helps you find it.

A related idea, transfer-appropriate processing, states that a way of studying is good not in the abstract but insofar as it matches the kind of test you will face.

For example, if a test will require recognising sounds, studying the sounds helps more than studying meanings, even though studying meanings is usually the deeper and generally better strategy.

Together these principles shift the focus from asking how strong a memory is to asking how well the conditions of learning and remembering line up, which is a subtler and more accurate way to think about memory.


19.1.3 The generation, spacing, and testing effects

Decades of research have produced several reliable techniques that strengthen encoding, and three of the best established are worth knowing by name.

The generation effect is the finding that you remember information better if you produce it yourself rather than simply reading it, so filling in a blank beats being handed the answer.

The spacing effect is the finding that learning spread out over time, with gaps between study sessions, produces far more durable memory than the same amount of study crammed into one block, an effect first noted by Hermann Ebbinghaus and confirmed thousands of times since.

The reason spacing helps is debated, but it seems that letting a memory partly fade and then retrieving it again forces more effortful processing than reviewing it while it is still fresh.

The testing effect, also called retrieval practice, is the finding that testing yourself on material, actively trying to recall it, strengthens memory more than restudying it for the same time.

This is initially surprising, because a test feels like a mere measurement of memory rather than a way of building it, yet the act of retrieving reshapes and reinforces the memory each time.

These three effects converge on a single practical message, that memory is built by effortful, active, spaced engagement rather than by passive, massed exposure, which is why rereading a textbook feels productive but works poorly.


19.2 Consolidation

Encoding creates a fragile memory, and consolidation is the set of processes that slowly turn that fragile trace into a stable, lasting one.

Consolidation happens on two very different scales, at individual synapses over hours and across whole brain systems over months and years, and sleep plays a special part in it.


19.2.1 Synaptic consolidation and reconsolidation

Synaptic consolidation is the fast form, the process over minutes to hours by which a newly formed memory becomes physically stabilised in strengthened connections between neurons.

Right after learning, a memory is vulnerable and can be wiped out by a blow, a drug, or a distraction, but as the synapses that carry it are strengthened through the building of new proteins, it becomes far more resistant.

This is why events just before a concussion are often lost, since the memory had not yet been consolidated when the injury struck.

Reconsolidation is a more surprising discovery, the finding that when an old, consolidated memory is reactivated by recall, it can briefly return to a fragile state and must be stabilised again.

This means remembering is not a neutral readout, because each time a memory is brought back it can be updated, strengthened, or even altered before it is restored.

Reconsolidation has raised the intriguing possibility of weakening painful memories, such as those in trauma, by reactivating them and then interfering with their restabilisation, though this remains an area of active and unfinished research.


19.2.2 Systems consolidation and the hippocampal-neocortical dialogue

Systems consolidation is the slow form, the process over weeks to years by which a memory's dependence gradually shifts from one part of the brain to another.

The standard model holds that new declarative memories at first depend on the hippocampus, a seahorse-shaped structure deep in the brain that is crucial for forming new memories, and that over time they are gradually transferred to the neocortex, the brain's outer sheet where long-term knowledge resides.

The proposed mechanism is a repeated dialogue, in which the hippocampus replays recent experiences and gradually trains the slower-learning cortex to hold them on its own, after which the memory no longer needs the hippocampus.

This idea is captured in the complementary learning systems framework, which pairs a fast-learning hippocampus with a slow-learning cortex so the brain can learn new things quickly without overwriting old knowledge.

There is a genuine scientific dispute here, because the multiple trace theory of Lynn Nadel and Morris Moscovitch argues that vivid episodic memories always keep the hippocampus involved, no matter how old they are, and that only the drier semantic gist is fully handed to the cortex.

Neuroimaging evidence tends to favour a continuing hippocampal role for detailed autobiographical memories, so the exact division of labour between hippocampus and cortex over time is still being worked out.


19.2.3 Sleep and the reorganisation of memory

Sleep is not merely rest for the memory system but appears to be an active period during which memories are strengthened and reorganised.

A large body of evidence shows that people remember material better after a night of sleep, or even a nap, than after an equal period of wakefulness, and that sleep protects memories against later interference.

During deep, non-dreaming sleep, the brain shows coordinated rhythms, including slow waves and brief bursts called sleep spindles, that are thought to orchestrate the transfer of memories from hippocampus to cortex.

A central piece of evidence is replay, the finding first seen in rats that patterns of neural firing from a recent experience are played back during sleep, as though the brain were rehearsing and filing the day's events.

Sleep also seems to do more than strengthen, since it can extract general rules and gist from specific experiences and can promote creative insight, suggesting it reorganises knowledge rather than merely preserving it.

The details of which sleep stages serve which functions are still debated, but the broad conclusion that sleep is essential for turning experiences into durable, well-organised memory is now widely accepted.


19.3 Retrieval

Retrieval is the final stage, the act of bringing a stored memory back into mind, and it is far more active and constructive than it feels.

This section covers the forms retrieval takes, the powerful role of context, the two feelings that can accompany recognition, and the surprising fact that the act of retrieval changes memory itself.


19.3.1 Recall and recognition

Retrieval comes in two broad forms that differ in how much help you are given.

Recall is bringing information back with few or no cues, as when an essay question asks you to produce an answer from scratch, and it is generally the harder form.

Recognition is identifying something as familiar when it is put in front of you, as in a multiple-choice question, and it is generally easier because the item itself acts as a strong cue.

The gap between them explains a common experience, that you may be unable to recall a name yet instantly recognise it when someone says it.

This difference has practical consequences, since recognition can succeed on weaker memories than recall can, which is why recognising a face is easier than producing the matching name.

The two forms are also thought to lean on somewhat different processes, a theme developed in the sub-section on dual-process accounts below.


19.3.2 Context-dependent and state-dependent retrieval

Following from the encoding specificity principle, retrieval is strongly helped when the surrounding conditions at recall match those at learning.

Context-dependent memory refers to the finding that external surroundings act as cues, so you remember material better in the place where you learned it.

A famous demonstration had divers learn lists of words either on land or underwater, and they recalled each list best in the same environment where they had learned it.

State-dependent memory refers to the parallel finding that your internal state acts as a cue, so material learned in a particular bodily or emotional state is best recalled in that same state.

For instance, information learned while in a certain mood tends to be recalled more easily when that mood returns, an effect called mood-dependent memory.

The practical upshot is that a poor memory is often not truly absent but merely inaccessible for lack of the right cue, and reinstating the original context, even mentally, can bring it back.


19.3.3 The dual-process account of recognition: recollection and familiarity

When you recognise something, the experience can take two quite different forms, and the dual-process account explains recognition as the blend of these two.

Familiarity is a fast, vague sense that you have encountered something before, without any accompanying details of when or where, like knowing a face is familiar but having no idea from where.

Recollection is a slower, richer retrieval that brings back the specific context of the earlier encounter, so you not only know the face is familiar but recall the party where you met them.

Researchers such as Andrew Yonelinas have modelled these as distinct processes, with familiarity behaving like a graded signal of memory strength and recollection behaving more like an all-or-none recovery of details.

One common laboratory method, the remember-know procedure, asks people to report whether they actually remember the details of encountering an item or merely know it is familiar, in order to separate the two.

There is debate about whether recollection and familiarity are truly two different processes or two points along a single continuum of memory strength, and this argument is not fully settled.

Even so, the distinction is useful and maps roughly onto different brain regions within the medial temporal lobe, with the hippocampus more tied to recollection and nearby cortex more tied to familiarity.


19.3.4 Retrieval as a cause of both strengthening and forgetting

The final and most counterintuitive point is that retrieving a memory is not a passive readout but an event that changes the memory itself.

On the one hand, as the testing effect showed, successfully retrieving a memory strengthens it, making it easier to retrieve again in future, so every act of recall is also an act of learning.

On the other hand, retrieval can also cause forgetting of related material, an effect called retrieval-induced forgetting.

Retrieval-induced forgetting is the finding that recalling some items from a set makes other, related but unretrieved items harder to recall later, as though pulling one memory forward pushes its competitors down.

The proposed explanation is that retrieving a target requires suppressing competitors that would otherwise interfere, and this suppression leaves those competitors weakened.

So retrieval is a double-edged process, sharpening the memories you practise while quietly weakening their neighbours, which means the very act of remembering actively reshapes the landscape of what you will be able to remember next.


CHAPTER 20. FORGETTING, RECONSTRUCTION, AND MEMORY ERROR (PROCESS)

This chapter is about the ways memory fails and distorts, which turn out to be as revealing as the ways it succeeds.

Forgetting is not simply the decay of a perfect recording, and remembering is not a faithful playback, so the failures of memory expose what memory really is.

This matters both scientifically, because errors reveal the machinery, and practically, because misplaced faith in memory, especially eyewitness memory, can ruin lives.

The chapter covers why we forget, why remembering is an act of reconstruction, and the characteristic errors that reconstruction produces.


20.1 Forgetting

Forgetting is the loss of access to information that was once stored, and there is more than one reason it happens.

This section distinguishes the main causes of forgetting, describes the classic shape of forgetting over time, and looks at whether we can forget on purpose.


20.1.1 Decay, interference, and cue-dependent forgetting

There are three main explanations for why memories become hard to reach, and they are not mutually exclusive.

Decay theory says memories simply fade with the passage of time if they are not used, weakening like a footprint slowly erased by wind.

Interference theory says forgetting is caused not by time itself but by other memories getting in the way, and it comes in two directions.

Proactive interference is when older memories disrupt the learning or recall of newer ones, such as when a previous phone number keeps intruding when you try to recall your new one.

Retroactive interference is the reverse, when newer learning disrupts the recall of older memories, such as when this year's parking spot makes last year's hard to recall.

Cue-dependent forgetting says the memory is not lost at all but merely inaccessible because the right retrieval cue is missing, and providing the cue restores it.

Evidence favours the view that much everyday forgetting is cue-dependent and interference-based rather than pure decay, because information that seemed forgotten often reappears the moment a suitable cue is supplied.


20.1.2 The forgetting curve and the relearning saving

The single most famous fact about forgetting comes from Hermann Ebbinghaus, who in the 1880s studied his own memory with painstaking rigour.

To avoid the influence of prior knowledge, he memorised long lists of nonsense syllables, meaningless three-letter combinations, and measured how much he retained over time.

The result was the forgetting curve, which shows that forgetting is rapid at first, with much lost within hours, and then levels off, so that what survives the first day tends to last much longer.

Ebbinghaus measured retention with a clever method called savings, which asks how much time or effort is saved when relearning a list compared with learning it fresh.

The savings method revealed that even material that could not be consciously recalled at all still left a trace, because it was relearned faster than brand-new material, showing that forgetting is often incomplete.

Ebbinghaus also documented the spacing effect and the benefits of overlearning, and his careful, quantitative approach essentially founded the experimental study of memory, so his curve remains a touchstone more than a century later.


20.1.3 Motivated and directed forgetting

A natural question is whether people can forget things on purpose, and the evidence suggests that intentional forgetting is real, though limited.

Directed forgetting is studied by explicitly instructing people to forget certain material, and such instructions do measurably reduce later memory for the to-be-forgotten items.

Two mechanisms are proposed, one in which people simply stop rehearsing and encoding the unwanted items, and another in which an active process inhibits or suppresses the memory at retrieval.

Motivated forgetting is the broader and more contested idea that people can push distressing memories out of mind because they want to, an idea with roots in the notion of repression associated with Sigmund Freud.

The scientific status of deep repression of traumatic memories is genuinely disputed, and many memory researchers are sceptical of it, while accepting that ordinary suppression and avoidance can reduce the accessibility of unwanted memories.

The honest summary is that some intentional control over memory is well demonstrated in the laboratory, but strong claims about wholesale burial and later perfect recovery of traumatic memories remain controversial and should be treated with caution.


20.2 Memory as reconstruction

The central lesson of modern memory research is that remembering is not replaying but rebuilding, and this section explains what that means.

We reconstruct memories using general knowledge structures, and this is both what makes memory efficient and what makes it prone to error.


20.2.1 Schemas and scripts as the scaffolding of recall

A schema is an organised packet of general knowledge about a type of thing or situation, built up from experience, such as your general idea of what a kitchen contains or how a restaurant works.

Schemas are useful because they let you fill in gaps, make sense of new situations quickly, and remember the gist of things without recording every detail.

A script is a particular kind of schema for a familiar sequence of events, such as the standard steps of eating at a restaurant, being seated, ordering, eating, and paying.

The idea traces to Frederic Bartlett, who in the 1930s had people recall an unfamiliar folk tale and found that they unconsciously altered it to fit their own cultural expectations, dropping strange details and adding familiar ones.

Schemas shape memory at every stage, guiding what you notice, how you store it, and how you later reconstruct it, so that when a detail is missing you tend to supply what your schema says should have been there.

This scaffolding is helpful most of the time, but it is exactly why memory can insert plausible things that never actually happened, which the next sub-section develops.


20.2.2 The reconstructive nature of remembering

Following Bartlett, the modern view is that each act of recall is an act of reconstruction, in which the mind assembles a memory from fragments plus general knowledge and expectation.

This is very different from the intuitive feeling that memory is like a video recording that we simply play back, a feeling that is compelling but mistaken.

Because reconstruction fills gaps with what is likely rather than what actually occurred, memories can be confidently held yet contain details that were never experienced.

Reconstruction also means memories can shift over time as your knowledge, mood, and later experiences change, so the same event may be remembered differently on different occasions.

This is not a rare malfunction but the normal way memory works, and it is the same flexibility that, as Chapter 18 noted, allows us to imagine the future by recombining stored pieces.

Recognising memory as reconstructive is the foundation for understanding the specific, systematic errors that follow.


20.3 The errors of memory

If memory is reconstructive, then certain kinds of error are predictable rather than random, and researchers have catalogued them.

This section presents a well-known taxonomy of memory failures, the laboratory methods that reliably create false memories, and the real-world stakes for eyewitness testimony.


20.3.1 The seven sins of memory as a taxonomy of failure

Daniel Schacter organised the ways memory goes wrong into a memorable list he called the seven sins of memory, published in 2001.

The first three are sins of omission, failures to bring something to mind.

Transience is the weakening or loss of memory over time, the ordinary fading captured by the forgetting curve.

Absent-mindedness is a failure at the meeting point of attention and memory, such as forgetting where you put your keys because you were not attending when you set them down.

Blocking is the temporary inability to retrieve something that is stored, most vividly the tip-of-the-tongue state where a word feels just out of reach.

The remaining four are sins of commission, distortions in what is remembered.

Misattribution is remembering something correctly but assigning it to the wrong source, such as recalling a fact but crediting the wrong person, or thinking an imagined event really happened.

Suggestibility is the incorporation of information from outside, such as a leading question, into your own memory of an event.

Bias is the distorting influence of your present knowledge, beliefs, and feelings on your memory of the past, so that you misremember the past as more consistent with your current self than it was.

Persistence is the unwanted, intrusive recall of memories you would rather forget, such as the repeated replaying of a distressing event.

Schacter's key insight is that these are not random defects but the by-products of a memory system that is otherwise well designed, so each sin is the flip side of a useful feature.


20.3.2 False memory and the laboratory paradigms that produce it

A false memory is a recollection of an event, or of details of an event, that did not actually happen, and researchers can reliably create them in the laboratory.

The most controlled method is the Deese-Roediger-McDermott paradigm, usually shortened to the DRM paradigm, which shows how easily the mind manufactures memories of things never presented.

In it, people study a list of words that are all associated with one missing word, for example bed, rest, tired, and dream, all linked to sleep, and afterwards a large proportion confidently remember having seen the word sleep, which was never on the list.

This happens because studying the related words activates the theme word, and the mind later cannot distinguish the internally generated theme from the actually presented items, a clear case of misattribution.

More dramatic are studies that implant whole false autobiographical memories, the best known being the lost in the mall study associated with Elizabeth Loftus, in which suggestion led a portion of participants to remember being lost in a shopping mall as a child, an event that never occurred.

Such studies show that entire, detailed, emotionally felt memories of nonexistent events can be created through suggestion, and that people often cannot tell these apart from real ones.

The general lesson is that vividness and confidence are not reliable guarantees that a memory is true, because false memories can be just as vivid and confidently held as accurate ones.


20.3.3 The misinformation effect and the fallibility of eyewitness memory

The misinformation effect is the finding that exposure to misleading information after an event can alter a person's memory of that event, and it is one of the most important results in memory science.

It was established through decades of work by Elizabeth Loftus and colleagues, beginning with a classic study by Loftus and John Palmer in 1974.

In that study, people watched a film of a car accident and were then asked how fast the cars were going, but the verb was varied, so some were asked how fast the cars were going when they smashed and others when they hit.

Those asked with the word smashed gave higher speed estimates, and a week later were more likely to falsely remember seeing broken glass that was never in the film, showing that the wording of a single question had reshaped their memory.

The practical stakes are enormous for eyewitness testimony, since a confident eyewitness is highly persuasive to juries, yet this research shows that eyewitness memory can be sincerely and completely mistaken.

Suggestive police procedures, such as leading questions or poorly conducted lineups, can inadvertently manufacture the very confident errors that lead to wrongful convictions, a link confirmed by later analyses of cases overturned by deoxyribonucleic acid, usually shortened to DNA, evidence.

The scientific response has been to develop safer interviewing and lineup methods and to educate courts that the confidence of a witness is not a reliable measure of accuracy, which is now a broad consensus among memory researchers.

PART FIVE. KNOWLEDGE AND CONCEPTS

================================================================================

CHAPTER 21. CONCEPTS AND CATEGORISATION (PROCESS)

This chapter is about one of the quietest but most important things your mind does: it sorts the world into kinds.

A concept is a mental idea of a kind of thing, such as "dog" or "chair" or "justice", and categorisation is the act of deciding that some particular thing you meet is an example of that kind.

You do this constantly, thousands of times a day, almost always without noticing.

When you glance at a new animal and instantly think "that is a dog", you have just categorised, and that single act lets you predict that it might bark, that it can be petted, and that it will not read your mail.

That is why categories matter so much: a category is a bundle of useful expectations, and putting a new thing into a category lets you treat the unknown as if it were familiar.

This chapter asks three plain questions: what is a concept made of inside the mind, how are categories arranged relative to one another, and how do we learn new categories in the first place.


21.1 The theories of conceptual structure

This section asks what a concept actually is, considered as something stored in the mind.

Over the last century researchers have offered several very different answers, and the story is a good example of science improving by discovering that its first neat idea was wrong.

We will walk through the main proposals in the order they arose, because each one was largely a reaction to the failures of the one before it.


21.1.1 The classical definitional view and its failure

The oldest idea, going back to Aristotle and taken for granted for over two thousand years, is that a concept is a definition.

On this view, to have the concept "bird" is to hold a checklist of features that something must have to count as a bird, for example "has feathers, has wings, lays eggs, has a beak".

These required features are called necessary and sufficient conditions, which is just a technical way of saying "each feature must be present, and having all of them together is enough to make something a member".

On this account category membership is all-or-nothing: a thing either ticks every box and is fully in, or misses a box and is fully out, with no in-between.

The trouble is that when psychologists actually looked, real everyday concepts almost never behave like this.

The philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein pointed out in the mid twentieth century that you cannot write a clean definition even for a simple word like "game": some games have winners and losers, some do not; some use a ball, some do not; some are competitive, some are just for fun.

Wittgenstein suggested that the members of a category are held together not by one shared essence but by "family resemblance", meaning they overlap in a criss-crossing web of features the way the members of a human family share a nose here and a chin there without any single feature running through them all.

There is also the problem of unclear cases: is a tomato a fruit or a vegetable, is a rug a piece of furniture, is a hot dog a sandwich.

If concepts were strict definitions, such questions would have crisp answers, but people hesitate and disagree, which suggests the underlying idea is not a strict definition at all.

Because of these failures, the definitional view is now generally regarded as inadequate as a description of ordinary human concepts, and the theories that follow were built to do better.


21.1.2 Prototype theory and graded typicality

Prototype theory, developed above all by the psychologist Eleanor Rosch in the 1970s, says that a concept is organised around a best example rather than a strict definition.

A prototype is an average or ideal member of the category, a kind of summary that captures the features most typical of the category even if no single real member has all of them.

For "bird" the prototype is something small that flies and sings and perches, close to a robin or a sparrow, and things are judged to be birds by how closely they resemble this prototype.

The key idea is graded typicality, which means membership comes in degrees: a robin is a very good example of a bird, a chicken is a poorer one, and a penguin is poorer still, even though all three really are birds.

This is not just armchair speculation.

Rosch showed in the 1970s that when you ask people to rate how good an example each item is, their ratings are consistent and predictable, and those ratings then forecast behaviour in other tasks.

For instance, in a sentence-verification task where people press a button to confirm statements like "a robin is a bird", they respond faster to typical members such as robin than to atypical members such as penguin, an effect called the typicality effect.

People also list typical members first when asked to name examples of a category, and children tend to learn typical members earlier.

The strength of prototype theory is that it naturally explains fuzzy boundaries and disagreement about odd cases, because if membership is a matter of degree there is no sharp line to defend.

Its main weakness is that a single averaged prototype throws away information about the actual variety within a category, and it can struggle to explain how people remember specific unusual members, which is where the next theory comes in.


21.1.3 Exemplar theory and instance-based categorisation

Exemplar theory offers a strikingly economical alternative: perhaps the mind does not form any summary or average at all.

On this view, put forward by Douglas Medin and Marguerite Schaffer in 1978 and developed in detail by Robert Nosofsky, a concept is simply the collection of specific remembered examples, called exemplars, that you have personally encountered.

You do not store an abstract idea of "dog"; you store memories of many individual dogs you have met.

To categorise a new animal you compare it, quickly and unconsciously, to all those stored examples at once, and you assign it to whichever category its remembered members most resemble.

If a new furry creature is very similar to many dogs you have seen and few cats, you call it a dog.

Nosofsky's well-known mathematical version of this idea is the Generalised Context Model (GCM), which grew out of the earlier context model of Medin and Schaffer.

The Generalised Context Model (GCM) adds a clever ingredient called attention weights, which let the learner emphasise whichever features happen to matter for telling the current categories apart, for example paying attention to size but ignoring colour.

Exemplar theory explains some things prototypes cannot, such as our sensitivity to specific unusual members and to how spread out or variable a category is.

The honest current picture, supported by decades of comparison studies, is that neither prototype nor exemplar theory wins outright; people seem to use exemplar-like memory in many laboratory tasks, but prototype-like summaries appear in others, and the mind probably has more than one way of representing categories.


21.1.4 The theory-theory and psychological essentialism

The theories so far all lean on surface similarity, on how much things look or feel alike, but a moment's reflection shows that similarity cannot be the whole story.

A toy dog can look more like a real dog than a hairless real dog does, yet you know which one is truly a dog, so your concept must rest on more than appearance.

The theory-theory, an idea associated with researchers such as Douglas Medin, Susan Gelman, and Frank Keil, proposes that concepts are embedded in intuitive theories, that is, informal everyday beliefs about how the world works and why things are the way they are.

The awkward name "theory-theory" simply means "the theory that concepts are like little theories".

On this view you categorise partly by explanation: you group things by the causes and functions you believe they have, not only by how they look.

A close companion idea is psychological essentialism, which is the tendency people show, from early childhood on, to assume that members of a natural category share a hidden inner "essence" that makes them what they are and causes their visible features.

For example, children and adults tend to believe that what makes a tiger a tiger is some deep inner tiger-nature, so that a tiger surgically altered to look like a lion is still, underneath, a tiger.

Susan Gelman's research with young children showed that they will insist on this hidden essence even when they cannot say what it is, treating the essence as a kind of placeholder to be filled in later by knowledge.

Essentialism seems to fit living kinds and natural substances better than it fits human-made objects, and it can be socially harmful when people wrongly apply essentialist thinking to human groups, imagining fixed inner essences behind race or gender where none exist.

The lasting contribution of the theory-theory is the reminder that a concept is not an isolated snapshot but a node in a web of causal belief.


21.2 The structure of categories

Concepts do not float about as an unordered heap; they are arranged, and one of the most robust findings in the field is that this arrangement is not flat.

This section looks at two facts about that arrangement: that categories come in layers with one layer being psychologically special, and that people can also invent brand-new categories on the spot to suit a goal.


21.2.1 The basic level of categorisation

Any single object can be named at several levels of generality at once.

The creature asleep on the sofa is, all at the same time, an "animal", a "dog", and a "Labrador".

Eleanor Rosch and her colleagues in the 1970s called these three layers the superordinate level (the broad one, "animal"), the basic level (the middle one, "dog"), and the subordinate level (the narrow one, "Labrador").

Their central discovery is that the middle layer, the basic level, is psychologically privileged: it is the level at which the mind prefers to work.

The evidence is consistent and varied.

People name objects at the basic level fastest and most often, so shown a picture you are far more likely to blurt out "dog" than either "animal" or "Labrador".

Children learn basic-level words earliest, adults verify basic-level membership most quickly, and the basic level is where the words tend to be short and common across the world's languages.

Rosch explained this with a trade-off she called cognitive economy: the basic level is the sweet spot where a category is still informative, because its members share a lot and even have a common shape you could draw, yet it is not so narrow that you drown in fine distinctions.

Go up to "animal" and the members share too little to be useful; go down to "Labrador" and you gain little over "dog" for most purposes.

One important qualification is that the special level shifts with expertise: a dog breeder or a bird-watcher becomes so fluent that the subordinate level ("Labrador", "chaffinch") starts to behave like the basic level for them, which shows the basic level reflects knowledge and use rather than a fixed fact about the world.


21.2.2 Ad hoc and goal-derived categories

Not every category is a settled, well-worn kind like "dog" or "furniture".

The psychologist Lawrence Barsalou showed that people can also build categories instantly to serve a momentary goal, and he called these ad hoc categories, the Latin phrase "ad hoc" meaning "for this particular purpose".

His famous example is the category "things to take out of your house in a fire".

Think about what belongs in it: your children, your pets, your passport, your laptop, a treasured photograph, perhaps some cash.

These items look nothing alike and would never sit together in an ordinary category, yet they form a perfectly sensible group the moment the goal of escaping a fire is in mind, united by the shared feature of being irreplaceable and worth saving.

Other everyday ad hoc categories include "foods to eat on a diet", "ways to get to the airport", and "things to pack for a holiday".

Barsalou's studies in the 1980s found something revealing about how these goal-derived categories are organised.

For ordinary categories, the best examples are the ones most similar to an average member, but for goal-derived categories the best examples are the ones closest to an ideal set by the goal.

For "foods to eat on a diet", the best example is not the average diet food but the one with the fewest calories, the ideal the goal points towards.

This matters for the bigger picture because it shows that categorisation is not only a matter of stored, permanent knowledge; it is a flexible, on-the-fly construction shaped by what you are trying to do right now.


21.3 Category learning

The previous sections described what categories are and how they are arranged; this section asks how a person comes to have a new category in the first place.

How does a radiologist learn to see a tumour on a scan, or a child learn to tell dogs from cats, when nobody hands them a definition.

Studying this in the laboratory has produced both precise mathematical models and an important discovery that the brain has more than one way of learning categories.


21.3.1 The computational models of category learning

To study category learning rigorously, researchers invent artificial categories, for example families of made-up cartoon creatures or blurry blobs, so they can control exactly what defines membership and watch a person learn it from scratch through trial and error with feedback.

A computational model, in this setting, is a precise mathematical recipe that tries to predict a learner's choices trial by trial, so that different theories can be tested against real behaviour rather than argued about in words.

The prototype and exemplar theories met earlier both have such model forms.

A prototype model assumes the learner gradually distils the training items into one summary per category and then judges new items by nearness to that summary.

An exemplar model, such as Nosofsky's Generalised Context Model, assumes the learner stores the individual training items and judges new items by their combined similarity to all of them.

These models are valued because they make numerical predictions that can be checked, and much of the field's progress has come from pitting them against each other on the same data.

A broader survey groups the many proposals into a handful of families, including rule-based, prototype-based, exemplar-based, and boundary-based models, and the present consensus is that no single model captures all human category learning; the best account depends on the task.


21.3.2 Rule-based against similarity-based learning

One of the clearest lessons from this research is that the mind appears to have two rather different ways of learning categories, and they seem to rest on different brain systems.

The first is rule-based learning: you work out an explicit rule you could say out loud, such as "if the line is wider than the gap, it belongs in category A".

This kind of learning is deliberate and effortful, it leans on working memory and reasoning, that is, on the mind's ability to hold and juggle information consciously, and you can usually explain what you did.

The second is similarity-based or, more precisely, information-integration learning: here the correct category depends on blending several features together in a way no simple spoken rule can capture, and learners improve gradually through feedback without being able to say how they do it, much like learning to recognise a friend's face.

The psychologist Gregory Ashby and colleagues built an influential theory of this split called COVIS, which stands for Competition between Verbal and Implicit Systems.

COVIS proposes an explicit, verbal, rule-seeking system that competes with an implicit, procedural system that learns slowly from reward and is tied to a brain circuit involving the basal ganglia, structures deep in the brain long known for habit learning.

The strong evidence for two systems comes from dissociations: manipulations that hurt one kind of learning often leave the other untouched.

For example, a delay between a response and its feedback badly disrupts the implicit information-integration learning, which needs prompt reward, but barely affects rule-based learning.

Not everyone accepts that there are two truly separate systems, and some argue a single flexible model can mimic the results, so the debate is not fully closed, but the idea that explicit rules and implicit similarity are at least partly distinct routes to a category is widely influential.


CHAPTER 22. SEMANTIC MEMORY AND ITS ORGANISATION (PROCESS)

This chapter is about your storehouse of general knowledge about the world, which psychologists call semantic memory.

Semantic memory is your knowledge of facts and meanings that are not tied to any particular moment in your life: that Paris is a city, that dogs are animals, that lemons are sour.

It is different from episodic memory, which is memory for specific events you lived through, such as the lemon tart you ate last Tuesday.

The great puzzle of this chapter is one of organisation: you hold an enormous amount of general knowledge, yet you can reach almost any piece of it in a fraction of a second, so how is it all arranged so that retrieval is so fast.

We will look at three families of answer: that meaning is a network of linked ideas, that meaning is a set of features or a position in a space, and that meaning is held in the brain by a hub drawing together many senses.


22.1 The network models

The oldest and most intuitive idea is that knowledge is a network, a web of concepts joined by links, rather like a mind map or the way pages on the internet link to one another.

This section covers the first serious network model and the more flexible one that replaced it.


22.1.1 Hierarchical semantic networks

The first influential network model was built by Allan Collins and Ross Quillian in 1969, and it grew out of an attempt to store knowledge efficiently in a computer.

In their hierarchical model, each concept is a node, a point in the network, and nodes are connected in a branching tree from general at the top to specific at the bottom: "animal" sits above "bird", which sits above "canary".

Facts are stored at the highest level where they apply, a trick called cognitive economy that saves space.

So "can breathe" is stored just once, up at "animal", rather than being copied onto every creature below it, and "canary" only stores what is special to canaries, such as "is yellow" and "can sing".

To check a fact you travel through the network, and this leads to a clean, testable prediction: facts that require more travel should take longer to confirm.

Confirming "a canary is a bird" means climbing one level, but confirming "a canary is an animal" means climbing two levels, and confirming "a canary can breathe" means climbing two levels and then fetching a stored fact.

Collins and Quillian found in sentence-verification experiments that people were indeed reliably slower for the statements requiring more steps, which was striking early support.

But the model soon ran into trouble.

It could not explain the typicality effect, that people confirm "a robin is a bird" faster than "a penguin is a bird" even though both are one step away.

It also mispredicted some distances, since people verify "a dog is an animal" surprisingly fast, and its strict tree could not easily hold the messy, criss-crossing associations of real knowledge.


22.1.2 Spreading activation

To fix these problems Collins, now working with Elizabeth Loftus, published a revised model in 1975 based on spreading activation.

The picture is still a network of concept nodes joined by links, but the tidy hierarchy is abandoned in favour of a web organised by relatedness, where the length of a link reflects how closely two ideas are associated in your experience.

Closely related ideas such as "red" and "fire" sit on short links; loosely related ones sit on long links.

Spreading activation is the core mechanism: when you think of a concept, that node lights up, and the activation flows outward along its links to neighbouring nodes, lighting them up too, more strongly for near neighbours than for distant ones.

This elegantly explains typicality, because a strong short link runs from "bird" to the well-connected "robin" and a weaker one to "penguin".

It also explains a famous laboratory finding called semantic priming: people recognise the word "nurse" faster if they have just seen the related word "doctor", because seeing "doctor" has already sent activation flowing to "nurse", giving it a head start.

The cost of this flexibility is that a network you can reshape at will is harder to prove wrong, but spreading activation remains one of the most durable and widely used ideas in the psychology of memory.


22.2 The feature and space models

A different tradition sets aside the picture of nodes and links and asks instead what a meaning is made of.

Perhaps the meaning of a word is a bundle of smaller features, or perhaps it is a location in a vast mental space.

This section covers both, ending with the modern computational version that now powers much of artificial intelligence.


22.2.1 Semantic feature comparison

In 1974 Edward Smith, Edward Shoben, and Lance Rips proposed that a concept is not a point in a network but a list of features, and that categorising works by comparing the features of two things.

They drew a useful distinction between two kinds of feature.

Defining features are the ones essential to a category, the ones every member must have, such as "has feathers" for birds.

Characteristic features are ones that are merely typical, common but not required, such as "can fly", which most birds have but ostriches and penguins do not.

To judge a statement like "a robin is a bird", the model runs in two stages: first a quick, rough comparison of all features of both kinds, and if that gives a clear yes or a clear no the person answers at once.

Only if the first stage is ambiguous does a slower second stage kick in that checks the defining features alone.

This two-stage design neatly explains the typicality effect: a robin shares both defining and characteristic features with birds, so it passes the fast first stage and gets a quick "yes", while a penguin lacks characteristic features like flying, fails the fast stage, and forces the slow careful check, producing the observed delay.

The feature-comparison model faded as a standalone theory, partly because it is hard to say which features are truly "defining" for everyday concepts, the very problem that sank the classical definitional view, but its idea that meaning is built from features lives on.


22.2.2 Distributional semantics and vector-space meaning

Distributional semantics is a powerful modern idea about meaning that turned out to be the engine behind much of today's artificial intelligence, and its slogan is memorably simple.

The linguist John Rupert Firth put it in 1957 as "you shall know a word by the company it keeps", meaning you can learn what a word means just by watching which other words it tends to appear near.

The word "dog" keeps company with "bark", "leash", "tail", and "vet", and that pattern of company is, on this view, most of what "dog" means.

The method turns each word into a vector, which is just a long list of numbers recording how often the word co-occurs with every other word, so that a word becomes a point in a space with hundreds of dimensions.

Words used in similar contexts end up as nearby points, so "dog" and "cat" sit close together while "dog" and "democracy" sit far apart, and closeness in the space captures similarity of meaning.

An early version was Latent Semantic Analysis in the 1990s, which used linear algebra to compress large bodies of text into such a space.

A famous later version was word2vec, introduced by Tomas Mikolov and colleagues at Google in 2013, which used a neural network and could even do rough analogies by arithmetic on the vectors, so that the vector for "king" minus "man" plus "woman" lands near "queen".

The great strength of this approach is that meaning is learned automatically from ordinary text with no human hand-labelling, and it is the direct ancestor of the word representations inside modern large language models.

Its much-debated weakness returns us to a theme of the next chapter: a system that has only ever seen words next to other words, and never touched a dog or seen the sky, may capture how words relate to each other without capturing what they are actually about.


22.3 The neural organisation of meaning

The models so far are about the mind's software; this section turns to the brain's hardware and asks where and how meaning is physically stored.

The evidence comes largely from what happens to knowledge when specific parts of the brain are damaged, which offers rare, if sad, natural experiments.


22.3.1 The hub-and-spoke model and the semantic hub

A central question about the brain is whether meaning lives in one place or is scattered.

The hub-and-spoke model, developed by Karalyn Patterson, Matthew Lambon Ralph, and colleagues, offers a "both" answer that has become the leading account.

The spokes are the scattered, modality-specific brain regions that hold the different kinds of sensory and motor knowledge about a thing: what a banana looks like sits near the visual areas, what it tastes like near the taste areas, how you peel it near the movement areas.

The term modality just means a channel of experience, such as sight, sound, or touch.

But scattered features are not enough, because knowing a banana means pulling all those strands into a single unified concept, and that is the job of the hub.

The hub is a region in the anterior temporal lobe, the front part of the temporal lobes which sit low on each side of the brain roughly behind the ears, and it draws the spokes together into a general, sense-independent meaning that captures the deep similarities between things.

The strongest evidence comes from a condition called semantic dementia, in which the anterior temporal lobes gradually waste away.

Patients with semantic dementia lose meaning itself in a broad, even way across all categories and all senses, which is exactly what you would expect if the shared hub, rather than any single spoke, were breaking down; they come to sort things by shallow appearance rather than deep meaning, for instance grouping all four-legged animals together.


22.3.2 Category-specific semantic deficits as evidence of structure

One of the most surprising discoveries in this field is that brain damage can rob a person of knowledge about one category of things while leaving other categories almost intact.

Elizabeth Warrington and Tim Shallice reported the landmark cases in 1984.

Some patients could recognise and name non-living objects like tools and furniture perfectly well, yet were badly impaired at living things such as animals and fruits, and, more rarely, other patients showed the opposite pattern.

When two patients show opposite patterns like this, researchers call it a double dissociation, and it is powerful evidence that the two abilities rest on at least partly separate machinery rather than one lumped-together store.

Warrington and Shallice offered an explanation called the sensory-functional theory.

Their idea was that we tell living things apart mainly by their sensory features, that is, by fine differences in shape, colour, and texture, whereas we identify non-living tools mainly by what they are for and how we act with them, their functional features.

If sensory knowledge and functional knowledge live in different parts of the brain, then damage to the sensory part would hit living things hardest, and damage to the functional part would hit tools hardest, which is roughly the observed pattern.

The theory is not the last word, and rival accounts stress other factors such as how familiar or how visually crowded the categories are, but the basic finding stands: the fact that knowledge can fracture along the seam between living and non-living things tells us semantic memory has real internal structure rather than being one undivided mass.


CHAPTER 23. GROUNDED, EMBODIED, AND DISTRIBUTED MEANING (FRAMEWORK)

This chapter steps back from the machinery of memory to ask a deep and stubborn question: what makes a thought about something actually be about that thing.

It is tagged as a framework because it supplies ideas and arguments that sharpen and constrain the process chapters around it, rather than describing a single mental capacity.

The question sounds abstract but it has become urgent in the age of artificial intelligence, because a chatbot can produce fluent sentences about apples without ever having seen, held, or tasted one.

The worry running through this chapter is whether meaning can live purely inside a system of symbols, or whether it must somehow be anchored, or grounded, in real experience of the world, in a real body acting in a real environment.


23.1 The symbol grounding problem

This section sets out the core problem plainly and traces it to the two thinkers who framed it, then surveys the main proposed escape routes.


23.1.1 Harnad's formulation and the Chinese Room

The symbol grounding problem was named and sharpened by the cognitive scientist Stevan Harnad in 1990.

The problem is this: if the meaning of a symbol in your head is given only by other symbols, the way a dictionary defines each word using more words, then the whole system seems to spin in a closed circle, with meaning never touching the world at all.

Harnad's own image is of trying to learn Chinese from a Chinese-to-Chinese dictionary alone: every definition sends you to more Chinese words you also do not know, and you could circle forever without ever learning what a single word means.

So the question is how any symbol inside a mind or a machine gets to be about a real thing out in the world, rather than just pointing at yet more symbols.

Harnad built directly on a famous earlier thought experiment by the philosopher John Searle in 1980, called the Chinese Room.

Searle imagined himself locked in a room with a huge rulebook, receiving slips of paper covered in Chinese characters and using the rulebook to send back other Chinese characters.

To the Chinese speakers outside, the room gives perfect answers and seems to understand Chinese, yet Searle inside understands nothing; he is just shuffling shapes by their form according to rules.

Searle's point was that manipulating symbols by their shape, which is what he argued a computer does, can never by itself add up to genuine understanding of what the symbols mean.

Harnad accepted the force of this and turned it into a constructive challenge: rather than just denying that machines understand, he asked how symbols could be given real meaning, and he suggested the answer must involve connecting symbols to the world through the senses.


23.1.2 Grounding by sensorimotor experience and by multimodal learning

Harnad's proposed way out of the circle is to tie at least some symbols directly to the world through sensory and motor experience, so that they are not defined by other words but by contact with the things themselves.

Sensorimotor means having to do with sensing and moving, that is, with perceiving the world and acting on it with a body.

The idea is that a basic word like "red" or "cup" gets its meaning grounded because the system can pick out red things and cups by seeing and handling them, and richer words can then be built on top of these grounded basics.

Harnad specifically proposed a hybrid system, one that joins a symbol-manipulating part to a pattern-learning neural network that connects those symbols to sensory images of the world, so you get the best of both.

A modern echo of this idea is multimodal learning in artificial intelligence, where "multimodal" means using several channels of input at once, such as pictures and text together rather than text alone.

Recent artificial intelligence systems that are trained on images paired with their captions learn to connect the word "dog" to actual pictures of dogs, which many researchers see as a partial, practical form of grounding that a text-only system lacks.

Whether this truly solves Harnad's problem or merely connects one set of symbols, words, to another, patterns of pixels, is still genuinely debated, and reasonable experts disagree, so it is fair to call this an open question rather than a settled one.


23.2 Grounded and perceptual symbol systems

This section presents the strongest positive theory in this area, the claim that concepts are not abstract at all but are re-enactments of experience, and then weighs the evidence honestly.


23.2.1 Concepts as simulations rather than amodal symbols

The traditional view in cognitive science held that concepts are amodal symbols.

Amodal means stripped of any particular sense, an abstract code standing for "dog" that is no more visual than it is auditory, like a word written in an internal language of thought.

The psychologist Lawrence Barsalou challenged this head-on in 1999 with his theory of perceptual symbol systems, part of a broader movement called grounded or embodied cognition.

Barsalou's proposal is that concepts are not abstract codes but simulations, partial re-enactments of the very brain states that occur when you actually perceive or act.

On this view, to think about a hammer you unconsciously and partly reactivate the visual experience of seeing a hammer and the motor experience of swinging one; the concept is a rehearsal of the experience rather than a description of it.

Barsalou calls the full stored capacity to run such re-enactments for a category a simulator, and any single running instance a simulation, so your "car" simulator can generate a simulation of a specific red sports car when needed.

The appeal of this theory is that it dissolves the grounding problem at a stroke: if concepts just are reactivated perception and action, they are grounded in the world automatically, with no gap to bridge.


23.2.2 The evidence for and against grounding

The evidence for grounded cognition is real but has been contested, so it is worth laying out both sides plainly.

On the supporting side, many experiments show that understanding language stirs up sensory and motor brain systems.

For example, reading action words like "kick", "pick", and "lick" activates the very regions of the motor cortex that control the foot, hand, and mouth, as if you faintly simulate the action to understand the word.

In behavioural studies, people are faster to judge a sentence sensible when the hand movement they must make to respond matches the movement the sentence describes, a result known as the action-sentence compatibility effect.

On the sceptical side, critics raise two main points.

First, activation is not the same as necessity: the fact that motor areas light up when you read "kick" does not prove that you need those areas to understand the word, since the activation might be a side effect that follows understanding rather than causing it.

Second, grounded theories struggle to explain abstract concepts like "justice", "seven", or "tomorrow", which have no obvious look, sound, or feel to simulate.

The current balanced view among many researchers is a middle position: sensory and motor simulation genuinely contributes to meaning, especially for concrete words, but it probably works alongside more abstract, language-based, and word-co-occurrence knowledge rather than replacing it entirely.

In short, the mind may be neither purely grounded nor purely abstract, but a blend, and pinning down that blend is active research.


23.3 Schemas, frames, and mental models

The final section of this chapter turns from single concepts to larger packages of structured knowledge, the ready-made mental frameworks that let you make sense of whole situations quickly.


23.3.1 Frames and scripts as structured knowledge

Much of the knowledge you use is not about lone objects but about how things typically hang together in familiar situations, and researchers proposed structured packages to capture this.

The artificial-intelligence pioneer Marvin Minsky introduced the idea of a frame in 1974.

A frame is a data structure for a stereotyped situation, made of slots that expect certain kinds of filler, with sensible default values ready when the details are missing.

Your "kitchen" frame has slots for a stove, a sink, and cupboards, and if someone mentions a kitchen you have not seen, you automatically assume it has these things unless told otherwise; that is a default value at work.

Closely related is the script, an idea from Roger Schank and Robert Abelson in 1977, which is a frame for a routine sequence of events.

Their famous example is the restaurant script: you know without being told that you enter, are seated, read a menu, order, eat, pay, and leave, in that order, with roles for the waiter and the cook.

Scripts explain why stories can leave so much unsaid, since if a tale says "she ate at the cafe and left a big tip", you effortlessly fill in the ordering and the eating from your script, and they also explain a memory quirk: people often misremember a story as having included typical script events that were never actually mentioned, because the script quietly supplied them.

Frames and scripts are important both as theories of human knowledge and as early blueprints for getting machines to reason about ordinary situations.


23.3.2 Mental models as manipulable internal representations

A mental model is a small working replica of some part of the world that you build in your head and can then run or manipulate to figure things out, rather than a static store of facts.

The idea was developed in depth by the psychologist Philip Johnson-Laird, building on an older insight from Kenneth Craik in 1943 that the mind works by carrying a small-scale model of reality that it can use to try out actions in imagination before committing to them in the flesh.

The key feature is that a mental model has a structure that mirrors the structure of the thing it represents, so relationships in the model line up with relationships in the world, which is what lets you "read off" new conclusions by inspecting the model.

Johnson-Laird applied this powerfully to reasoning: he argued that when people work through a logic problem they do not follow formal rules of logic but instead imagine concrete example situations, that is, build mental models of the possibilities, and then check what holds across them.

This theory neatly predicts why people make certain reasoning errors, because they tend to build only one or a few models and overlook other possibilities that a fuller search would reveal, so the errors come from limited model-building rather than from broken logic.

Mental models also explain everyday understanding, such as how you predict what a set of gears will do by mentally turning them, and the idea connects outward to the broader theme of Chapter One, that a mind works largely by building and running internal models of its world.


CHAPTER 24. MENTAL IMAGERY AND ANALOG REPRESENTATION (PROCESS)

This chapter is about the pictures in your head.

Mental imagery is the experience of perceiving something in its absence, most familiarly "seeing" something with your mind's eye, as when you picture your front door or count the windows on your house from memory.

Almost everyone has some version of this experience, and it raises a genuinely deep question about the mind: when you picture something, is there really a picture-like thing in your head, or is that just a figure of speech for a process that is actually more like describing.

That question drove one of the longest and most instructive debates in cognitive science, and this chapter lays out the striking experiments first and then the debate they fed.

The word analog in the chapter title means a representation that varies smoothly and resembles what it stands for, the way the length of a mercury thermometer's column varies in step with the temperature, as opposed to a digital or symbolic code that stands for things by arbitrary labels.


24.1 The phenomena of imagery

Before the theories, this section presents the two classic experimental findings that made imagery a respectable scientific topic, because both produced clean, orderly numbers rather than mere reports of private experience.


24.1.1 Mental rotation and its linear signature

The most celebrated imagery experiment was carried out by Roger Shepard and Jacqueline Metzler in 1971, and its result is beautifully simple.

They showed people pairs of drawings of three-dimensional shapes built from little cubes, and the task was just to decide whether the two shapes were the same object seen from different angles, or genuinely different mirror-image shapes.

The crucial trick was that when the two shapes were the same, one was shown rotated by some amount relative to the other, anywhere from zero up to 180 degrees.

The striking finding was a straight-line relationship: the more one shape was rotated away from the other, the longer people took to decide they matched, and the increase was remarkably steady, adding a roughly constant amount of time for each extra degree of rotation.

This orderly straight-line pattern is the "linear signature" of the chapter title.

The natural interpretation, and the one Shepard and Metzler drew, is that people literally rotate a mental image of one shape, smoothly and at a fairly constant speed of very roughly 60 degrees per second, until it lines up with the other and they can compare them.

The importance of this result is that the timing behaves as if a real object were being physically turned in space, which is hard to explain if the mind were only shuffling abstract symbols, and it strongly suggested that imagery is an analog process that preserves the spatial structure of what it represents.


24.1.2 Image scanning and the preservation of metric structure

The second classic finding came from Stephen Kosslyn in the 1970s, and it concerns not rotating an image but scanning across one.

Kosslyn had people memorise a map of a made-up island dotted with landmarks such as a hut, a tree, and a well, and then, with eyes closed, picture the map and mentally move their attention from one named landmark to another.

The result mirrored the rotation studies: the greater the real distance between two landmarks on the original map, the longer people took to scan between them in their mind's eye.

Again the times rose in a steady, straight-line fashion with distance.

The phrase "preservation of metric structure" means that the mental image keeps the actual distances of the real thing, so that things far apart on the map are far apart in the image and take longer to travel between.

Kosslyn argued that this is exactly what you would expect if a mental image is genuinely laid out like a picture in a space, with the mind's eye moving across it much as real eyes move across a real scene.

Taken together with mental rotation, image scanning built a strong case that mental images are not just vague inner talk but structured, space-like representations you can move around in, which set up the great debate that follows.


24.2 The imagery debate

The experiments above were dramatic, but they did not by themselves settle what a mental image really is, and for decades two camps drew opposite conclusions from the same data.

This section lays out the two positions and then gives an honest account of what was and was not resolved.


24.2.1 The depictive account

The depictive account, championed by Stephen Kosslyn, takes the experiments largely at face value.

Depictive means picture-like, representing by resemblance the way a photograph does, so that parts of the representation correspond to parts of the thing and spatial layout is genuinely preserved.

On this view a mental image really is a special kind of picture in the head, displayed on an internal space-like medium that Kosslyn compared to a screen, which the rest of the mind can inspect much as an eye inspects a scene.

This account explains the rotation and scanning results very naturally: they take time in an orderly, distance-dependent way precisely because a real spatial layout is being traversed step by step, just as it would take you longer to walk across a bigger room.

Kosslyn's stronger claim, developed later, was that these mental pictures are actually laid out on the maps in the early visual areas of the brain, the same regions that light up when you really see, so that imagining and seeing share hardware.


24.2.2 The propositional account

The opposing view was pressed hardest by Zenon Pylyshyn, and it denies that there is any real picture in the head at all.

A proposition is an abstract, language-like description of a fact, something like "the hut is north of the tree", with no pictorial quality of its own.

Pylyshyn argued that all knowledge, including so-called images, is really stored in this abstract propositional form, and that the feeling of seeing a picture is just that, a feeling, not evidence of an actual internal picture doing the work.

His sharpest objection was ingenious.

He suggested that the scanning and rotation results might come not from any picture but from what he called tacit knowledge, meaning people's unconscious knowledge about how real objects behave.

The idea is that participants know, without realising they are using it, that in the real world scanning a longer distance or rotating a larger angle takes more time, and they unconsciously reproduce that expected timing when asked to imagine, so the neat results reflect their beliefs about the world rather than the mechanics of a mental image.

Pylyshyn backed this with the finding that the results can change when you change the instructions or what people expect, which is awkward for the idea that you are simply reading off a fixed internal picture.


24.2.3 What the debate settled and what it did not

After decades of argument, the imagery debate reached a partial and honest resolution rather than a clean victory for either side.

What the newer evidence, especially brain imaging, did settle for many researchers is that imagery is not purely abstract description.

When people form vivid visual images, the early visual areas of the brain, including the primary visual cortex that also processes real sight, often become active, and the pattern of activity even reflects the size and shape of what is imagined, which fits the depictive account and is hard to square with a purely propositional one.

Damage to visual brain areas can impair imagery in ways that parallel its effect on perception, further tying the two together.

What the debate did not fully settle is the deeper philosophical point, and Pylyshyn and his allies were never entirely refuted, because one can always insist that the brain activity is a by-product and that the real computations underneath are still symbol-like.

There is also a genuine puzzle the debate did not anticipate: people vary enormously in their imagery, and some individuals, described only in recent years under the name aphantasia, report no conscious visual imagery at all yet can still do many imagery tasks, which suggests the vivid inner picture may not be doing all the work we once assumed.

The lasting lesson is a good one for a beginner to carry away: two careful camps looked at the same solid data and disagreed for years, and progress came less from winning the argument than from inventing new methods, here brain imaging, that could see past the private nature of the experience.


================================================================================

PART SIX. LANGUAGE

================================================================================

CHAPTER 25. THE STRUCTURE AND FACULTY OF LANGUAGE (PROCESS)

Language is the system that lets one mind put a thought into another mind using sound, sign, or written marks.

This chapter is about what language is made of and whether the ability to use it is a special piece of mental machinery all its own.

We will start with the layers that every language is built from, then look at the features that make human language so powerful, and finish by asking whether language is a separate faculty or just ordinary thinking put to use.

The reason any of this matters is simple: understanding how language is structured is the first step toward understanding how a mind, human or machine, could ever produce and understand it.


25.1 The levels of linguistic structure

Language looks like a single smooth stream, but underneath it is organised into separate layers, each with its own rules.

Linguists find it useful to peel these layers apart, because a problem at one layer can be studied without solving the others.

The sections below walk up from the smallest pieces, the sounds, to the largest, whole conversations.


25.1.1 Phonology and morphology

Phonology is the study of the sound system of a language, meaning the set of sounds it uses and the rules for how those sounds may be combined.

The smallest unit of sound that can change the meaning of a word is called a phoneme, and swapping one phoneme for another turns "bat" into "pat" or "cat".

A phoneme is not a letter and not an exact acoustic recording; it is a category of sound that speakers of a language treat as "the same", even when the actual noise varies from person to person and moment to moment.

Different languages carve the sound world up differently, so a distinction that matters in one language can be invisible in another.

For example, English treats the "r" and "l" sounds as two different phonemes, while Japanese does not draw that line in the same way, which is why the contrast is famously hard for some Japanese learners of English.
