Phonology also covers rules about which sound sequences are allowed, so an English speaker senses that "blick" could be a word but "bnick" could not, even though neither is real.

Morphology is the study of the internal structure of words, meaning how words are built out of smaller meaningful pieces.

The smallest unit that carries meaning is called a morpheme, and a single word can contain several of them.

The word "cats" contains two morphemes, the root "cat" and the plural marker "s", and the word "unhappiness" contains three, namely "un", "happy", and "ness".

Morphemes come in two broad kinds, free morphemes that can stand alone as words, like "dog", and bound morphemes that must attach to something else, like the past-tense "ed".

Morphology is why you can hear a brand new word like "to google" and instantly know that "googled" means it happened in the past, without anyone teaching you that specific form.

Together, phonology and morphology handle the raw materials of language, the sounds and the word-parts, before any sentence is built.


25.1.2 Syntax

Syntax is the set of rules that govern how words are combined into phrases and sentences.

It is the reason "the dog chased the cat" and "the cat chased the dog" mean different things even though they contain exactly the same words.

Syntax shows that meaning does not live in words alone; it lives partly in the arrangement, in who is placed where.

A key idea in syntax is that sentences are not flat strings of words but have hidden hierarchical structure, meaning words group into phrases, and phrases group into larger phrases, like nested boxes.

In "the old man in the corner smiled", the words "the old man in the corner" form one group that acts as a single unit, the thing that did the smiling.

This grouping is invisible in the sound but real in the grammar, and it is what lets us understand sentences we have never heard before.

Syntax also captures the fact that some strings of words are well formed and others are not, so "she quickly ran home" is fine while "quickly she home ran" feels broken to an English ear.

A grammar, in the technical sense, is a finite set of such rules that can describe an unlimited number of possible sentences.

Noam Chomsky, the linguist whose work reshaped this field starting in the 1950s, argued that the deep patterns of syntax are surprisingly similar across the world's languages, hinting at a shared underlying design.

Syntax is often treated as the engine room of language, the part that assembles small meaningful pieces into the endless variety of things we can say.


25.1.3 Semantics, pragmatics, and discourse

Semantics is the study of meaning: what words, phrases, and sentences actually refer to and how their meanings combine.

At the word level, semantics asks what "dog" picks out in the world, and at the sentence level it asks how the meanings of the parts add up to the meaning of the whole.

A central principle here is compositionality, the idea that the meaning of a sentence is built up in a regular way from the meanings of its words and the way they are arranged.

Compositionality is why, once you know the words and the grammar, you can understand "the purple elephant sneezed" even though no one has ever said it to you.

Pragmatics is the study of meaning in context, meaning what a speaker actually intends beyond the literal words.

If someone at the dinner table says "can you pass the salt?", the literal question is about your ability, but the intended meaning is a polite request, and pragmatics is what explains the gap.

Pragmatics covers things like sarcasm, hinting, politeness, and the way "it is cold in here" can be a request to close the window.

Discourse is the level above the single sentence, the study of how sentences link together into a coherent stretch of language, such as a paragraph, a story, or a conversation.

At the discourse level we track things like who "she" refers to three sentences later, and how one sentence sets up an expectation that the next one fulfils.

These three levels, semantics, pragmatics, and discourse, are where language stops being a formal puzzle and starts being about communication between real people with intentions and shared history.


25.2 The defining properties

Having seen the layers, we can now ask what makes human language special compared with other communication systems in nature.

The properties in this section are the features most often named as the signature of human language, the things a honeybee's dance or a vervet monkey's alarm call does not fully share.


25.2.1 Generativity, productivity, and recursion

Generativity, also called productivity, is the ability of a language to produce and understand an unlimited number of new sentences from a limited set of words and rules.

You are almost certainly reading sentences right now that you have never encountered before, and you understand them effortlessly, which is generativity in action.

This is what separates human language from a fixed list of calls or signals, where an animal has, say, a few dozen fixed messages and no way to make new ones.

Recursion is a specific and powerful trick that helps make this openness possible: it is the ability to place a structure inside another structure of the same kind.

For example, you can put a sentence inside a sentence, as in "she said that he thought that they knew that it would rain".

Because recursion can in principle be repeated without a fixed limit, it lets a finite grammar describe an infinite range of possible sentences.

In an influential 2002 paper in the journal Science, Marc Hauser, Noam Chomsky, and W. Tecumseh Fitch proposed that recursion might be the one core ingredient of the language faculty that is uniquely human.

This claim became the centre of a heated debate, because in 2005 the linguist Daniel Everett argued that Piraha, a language of the Amazon, lacks recursive embedding, which he attributed to the culture rather than to a different brain.

Critics replied on several fronts, some disputing Everett's data, and others pointing out that Piraha speakers readily learn Portuguese, a language that clearly uses recursion, so their minds must be capable of it even if their own language rarely displays it.

The honest current state of the matter is that the special status of recursion is still contested, and experts have not reached full agreement, though the broader point that human language is open ended in a way animal signals are not is widely accepted.


25.2.2 Competence against performance

Competence and performance is a distinction, introduced by Chomsky, between what a speaker knows about their language and how they actually use it in real time.

Competence is the idealised underlying knowledge, the internal grammar that in principle allows a speaker to produce and judge an unlimited set of sentences.

Performance is the actual behaviour, the messy real-world talking and listening that is shaped by memory limits, tiredness, distractions, and slips of the tongue.

The distinction matters because our performance often falls short of our competence, and a scientist must decide which one is the real target of study.

Consider a sentence like "the cat the dog the rat bit chased ran", which is grammatical by the rules yet almost impossible to understand because it overloads memory.

By the competence view, that sentence is a legitimate product of the grammar, and its difficulty is a performance problem about the limited working memory of a real brain, not a flaw in the grammar itself.

Chomsky argued that linguistics should aim first at describing competence, the pure knowledge, treating performance factors as a separate matter.

Many psychologists pushed back, arguing that the limits of real-time processing are not a nuisance to be set aside but a central fact about how the mind actually works.

This tension runs through the whole field, and it is one reason cognitive scientists and formal linguists sometimes talk past one another, since they are aiming at different targets.


25.3 The modularity question

We now reach the deepest question of the chapter: is the ability to use language a special, dedicated system in the mind, or is it just general intelligence applied to words?

This is called the modularity question, and how you answer it shapes how you would try to build or model a language user.


25.3.1 Language as a distinct faculty

A faculty, in this context, means a distinct mental capacity with its own dedicated machinery, as opposed to a general-purpose ability used for many things.

The claim that language is a distinct faculty says that the mind contains specialised equipment for language that is not simply the same equipment we use for vision, memory, or reasoning.

The philosopher Jerry Fodor sharpened this idea in 1983 with the notion of a mental module, a processing system that is specialised for one kind of input and runs somewhat automatically and independently of the rest of thought.

A module, in Fodor's sense, is fast, mandatory, and informationally encapsulated, meaning it does its job without waiting for the rest of your knowledge and beliefs to weigh in.

The classic evidence for encapsulation is that you cannot help understanding a sentence in your native language when you hear it, just as you cannot choose to stop seeing an optical illusion.

On the strongest version of this view, associated with Chomsky, humans are born with a language-specific endowment, sometimes called universal grammar, that guides how any child acquires whatever language surrounds them.

The opposing camp holds that language is built out of more general abilities, such as learning statistical patterns, imitating others, and reading intentions, rather than from a dedicated grammar organ.

This disagreement is genuine and ongoing, and researchers of good faith line up on both sides, so the fair summary is that the question of a distinct language faculty remains open.


25.3.2 The evidence from dissociation and development

Two main streams of evidence are used to argue that language is at least partly its own system: dissociation and development.

A dissociation, in this field, is a case where one ability is damaged while another is spared, which suggests the two rely on at least partly separate machinery.

The strongest form is a double dissociation, where in one group ability A is lost but ability B survives, and in another group the reverse is true, which is powerful evidence that A and B are separate.

Language provides a striking dissociation between grammar and general intelligence, and between different parts of language itself.

In a condition called Broca's aphasia, caused by damage usually toward the front of the left side of the brain, people can often still understand meaning but produce halting, grammatically stripped-down speech, a pattern called agrammatism.

In another pattern linked to damage further back, people may produce fluent, smoothly structured speech that is oddly empty of correct meaning, roughly the mirror image.

Recent brain-mapping studies have supported a genuine double dissociation of this sort, with grammatical production and meaning leaning on partly different tissue, which many take as evidence that the language system has separable internal parts.

There is also a developmental disorder called developmental language disorder, once widely known as specific language impairment, in which children struggle with grammar despite otherwise typical intelligence and hearing.

Cases like this, where language lags while general reasoning proceeds normally, are used to argue that language draws on some machinery of its own rather than riding entirely on general smarts.

It is important to be careful here, because the brain regions involved are not neat single-purpose boxes, and later research has shown these areas also take part in other tasks, so the evidence points to specialisation of degree rather than to a perfectly sealed language organ.

The developmental evidence adds a second angle: children the world over acquire language on a broadly similar timetable, rapidly and without formal teaching, which supporters of a language faculty read as a sign of built-in guidance.

Skeptics answer that powerful general learning, plus the rich social input children receive, could produce the same regularities, so this evidence too is read in more than one way.

Taken together, the dissociation and development findings make a serious case that language has some dedicated machinery, while stopping well short of proving that it is a fully separate and self-contained organ of mind.


CHAPTER 26. SPEECH PERCEPTION AND WORD RECOGNITION (PROCESS)

When someone speaks to you, your ears receive nothing but a continuously changing wave of air pressure, yet you hear crisp, separate words.

This chapter is about the remarkable and largely unconscious work that turns that smeared, noisy sound stream into recognised words.

We look first at how the mind hears individual speech sounds, then at how it identifies spoken words as they unfold in time, and finally at how the same recognition problem plays out for written words on a page.

The theme throughout is that recognition is an active guessing process, not a passive recording, because the raw signal is far too messy to read off directly.


26.1 Speech perception

Speech perception is the process by which the sounds of speech are mapped onto the units of language, such as consonants and vowels.

It is harder than it sounds, because the acoustic signal for a given speech sound is never exactly the same twice.

The two sections here cover the mind's tidy solution to that messiness and the surprising fact that seeing a speaker's face changes what you hear.


26.1.1 Categorical perception and the lack of invariance

The lack of invariance problem is the fact that there is no single fixed acoustic pattern that always corresponds to a given speech sound.

The exact sound waves for the consonant "d" differ depending on the vowel that follows it, the speaker's voice, the speed of talking, and the surrounding words, yet listeners hear "d" every time.

This is a deep puzzle, because it means the mind cannot simply match incoming sound against a stored template, since there is no one true template to match.

Categorical perception is part of the mind's answer, and it means we tend to hear speech sounds as belonging to distinct categories rather than as points on a smooth continuum.

The classic demonstration uses a cue called voice onset time, which is the gap between when a sound is released and when the vocal cords start buzzing.

A short voice onset time near zero milliseconds is heard as "b", while a longer one around forty milliseconds is heard as "p", with a fairly sharp boundary near twenty milliseconds.

The striking finding is that if you slowly slide the voice onset time from zero upward, listeners do not hear a gradual blend; they hear a clear "b" right up to the boundary and then abruptly a clear "p".

Two sounds that sit on the same side of the boundary are hard to tell apart, while two sounds the same physical distance apart but straddling the boundary are easy to tell apart.

The practical effect is that the mind throws away fine within-category detail and keeps only the category identity, which is exactly what you want if your goal is to recover the intended word rather than the exact noise.

Later research has softened the original strict picture, showing listeners retain more graded, within-category sensitivity than once believed, and can use it when the task demands, so the perception is less all-or-nothing than the early studies suggested.

Even so, the core insight stands: speech perception imposes stable categories on an unstable signal, which is a large part of how we cope with the lack of invariance.


26.1.2 The multimodal nature of speech and the McGurk effect

Speech perception is multimodal, meaning it uses more than one sense at once, in particular sight as well as hearing.

We are usually unaware of it, but when we can see a talker's lips, we use that visual information to help decide what we heard, which is why a noisy phone call is harder than a face-to-face chat.

The most famous demonstration is the McGurk effect, first reported by Harry McGurk and John MacDonald in 1976.

In the classic setup, a listener hears the sound "ba" while watching a video of a mouth silently articulating "ga", and the surprising result is that most people report hearing "da", a third sound that matches neither the ears nor the eyes exactly but splits the difference.

The effect is compelling because closing your eyes instantly restores the true "ba", proving that vision was actively shaping what felt like a purely auditory experience.

McGurk and MacDonald originally reported that around ninety-eight percent of adults experienced the illusion, though more recent studies find the rate varies widely, often much lower, depending on the exact stimuli and person.

That variability is itself informative, because it shows the brain is weighing the reliability of each sense rather than blindly merging them.

Brain research locates much of this audiovisual blending in a region called the superior temporal sulcus, a groove on the side of the brain that combines information across the senses.

One influential way to understand the effect is that the brain estimates whether the sound and the lip movements came from the same source, and if it judges that they did, it fuses them into a single best guess.

The broad lesson is that hearing speech is not a pure ear task but a whole-perception task, in which the brain integrates every clue it can get to recover what was said.


26.2 Spoken-word recognition

Spoken-word recognition is the process of identifying which word a speaker is producing as the sound arrives over time.

Its defining challenge is that speech unfolds moment by moment, so the listener must work with fragments and cannot wait for the whole word before starting.

The two models below are the most influential attempts to describe how the mind narrows down the possibilities as the sound comes in.


26.2.1 The cohort model

The cohort model, developed by William Marslen-Wilson and colleagues starting around 1980, describes word recognition as a process of rapid narrowing from many candidates to one.

The core idea is that as soon as you hear the beginning of a word, your mind activates a whole set of words that start that way, and this set is called the cohort.

When you hear the first sounds "ele", your mental cohort might include "elephant", "elegant", "eleven", "elevator", and "element", all lit up at once.

As more of the word arrives, candidates that no longer fit drop out of the running, so hearing the next sound "eleph" knocks out "elegant" and "eleven" and leaves "elephant".

The moment when only one candidate remains is called the uniqueness point, the point at which enough sound has been heard that no other word in your vocabulary could continue that way.

A key and testable prediction is that a word is effectively recognised at its uniqueness point, which can arrive before the word has finished, so you often know the word before the speaker stops saying it.

This explains the everyday feeling of finishing someone's word in your head a beat before they do.

The original model was strict about word beginnings, holding that a mispronounced first sound would launch the wrong cohort and derail recognition, and later versions softened this to allow the system to recover and to let context and word frequency tilt the competition.

The lasting contribution of the cohort model is the picture of recognition as a race among competitors that is settled the instant the winner becomes unique.


26.2.2 Interactive-activation and competition models

Interactive-activation and competition models describe recognition using a network of simple units that excite and inhibit one another.

The best known example for speech is the TRACE model, built by James McClelland and Jeffrey Elman in 1986.

In this kind of model, there are layers of units, one layer for features of the sound, one for phonemes, and one for whole words, and units are connected within and across the layers.

Two things happen at once: units that are consistent with each other send excitement upward and downward, while units that compete at the same level send inhibition sideways to suppress their rivals.

Interactive means the flow runs in both directions, so higher-level word knowledge can reach back down and influence how the lower-level sounds are perceived.

This top-down influence lets the model explain how listeners can restore a sound that was covered by a cough, because the activated word fills in the missing piece.

The competition part, the sideways inhibition, is how the model settles on a single winner, as the strongest word unit gradually silences its neighbours.

The main difference from the cohort model is this two-way, top-down flow, since the strict early cohort model let information travel mainly bottom up, from sound to word.

The debate between strictly bottom-up accounts and interactive accounts has been one of the long-running arguments in the field, and both camps still have serious support, with the disagreement centring on exactly how much and how early higher knowledge reaches down to shape perception.


26.3 Visual word recognition and reading

Reading is recognising words from marks on a surface, and it is a skill humans invented far too recently for evolution to have built special equipment for it.

That makes reading a fascinating case of the brain repurposing older machinery, chiefly vision and spoken language, for a brand new job.

The two sections here cover the main theory of how we turn letters into sound and meaning, and how tracking the eyes reveals the hidden work of reading.


26.3.1 The dual-route and connectionist accounts

The dual-route model proposes that there are two different pathways from a written word to its pronunciation, working side by side.

The first pathway is the lexical route, which recognises a whole familiar word directly and looks up its stored pronunciation, rather like recognising a friend's face at a glance.

The second is the non-lexical route, which sounds a word out letter by letter using the regular rules that link letters to sounds, rather like a beginner decoding "cat" one piece at a time.

The two routes explain a neat pattern in the words themselves.

Regular words that follow the usual spelling rules, like "mint", can be handled by either route, while a made-up nonword like "blorp" can only be read by sounding it out, since there is no stored entry for it.

Irregular words that break the rules, like "yacht" or "pint", must go through the lexical whole-word route, because sounding them out gives the wrong answer.

This model gains strong support from patients with reading disorders, where damage can knock out one route while sparing the other, producing people who can read familiar irregular words but not new nonwords, or the reverse.

The connectionist account, most associated with the "triangle model" of David Plaut, James McClelland, and colleagues, challenges the idea of two separate routes.

It uses a single network of interconnected units that learns the statistical links among spelling, sound, and meaning all at once, so regular and irregular words are handled by the same learned system rather than by two boxes.

Which picture is closer to the truth is still argued, and the debate mirrors the larger clash in the field between rule-based, box-and-arrow models and single-network learning models.


26.3.2 Eye movements as a window on reading

While reading feels like a smooth glide across the page, the eyes actually move in quick jumps with brief pauses in between.

The jumps are called saccades, and they are so fast that vision is essentially suppressed during them, so no useful reading happens while the eye is in motion.

The pauses are called fixations, and they are when the eye holds still and information is actually taken in, typically for a fraction of a second each.

Because fixation times and jump lengths can be measured very precisely, tracking the eyes gives researchers a moment-by-moment window into the hidden effort of reading.

The region from which useful information is gathered in a single fixation is called the perceptual span, and in English it stretches only about three to four letters to the left of where you are looking but around fourteen to fifteen letters to the right.

This lopsided span, biased in the direction of reading, shows that the mind is already previewing the upcoming word before the eyes land on it.

The measurements reveal that we do not fixate every word; short, common, and predictable words are often skipped entirely, while long or unexpected words get longer looks.

The fact that a word's frequency and predictability change how long the eye lingers is powerful evidence that recognition and comprehension are happening right there, tied to the eye in real time.

When comprehension stumbles, the eyes make a backward jump called a regression, returning to an earlier word to sort out a difficulty, which lets researchers catch the exact spot where reading broke down.

Detailed computational models, such as the E-Z Reader model of Erik Reichle and colleagues, tie all this together by proposing that attention moves to a word, lexical processing of that word triggers the next eye movement, and the cycle repeats, capturing the timing patterns seen in real readers.


CHAPTER 27. SENTENCE AND DISCOURSE COMPREHENSION (PROCESS)

Recognising words is only the start, because the real payoff of language is understanding whole sentences and connected stretches of talk.

This chapter is about how the mind assembles words into structured meaning and then knits sentences together into a coherent understanding of a situation.

We begin with parsing, the building of sentence structure, move to how the mind handles ambiguity and prediction, and end with the broader skills of drawing inferences and reading between the lines.

The recurring lesson is that comprehension is fast, forward-looking, and often just good enough rather than perfect.


27.1 Parsing

Parsing is the mental process of working out the grammatical structure of a sentence as it is read or heard.

Because words arrive one at a time, the mind cannot wait for the end; it must build structure on the fly, committing to an interpretation before all the evidence is in.

The two sections here present the two great families of theory about how it does this: a fast first-guess approach and a many-clues-at-once approach.


27.1.1 The garden-path model and structural principles

The garden-path model, developed by Lyn Frazier, says the mind builds sentence structure quickly using a single first-choice guess based on simple grammatical rules.

The name comes from the phrase "to be led up the garden path", meaning to be misled, because the model explains sentences that fool us into the wrong structure.

A famous example is "the horse raced past the barn fell", which feels broken at the word "fell" because we first read "raced" as the main verb and then have to backtrack.

The model proposes that the parser follows two guiding principles to make its snap decision.

The first is minimal attachment, which says the parser prefers the simplest possible structure, adding new words with the fewest extra grammatical nodes.

The second is late closure, which says the parser prefers to attach an incoming word to the phrase it is currently working on rather than starting a new one.

Crucially, this model is a two-stage story: the parser first commits to one structure using only grammar, fast and blind to meaning, and only afterward checks whether that structure makes sense.

When the first guess turns out wrong, as in the horse sentence, the reader hits a snag and must reanalyse, which is measurable as a slowdown in reading.

The strength of the garden-path model is that it makes clear, testable predictions about exactly which sentences will cause trouble, and many of those predictions have held up.

Its central claim, that the first pass ignores meaning and uses grammar alone, is exactly what its rivals dispute.


27.1.2 Constraint-satisfaction and good-enough processing

Constraint-satisfaction models offer a rival to the garden-path view, arguing that the mind uses many sources of information at once rather than grammar first.

On this account, from the very first moment the parser weighs grammar, word meanings, how often a word takes a particular role, and the wider context, all in parallel, and settles on whichever interpretation the combined evidence best supports.

Under this view there is no strictly grammar-only first stage; a plausible meaning or a strong context can steer the interpretation right away and prevent the garden-path stumble that the two-stage model predicts.

Evidence for this comes from findings that a rich context or the plausibility of the words can reduce or erase the difficulty of otherwise tricky sentences.

The debate between the grammar-first garden-path model and the everything-at-once constraint-satisfaction model has not been fully settled, and it remains one of the live arguments in the psychology of language.

A related and important idea is good-enough processing, put forward by Fernanda Ferreira and colleagues around 2002.

The good-enough view says that in everyday life the mind often does not build a complete, fully accurate structure, but instead settles for an interpretation that is good enough for the current purpose.

For example, when people are asked "the dog was bitten by the man, who got hurt?", a surprising number answer "the dog", because they extract a rough gist rather than parse every relationship exactly.

This shows that comprehension is often shallow and pragmatic, aimed at getting the point rather than achieving a perfect analysis, which is efficient for a busy mind but leaves room for misunderstanding.

Good-enough processing is a helpful corrective to the older assumption that understanding always means building a complete and correct representation.


27.2 Ambiguity and prediction

Language is riddled with ambiguity, where a word or structure could mean more than one thing, yet we barely notice because the mind resolves it so smoothly.

At the same time, the mind is constantly running ahead of the incoming words, predicting what is likely to come next.

The two sections here examine how ambiguity gets resolved and how prediction shows up even in the electrical signals of the brain.


27.2.1 Lexical and syntactic ambiguity resolution

Lexical ambiguity is when a single word has more than one meaning, such as "bank", which can mean a riverside or a place for money.

Syntactic ambiguity is when a whole sentence structure can be built in more than one way, such as "I saw the man with the telescope", where the telescope could belong to the seeing or to the man.

The mind resolves lexical ambiguity astonishingly fast, and research suggests that for a brief instant both meanings of an ambiguous word are activated, even the one that does not fit, before context quickly suppresses the wrong one.

This momentary activation of an irrelevant meaning, detectable in the lab within a fraction of a second, is strong evidence that meaning access is at first automatic and only later filtered by context.

How quickly context wins depends on factors like how common each meaning is, so a rare meaning may take longer to settle even when the context strongly favours it.

Syntactic ambiguity is resolved using the same tools discussed under parsing, whether a fast structural first guess or a weighing of many constraints together.

The general finding is that the mind does not enjoy holding two interpretations open; it commits quickly and, when the commitment proves wrong, pays a measurable cost to revise.

Ambiguity resolution is therefore a good example of the mind trading a small risk of error for the large benefit of keeping up with the incoming stream.


27.2.2 Prediction in comprehension and its electrophysiological signatures

For a long time comprehension was pictured as purely reactive, with the mind responding to each word as it arrived, but the modern view is that the mind actively predicts upcoming words.

Prediction means the brain uses the context so far to pre-activate what is likely to come next, so that a fitting word is processed faster and an unexpected one causes a jolt.

The evidence comes largely from a technique called electroencephalography, often shortened to EEG, which records the brain's electrical activity through sensors on the scalp.

Averaging this activity across many trials yields an event-related potential, abbreviated ERP, which is the brain's electrical response time-locked to a specific word or event.

One famous ERP signature is the N400, a dip in the electrical trace occurring about four hundred milliseconds after a word, whose size reflects how hard the word is to fit with the meaning built up so far.

A sentence like "he spread the warm bread with socks" produces a large N400 at "socks", because that word clashes with the expectation set up by the context, whereas "butter" would produce a small one.

The N400 is thus read as an index of semantic processing, essentially a measure of how surprising or ill-fitting a word's meaning is.

A second signature is the P600, a rise in the trace around six hundred milliseconds after a word, classically linked to grammatical trouble, such as a word that breaks the sentence's syntax.

The rough division of labour, with the N400 tracking meaning problems and the P600 tracking structural problems, has been enormously useful, though researchers stress it is not clean, since meaning violations can sometimes produce a P600 too.

The deeper significance of these signals is that they appear even before a predicted word arrives or is completed, which is strong evidence that comprehension is a forward-looking, predictive act rather than a purely reactive one.

This predictive view of the mind connects language comprehension to a broader modern theme in which the brain is seen as a prediction machine that is always anticipating its next input.


27.3 Discourse and pragmatics

Understanding goes well beyond single sentences, because real language comes in connected chunks that describe situations and carry meanings the words never literally state.

Discourse processing is how we build a joined-up understanding across sentences, and pragmatics is how we recover what a speaker means beyond what they say.

The two sections here cover the mental picture we build of a described situation and the social reasoning that lets us grasp implied meaning.


27.3.1 Inference, coherence, and the situation model

A situation model is the mental representation a reader or listener builds of the state of affairs that a text or conversation is about.

The key insight is that skilled comprehension is not about storing the exact words or even the exact sentences, but about constructing a model of the world the language describes.

If you read "Jane took the picnic basket out of the car. The beer was warm.", you effortlessly understand that the beer was in the basket, even though no sentence said so.

That understanding comes from an inference, a piece of information you supply yourself by drawing on your general knowledge to fill the gaps between sentences.

Inferences are what make a text feel coherent, meaning connected and sensible rather than a list of unrelated facts, and readers generate them constantly and mostly without noticing.

The situation model tracks several dimensions of the described world at once, including who the characters are, where and when events happen, causes, and goals, and readers slow down when any of these shifts, such as a jump to a new location or time.

Evidence that people build situation models rather than word lists includes the finding that, days later, readers often remember the gist of what a passage meant while forgetting its exact wording.

The situation model is therefore the level at which language finally becomes understanding of the world, rather than mere processing of symbols.


27.3.2 Grice's maxims and the computation of common ground

Much of what we mean is not in our words at all, and the philosopher Paul Grice offered the most influential account of how listeners recover that unspoken meaning.

Grice proposed the cooperative principle, the assumption that people in a conversation are generally trying to communicate helpfully and cooperatively.

From this he drew four maxims, or rules of thumb, that cooperative speakers are expected to follow.

The maxim of quantity says to give the right amount of information, neither too little nor too much.

The maxim of quality says to be truthful and not say what you believe to be false.

The maxim of relation, or relevance, says to say things that bear on the matter at hand.

The maxim of manner says to be clear, brief, and orderly, avoiding obscurity and confusion.

The clever part is what happens when a speaker openly breaks one of these maxims, which Grice called flouting, because the listener assumes cooperation is still intended and reasons out an extra hidden meaning.

If you ask "how was the meeting?" and I sigh and say "well, the coffee was nice", I have flouted the maxim of quantity by dodging the real question, and you infer that the meeting itself went badly.

This inferred, unstated meaning is called an implicature, and computing implicatures is a large part of everyday understanding.

Underpinning all of this is common ground, the body of knowledge, beliefs, and assumptions that the speakers treat as shared between them.

Common ground is why you can say "did you see it?" to a friend and both know exactly what "it" means, and skilled communicators constantly track what is and is not shared so they can leave the obvious unsaid.

Modern researchers try to make this precise, sometimes modelling a listener as reasoning about what a rational, cooperative speaker would have chosen to say, which turns Grice's insight into a computation about other minds.

Pragmatics, in the end, shows that understanding language is inseparable from understanding people, since to grasp what is meant you must model the mind of the one who is speaking.


CHAPTER 28. LANGUAGE PRODUCTION (PROCESS)

Producing language is the mirror image of understanding it, turning a private thought into a public stream of sounds or signs.

This chapter is about that outward journey, from a fuzzy idea to a fully articulated sentence, and about what the mind's slips and stumbles reveal about the machinery doing the work.

We look first at the stages a thought passes through on its way to speech, and then at the errors and blockages that expose those stages in action.

Because we cannot directly watch the steps of speaking, much of what we know comes from the clever study of when speaking goes wrong.


28.1 The architecture of production

The architecture of production means the arrangement of processing stages that transform an intention into spoken words.

Researchers generally agree that production moves through several levels, from planning the meaning, to choosing and shaping words, to controlling the mouth.

The two sections here describe the overall flow and then zoom in on a key two-step within it, the split between a word's meaning and its sound.


28.1.1 From message to articulation

The most influential map of speech production comes from Willem Levelt, whose model lays out a sequence of stages from idea to sound.

The journey begins in the conceptualizer, the stage where the speaker decides what they want to express and builds a preverbal message, meaning a plan of the intended meaning that does not yet contain any actual words.

This preverbal message then passes to the formulator, the stage that gives the message linguistic form by selecting words and arranging them grammatically and then working out their sound.

Within the formulator, grammatical encoding chooses the words and builds the sentence frame, and phonological encoding fills in the actual speech sounds and rhythm.

The output of the formulator is a phonetic plan, essentially a detailed set of instructions for the mouth, sometimes described as inner speech.

Finally, the articulator takes that plan and drives the muscles of the lips, tongue, and vocal cords to produce the audible speech.

A key feature of Levelt's model is that production is incremental, meaning the speaker does not fully plan the whole sentence before starting, but begins uttering the first part while later parts are still being prepared.

Incremental production is why we can start a sentence confidently and figure out the ending on the way, and it is also why we sometimes paint ourselves into a grammatical corner.

The model also includes a monitor, a self-checking loop by which speakers listen to their own inner and outer speech and catch errors, which is how you sometimes stop yourself mid-word.

This staged picture, from meaning to grammar to sound to muscle, provides the framework within which most production research is understood.


28.1.2 The lemma and the lexeme

A central claim in Levelt's model, and in production research generally, is that retrieving a word happens in two distinct steps rather than one.

The first step retrieves the lemma, which is the word considered as a unit of meaning and grammar, but without its sound yet attached.

The lemma of the word "sheep" carries its meaning and grammatical facts, such as that it is a noun, but not yet the actual sounds "sh-ee-p".

The second step retrieves the lexeme, sometimes called the word form, which is the word's actual sound shape, its phonemes and syllables and stress.

So producing a word means first selecting the right concept-and-grammar unit, the lemma, and then, as a separate stage, looking up how it sounds, the lexeme.

This two-step idea is not just a tidy diagram; it makes predictions that can be tested, and much of the evidence comes from the kinds of errors and states discussed later in this chapter.

The strongest support is the tip-of-the-tongue state, where you have clearly retrieved the lemma, since you know exactly which concept you want and often its grammar, yet the lexeme, the sound, refuses to come.

That everyday experience of knowing a word's meaning while its sound eludes you is hard to explain unless meaning and sound are stored and accessed as separate steps.

The lemma-lexeme distinction is therefore one of the better-supported ideas about the fine structure of producing a single word.


28.2 The evidence from error

Because the stages of production happen silently and fast, one of the best ways to study them is to examine what happens when they misfire.

Errors are not random noise; they follow strict patterns, and those patterns are like fingerprints left by the hidden machinery.

The two sections here cover slips of the tongue and the frustrating tip-of-the-tongue state, each of which exposes a different part of the production process.


28.2.1 Speech errors as a window on the plan

Speech errors, or slips of the tongue, are the small mistakes we all make when talking, and their regularities reveal how speech is planned.

The crucial observation is that errors are not chaotic; they obey rules, and those rules tell us about the units and stages of production.

In an exchange error, two elements swap places, as in saying "you have hissed all my mystery lectures" when meaning "missed all my history lectures", a type of slip collected famously and named the spoonerism after Reverend William Spooner.

The fact that whole sounds can trade places across several words shows that the speaker had planned that whole stretch in advance, since you cannot swap two things unless both are already prepared.

Errors also respect linguistic categories, so sounds swap with sounds and whole words swap with whole words, but the two kinds rarely mix, which supports the idea of separate levels for sound and for word selection.

Sound errors also obey the sound rules of the language, so a slip almost always produces a pronounceable sequence rather than an illegal one, showing that even mistakes pass through the phonological system.

Another type is the word-substitution error, where a wrong word pops out, and these split revealingly into two kinds.

Some substitutions are based on meaning, like saying "fork" for "spoon", which points to an error at the lemma stage where meaning-based selection happens.

Others are based on sound, like saying "historical" for "hysterical", which points to an error at the lexeme stage where sound is retrieved.

That the two kinds of substitution exist and stay separate is further evidence for the two-step lemma-then-lexeme picture from earlier.

The systematic study of speech errors, pioneered by researchers such as Victoria Fromkin in the 1970s, turned slips from mere bloopers into a serious scientific window on the plan behind speaking.


28.2.2 The tip-of-the-tongue state

The tip-of-the-tongue state is the maddening experience of being certain you know a word while being temporarily unable to produce its sound.

It is a nearly universal experience, and it was first studied carefully by Roger Brown and David McNeill in 1966.

Their method was to read people the definitions of rare words and watch for those who fell into the tip-of-the-tongue state, then ask what they could recover about the missing word.

The striking finding was that people in this state are not in a total blackout; they often correctly know the first letter, the number of syllables, and the stress pattern of the word they cannot quite say.

This partial access is powerful evidence for the two-step model, because it shows the meaning and grammar of the word, the lemma, have been fully retrieved while only the full sound, the lexeme, is stuck.

In other words, the tip-of-the-tongue state is a production failure caught in the very act of crossing from meaning to sound.

Researchers have debated what causes the block, and two main explanations compete.

The blocking hypothesis says an unwanted similar-sounding word gets in the way and jams retrieval of the target, and some experiments do find more tip-of-the-tongue states when a similar-sounding distractor word is present.

The transmission-deficit hypothesis says there is no active blocker; instead the connection carrying activation to the word's sounds is simply too weak at that moment to fully light them up.

The transmission-deficit view fits the finding that tip-of-the-tongue states grow more common with age and with rarely used words, both of which would weaken those sound connections, and it is the account many researchers now favour, though the matter is not fully closed.

Either way, the tip-of-the-tongue state remains one of the clearest everyday demonstrations that knowing what you mean and knowing how it sounds are two genuinely separate things in the mind.

CHAPTER 29. LANGUAGE ACQUISITION AND THE LANGUAGE-THOUGHT RELATION (PROCESS)

This chapter is about two of the deepest puzzles in the science of the mind.

The first puzzle is how a small child, without lessons or grammar drills, comes to speak a full human language in just a few years.

The second puzzle is whether the language you speak shapes the way you think, or whether thought runs on its own track underneath language.

Both questions matter for konnectome because building a humanlike mind means understanding how language gets into a mind in the first place, and how tightly language and thought are bound together.

We will move from how children learn to how words and thoughts relate, keeping everything grounded in plain examples.


29.1 The acquisition of language

Language acquisition is the process by which a person, usually a young child, comes to understand and produce a language.

What makes it remarkable is its speed and its reliability: nearly every healthy child, in every culture, masters their native tongue on a roughly similar timetable, with very little explicit teaching.

This section lays out the main competing explanations for how that happens, from the idea that language is largely built into us to the idea that it is learned from patterns in what we hear.


29.1.1 Nativism, universal grammar, and the poverty of the stimulus

Nativism is the view that a large part of our capacity for language is inborn, present in the mind before experience rather than learned from scratch.

The most famous version comes from the linguist Noam Chomsky, who argued starting in the late 1950s that humans are born with a specialised mental endowment for language.

Universal grammar is Chomsky's name for that inborn endowment: a set of abstract structural principles, shared by every human language, that a child brings to the task of learning.

In plain terms, the claim is that a baby does not arrive as a blank slate but with a rough template for how any human language can be built, so the child only has to figure out which specific language is being spoken around them.

The central argument for this view is called the poverty of the stimulus.

The argument runs like this: the speech a child actually hears is limited, messy, and full of errors and unfinished sentences, yet children reliably end up knowing subtle grammatical rules that were never explicitly present in what they heard.

A standard example is that children rarely hear the exact sentences they later produce, and they almost never get clear correction for grammatical mistakes, yet they still converge on the right rules.

If the input is too thin to fully specify the grammar, the reasoning goes, then some of the knowledge must have been supplied by the child's own mind, that is, by innate structure.

It is important to be honest that this is a contested claim rather than a settled fact.

Critics argue that the input to children is far richer than the poverty-of-the-stimulus argument assumes, and that modern statistical learning can extract more from that input than was once thought possible.

Supporters reply that certain deep regularities, such as the way questions are formed around the structure of a sentence rather than by counting words, still seem to be known without direct evidence in the input.

The current state of the debate is genuinely open: most researchers accept that humans have some special biological readiness for language, while disagreeing sharply about how much specific grammatical content is built in versus learned.


29.1.2 Usage-based and statistical learning

The usage-based approach is the main rival to strong nativism.

It holds that children learn language not from an inborn grammar but from the actual use of language around them, by detecting patterns, generalising from examples, and gradually building rules out of concrete instances.

In this view, championed by researchers such as Michael Tomasello, grammar is an emergent product of general learning abilities and social understanding, not a pre-installed module.

A key engine of this account is statistical learning, which is the mind's ability to pick up on the frequencies and co-occurrences of things in the world without trying to.

The landmark demonstration came from Jenny Saffran, Richard Aslin, and Elissa Newport in 1996, who showed that eight-month-old infants could find word boundaries in a continuous stream of speech after only about two minutes of passive listening.

To understand what they did, imagine hearing a made-up language with no pauses between words, like "bidakupadotigolabubidaku".

The infants tracked a statistical cue called the transitional probability, which is simply how likely one syllable is to follow another.

Within a real word the syllables follow each other very reliably, while across a word boundary the next syllable is less predictable, so a dip in predictability signals "a word probably ends here".

The infants used exactly these dips to segment the stream, which showed that a core part of learning language can be accomplished by tracking statistics alone.

This finding was hugely influential because it showed that powerful learning does not require an inborn grammar for at least some tasks, only a sensitivity to patterns.

The honest summary is that usage-based and statistical learning clearly do a great deal of the work, especially for vocabulary and sound patterns, while the debate continues over whether they are enough to explain the most abstract parts of syntax, which is the system of rules for combining words into sentences.


29.1.3 The critical period and bilingualism

A critical period is a window of time early in life during which the brain is especially ready to learn something, after which learning the same thing becomes harder and often less complete.

The biologist Eric Lenneberg proposed in his 1967 book that language has such a window, roughly from early childhood to around puberty.

The everyday evidence people point to is that young children pick up a new language effortlessly and end up sounding like natives, while adults who move to a new country often learn to communicate well yet keep an accent and struggle with fine points of grammar.

More striking evidence comes from rare and tragic cases of children deprived of language early in life, who then have great difficulty acquiring normal grammar even with later help, and from studies of deaf signers who acquired sign language at different ages.

The strength and even the existence of a sharp critical period remain debated.

Many researchers now prefer to speak of a gradual decline in language-learning ability with age rather than a hard cutoff, and they argue about whether the cause is biological maturation, changes in learning strategy, or simply reduced exposure and motivation.

Johnson and Newport's influential 1989 study found that the age at which people arrived in a new country strongly predicted their later grammar, consistent with a maturational window, but the interpretation of such data is still argued over.

Bilingualism is the ability to use two languages, and it is the norm rather than the exception across the world's population.

Growing up with two languages does not confuse children or delay their language development in any lasting way, contrary to an old worry, though bilingual children may know slightly fewer words in each single language while knowing more words overall.

For years many scientists reported a "bilingual advantage", the claim that juggling two languages strengthens executive control, which is the set of mental skills for focusing, switching, and holding back impulses.

That claim has since been seriously challenged, because large and carefully controlled studies often fail to find the advantage, and studies that do find it may reflect publication bias, meaning positive results get published while null results sit in drawers.

The fair current view is that any cognitive benefit of bilingualism, if it exists, is small and inconsistent, while the communicative and cultural benefits of speaking two languages are real and large.


29.2 Language and thought

This section turns from how we learn language to how language relates to thinking itself.

The core question is old and stubborn: does the particular language you speak mould the concepts you can form and the way you reason, or is thought largely independent of language and merely expressed through it?

We will look at the modern evidence on that question, at the idea that thought has its own internal language, and at how language may have evolved in the first place.


29.2.1 Linguistic relativity and its modern evidence

Linguistic relativity is the idea that the language you speak influences the way you perceive and think about the world.

It is often called the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, after the linguists Edward Sapir and Benjamin Lee Whorf who wrote about it in the early twentieth century.

There is a strong version and a weak version, and keeping them apart is essential.

The strong version, linguistic determinism, says language completely determines thought, so that you cannot think what your language cannot express.

That strong version is now rejected by almost everyone, because people clearly can think about things their language has no single word for, and can learn new distinctions.

The weak version says language influences or nudges thought, making some distinctions easier or more habitual, and this weaker claim has real experimental support.

One well-studied domain is colour: languages divide the colour spectrum differently, and speakers of a language that has separate basic words for light blue and dark blue, such as Russian, are slightly faster at telling those shades apart than English speakers who call both "blue".

Another domain is space: some Aboriginal Australian languages describe location using fixed compass directions like north and south rather than "left" and "right", and speakers of those languages show a remarkable, constant awareness of their orientation.

A third domain is grammatical gender, where the gender a language assigns to an object can subtly colour how people describe it.

The modern consensus, associated with researchers such as Lera Boroditsky, is that language does shape thought in measurable but bounded ways, more like tinting a lens than building the eye.

Language seems to influence thinking most when a task lets people lean on verbal labels, and its influence shrinks when people are prevented from using language or when the task is purely perceptual.


29.2.2 The language of thought hypothesis

The language of thought hypothesis is a very different idea about the language-thought relation, proposed by the philosopher Jerry Fodor in his 1975 book.

It claims that thinking happens in an internal mental code, a kind of inner language, that is separate from any spoken language like English or Japanese.

This inner code is often nicknamed "Mentalese".

The core claim is that thoughts have parts that combine according to rules, much as words combine into sentences, and that this combining is what lets us think an unlimited number of new thoughts.

Two properties are central to the argument.

Productivity means you can understand and produce endlessly many new thoughts you have never encountered, just as you can understand a sentence you have never heard before.

Systematicity means that if you can think "the dog chased the cat", you can automatically also think "the cat chased the dog", because the same parts recombine in an orderly way.

Fodor argued that only a structured, symbol-like internal language could explain these properties, which is why the language of thought hypothesis is a foundational idea for the symbolic tradition in cognitive science.

Notice how this differs from linguistic relativity: relativity is about whether your spoken language shapes thought, while the language of thought hypothesis is about whether thought itself has a language-like structure underneath all spoken languages.

The hypothesis remains influential but contested, because rival approaches, especially connectionism which models the mind as networks of simple units, argue that structured thought can emerge without a literal inner symbolic language.


29.2.3 The evolution of language

The evolution of language asks how our species came to have language at all, when no other animal has anything close to it.

This is one of the hardest questions in science because language does not fossilise, so there is no direct record of when or how it appeared.

Researchers piece together indirect clues from anatomy, genetics, archaeology, and comparisons with other animals.

One long-running debate is whether language evolved gradually as a communication tool shaped by natural selection, or appeared more suddenly as a side effect of some other change in the brain.

The linguist Steven Pinker, with Paul Bloom in an influential 1990 paper, argued that language is a biological adaptation gradually shaped by selection for communication, much like the eye.

Chomsky and some colleagues have argued instead that the core computational ingredient of language, the ability to combine elements into ever larger structures, may have arisen relatively suddenly and was not primarily selected for communication.

Genetics adds a piece to the puzzle: a gene called FOXP2, which stands for forkhead box protein P2, was found to be disrupted in a family with severe speech and language difficulties, and it plays a role in the brain circuits for fine motor control of speech.

Early excitement that FOXP2 was "the language gene" has been tempered, because the gene is involved in many species and many functions, so it is better understood as one contributor among many rather than a single switch for language.

A separate and important debate concerns whether language evolved first for communicating with others or first as a tool for thinking, and the evidence does not yet settle this.

The honest bottom line is that the evolution of language is genuinely unresolved, with reasonable scientists disagreeing about timing, cause, and mechanism, and with the field relying on careful inference rather than direct evidence.

PART SEVEN. LEARNING

================================================================================

CHAPTER 30. NON-ASSOCIATIVE AND ASSOCIATIVE LEARNING (PROCESS)

This chapter covers the most basic ways that experience changes behaviour, the building blocks on which more complex learning is built.

Learning, at its simplest, means a lasting change in behaviour or knowledge that comes from experience.

We start with the simplest forms, in which an animal adjusts its response to a single repeated event, and then move to forms in which the mind links two things together.

These mechanisms are ancient and shared across the animal kingdom, and they turn out to be described by surprisingly precise mathematical rules, which is why they matter for a computational understanding of mind.


30.1 Non-associative learning

Non-associative learning is the simplest kind of learning, in which your response to a single stimulus changes just because you have encountered it repeatedly.

It is called non-associative because it does not involve linking two different things together, only adjusting to one thing on its own.

Despite its simplicity, it is the foundation of how nervous systems tune themselves to their environment, filtering out the unimportant and staying alert to the important.


30.1.1 Habituation and sensitisation

Habituation is the fading of a response to a stimulus that is repeated over and over without consequence.

A homely example is a clock that ticks loudly when you first enter a room, but which you stop noticing after a while, even though the sound never changed.

Habituation is useful because it lets an animal ignore harmless, familiar events and save its attention for things that matter.

It is not the same as sensory fatigue or simple tiredness, and scientists distinguish it by specific signatures, such as the fact that the response comes back if the stimulus changes, a phenomenon called dishabituation.

Sensitisation is the opposite process, in which a response grows stronger rather than weaker.

This typically happens after an intense, painful, or threatening stimulus, which leaves the animal more reactive to everything for a while.

For example, after a sudden loud bang, you may jump at small sounds that would not normally startle you at all.

Sensitisation is useful because a dangerous event should raise an animal's overall vigilance.

Much of what we know about the cellular basis of these processes comes from the neuroscientist Eric Kandel's work on the sea slug Aplysia, a simple animal whose large nerve cells let researchers trace exactly how habituation and sensitisation change the strength of connections between neurons.

That work, which earned a share of the Nobel Prize in 2000, showed that even the simplest learning is stored as changes in the connections between nerve cells, a principle that scales up to more complex memory.


30.2 Classical conditioning

Classical conditioning is a form of associative learning in which an animal learns that one event predicts another.

Associative learning means learning a link between two things, so that one comes to stand for or signal the other.

This kind of learning lets an animal use a cue in the world to prepare for something important that reliably follows it, which is enormously adaptive.


30.2.1 The Pavlovian paradigm and its phenomena

Classical conditioning is also called Pavlovian conditioning after the Russian physiologist Ivan Pavlov, who discovered it around the turn of the twentieth century while studying digestion in dogs.

Pavlov noticed that his dogs began to salivate not just when food arrived but at signals that food was coming, such as the footsteps of the person who fed them.

The basic setup uses four terms that are worth defining clearly.

The unconditioned stimulus is something that naturally triggers a response without any learning, such as food in the mouth.

The unconditioned response is the natural, unlearned reaction to it, such as salivating to food.

The conditioned stimulus is a neutral signal, such as a bell, that the animal learns to associate with the unconditioned stimulus.

The conditioned response is the learned reaction to that signal, such as salivating to the bell alone.

After the bell is paired with food many times, the animal salivates to the bell by itself, which shows it has learned that the bell predicts food.

Several further phenomena flesh out the picture.

Acquisition is the gradual building up of the conditioned response over repeated pairings.

Extinction is the fading of the conditioned response when the signal is presented many times without the food, so the animal learns the bell no longer predicts anything.

Spontaneous recovery is the surprising reappearance of the response after a rest, which shows that extinction does not erase the original learning but rather overlays it with new learning.

Generalisation means the animal responds to signals similar to the trained one, while discrimination means it learns to respond only to the specific signal and not to others.


30.2.2 The Rescorla-Wagner model and prediction error

The Rescorla-Wagner model, published by Robert Rescorla and Allan Wagner in 1972, is one of the most important theories in the whole of learning science.

Before it, people often assumed that learning happened simply because two things occurred close together in time, an idea called contiguity.

The Rescorla-Wagner model made a deeper and more powerful claim: learning is driven by surprise, not merely by togetherness.

The central idea is prediction error, which is the gap between what actually happens and what the animal expected to happen.

When an outcome is fully expected, the prediction error is zero, and no new learning occurs, because there is nothing to update.

When an outcome is surprising, either better or worse than expected, the prediction error is large, and learning is strong, because the animal must revise its expectations.

In plain terms, you learn about a cue only to the extent that the outcome it predicts caught you off guard.

The model can be stated as a simple rule: the change in the strength of an association depends on how salient the cue and outcome are, multiplied by the difference between the maximum possible learning and how much has already been learned.

This one idea, that learning tracks prediction error, turned out to be extraordinarily fruitful, and as later chapters show, it became the bridge between animal conditioning and modern theories of how the brain and artificial systems learn from rewards.


30.2.3 Blocking, overshadowing, and the primacy of contingency over contiguity

Blocking is the single most important piece of evidence for the prediction-error view of learning, and it was discovered by Leon Kamin around 1969.

In a blocking experiment, an animal first learns that one cue, say a light, reliably predicts a shock.

Then a second cue, say a tone, is added, so the light and tone appear together and are followed by the same shock.

Common sense might expect the animal to learn that the tone also predicts shock, since the tone was always paired with it.

Instead, the animal learns little or nothing about the tone, because the shock was already fully predicted by the light, so there was no surprise and no prediction error to drive learning about the tone.

The prior learning about the light "blocks" learning about the tone, which is exactly what the Rescorla-Wagner model predicts and what a simple contiguity account cannot explain.

Overshadowing is a related effect: when two cues of unequal salience are trained together from the start, the more noticeable cue captures most of the learning and overshadows the weaker one.

Together these findings establish the primacy of contingency over contiguity.

Contiguity means two things merely occurring close together in time.

Contingency means one thing genuinely predicting another, that is, the outcome being more likely when the cue is present than when it is absent.

Rescorla showed in a classic experiment that animals learn about a cue only when it actually changes the odds of the outcome, not simply when the cue and outcome happen to co-occur.

The lesson, which reshaped the field, is that brains are not passive recorders of what happens together but active predictors that learn from the mismatch between expectation and reality.


30.3 Instrumental conditioning

Instrumental conditioning, also called operant conditioning, is learning from the consequences of your own actions.

In classical conditioning the animal learns a relationship between two events it does not control, but in instrumental conditioning the animal learns that its own behaviour produces outcomes.

This is the kind of learning behind training a dog to sit for a treat, or a person forming a habit because it pays off, and it is central to how goals and rewards shape behaviour.


30.3.1 The law of effect and schedules of reinforcement

The law of effect was formulated by the psychologist Edward Thorndike around 1898, based on experiments with cats learning to escape from puzzle boxes.

The law states, in plain form, that actions followed by satisfying outcomes become more likely to be repeated, while actions followed by unpleasant outcomes become less likely.

Thorndike's cats did not solve the box in a flash of insight but gradually got faster over many trials, as successful actions were stamped in by their rewarding consequences.

Reinforcement is anything that makes a behaviour more likely in the future, while punishment is anything that makes it less likely.

The psychologist B. F. Skinner built an entire research programme on these ideas, using a device now called the Skinner box in which an animal presses a lever for food.

A key discovery was that the pattern, or schedule, on which reinforcement is delivered has powerful and predictable effects on behaviour.

A fixed-ratio schedule gives a reward after a set number of responses, such as one treat per five lever presses, and produces high, steady rates of responding.

A variable-ratio schedule gives a reward after an unpredictable number of responses, and produces very high and persistent responding, which is why slot machines, built on exactly this schedule, are so compelling.

A fixed-interval schedule rewards the first response after a set time has passed, producing a burst of responding as the deadline approaches.

A variable-interval schedule rewards the first response after an unpredictable amount of time, producing slow, steady responding.

These schedules matter because they reveal that behaviour is finely tuned to the statistics of reward, a theme that connects directly to the reinforcement-learning theories of the next chapter.


30.3.2 Goal-directed against habitual control

A crucial insight of modern learning science is that instrumental behaviour is not one thing but is controlled by two different systems.

Goal-directed control means acting because you expect the action to lead to a specific outcome that you currently want.

If you press a lever because you know it delivers a particular food and you are hungry for that food, your behaviour is goal-directed.

Habitual control means acting out of ingrained routine, triggered by the situation, without weighing the current value of the outcome.

If you keep pressing the lever automatically even after the food has been made worthless, your behaviour has become a habit.

Researchers tease these apart with a clever manipulation called outcome devaluation.

They make the reward worthless, for example by letting the animal eat it to full satiation or by making it mildly sickening, and then see whether the animal still performs the action.

A goal-directed animal immediately stops, because it no longer wants the outcome, while a habitual animal keeps going, because its behaviour is no longer tied to the outcome's value.

A central finding, associated with researchers such as Anthony Dickinson, is that behaviour tends to start out goal-directed and become habitual with extended practice.

This distinction is deeply important, because it maps onto the difference between flexible, thoughtful action and automatic routine, and, as the next chapter describes, onto two computational strategies known as model-based and model-free learning.


CHAPTER 31. REINFORCEMENT LEARNING AS A THEORY OF COGNITION (FRAMEWORK)

This chapter presents one of the most successful bridges ever built between artificial intelligence, psychology, and neuroscience.

Reinforcement learning is a mathematical framework for how an agent should learn to act in order to maximise reward over time, through trial and error.

It began as an engineering method for training machines, but it turned out to describe, with startling accuracy, how real brains learn from reward, using the very prediction-error idea introduced in the last chapter.

Because it is precise, testable, and shared across biological and artificial minds, reinforcement learning is a central framework for konnectome's aim of understanding humanlike intelligence.


31.1 The formal framework

This section lays out the basic mathematical machinery of reinforcement learning in plain terms.

The goal is to give you the core concepts, an agent, states, actions, rewards, and value, without heavy equations, so the later sections make sense.

Do not worry if the vocabulary is new; each term names a simple, intuitive idea.


31.1.1 Markov decision processes and value functions

A Markov decision process is the standard formal description of the situation a learning agent faces.

It sounds technical, but the idea is simple: it is a way of describing a world made of situations you can be in, actions you can take, and rewards you can receive.

A state is the situation the agent is currently in, such as a particular square on a game board.

An action is a choice the agent can make, such as moving left or right.

A reward is a number signalling how good the immediate outcome was, such as plus one for finding food or minus one for hitting a wall.

The word Markov refers to a simplifying assumption: that the future depends only on the present state, not on the whole history of how you got there.

In other words, if you know where you are now, you know everything you need to decide what to do next, and the path you took to get there does not add information.

The agent's job is to find a policy, which is a rule that says which action to take in each state.

To choose well, the agent needs to think beyond the immediate reward, because a small reward now might lead to a big reward later, or a tempting reward now might lead to disaster.

This is captured by the value function, which is the heart of the framework.

The value of a state is the total amount of reward the agent can expect to collect in the long run, starting from that state and following its policy.

Value is distinct from immediate reward: a state can feel unrewarding right now yet have high value because it leads somewhere good.

Because future rewards are less certain and less pressing than present ones, they are usually discounted, meaning a reward far in the future counts for a little less than the same reward now.

Learning good value estimates is the key to acting well, and the next sub-section describes the elegant trick that makes such learning possible.


31.1.2 Temporal-difference learning and its variants

Temporal-difference learning is the central algorithm of reinforcement learning, developed largely by Richard Sutton and Andrew Barto in the 1980s.

It solves a hard problem: how can an agent learn the long-run value of situations when the rewards may come much later, without waiting to see the entire future?

The clever answer is to learn from the difference between successive predictions, which is where the name temporal difference comes from.

Here is the idea in plain words.

At each step, the agent has a prediction of how much reward is coming.

A moment later, it has a new, slightly better-informed prediction, plus whatever reward it just received.

If the new estimate is higher than the old one, the agent was pleasantly surprised, and it nudges the earlier prediction upward; if lower, it nudges it downward.

This nudge is the temporal-difference error, and it is a form of the very same prediction error we met in classical conditioning.

The beauty of this method is that the agent learns continually, step by step, using each prediction to correct the one before it, without ever needing to know the full outcome in advance.

There are several variants worth naming.

In one variant, called Q-learning, the agent learns the value of taking a particular action in a particular state, which directly tells it which action is best.

Q-learning is called off-policy because it can learn about the best possible actions even while behaving more cautiously or randomly.

Another variant, called SARSA, learns the value of the actions the agent actually takes, and is called on-policy.

The deep significance of temporal-difference learning, spelled out later in this chapter, is that the brain appears to use exactly this kind of error signal, carried by the chemical dopamine.


31.1.3 The exploration and exploitation trade-off

The exploration-exploitation trade-off is a fundamental dilemma that every learning agent, biological or artificial, must face.

Exploitation means using what you already know to get the best reward you can right now.

Exploration means trying something new and uncertain, giving up guaranteed reward now for the chance of discovering something better.

The tension is easy to feel in everyday life.

Imagine you have a favourite restaurant you know is good; going there is exploitation.

Trying a new restaurant that might be wonderful or might be terrible is exploration.

If you only ever exploit, you may never discover a better option and get stuck in a rut.

If you only ever explore, you never settle down to enjoy what you have found, and you waste chances on bad options.

A good learner must balance the two, exploring more when it is ignorant and exploiting more as it grows confident.

Researchers have formalised several strategies for striking this balance.
