43.2.1 Subliminal perception and priming

Subliminal perception means perceiving a stimulus that is too weak, too brief, or too hidden to be consciously seen, yet which still affects the mind.

The main laboratory tool for studying it is priming, which means showing one stimulus and measuring how it changes the response to a later one.

In a typical masked priming experiment, a word is flashed very briefly and then immediately covered by a jumble of symbols called a mask, so that the person reports seeing nothing, yet that hidden word can still speed up the recognition of a related word afterward.

Work by Stanislas Dehaene and others has shown that such masked words can be processed surprisingly deeply, including at the level of meaning, and not merely as visual shapes.

This is genuinely important evidence that a good deal of processing happens before and without consciousness.

However, this is an area where healthy scepticism is essential, and the science has become more careful over time.

A recurring problem is that experiments meant to hide a stimulus completely often fail to do so, and participants may have had a faint, above-chance awareness that was not properly measured.

Recent meta-analyses of subliminal linguistic priming have found evidence of weak statistical power and of residual awareness in many classic studies, which means some famous subliminal effects are smaller or less certain than they were once claimed to be.

The balanced conclusion is that unconscious processing of simple, well-learned stimuli is real, but that dramatic claims about the unconscious mind absorbing complex hidden messages are not well supported, and measuring true unawareness is the hard part.


43.2.2 Implicit cognition and the dissociations that reveal it

Implicit cognition refers to mental processes that influence our thoughts, feelings, and actions without our being aware of the process or sometimes even of its results.

The main way researchers argue that something is implicit is by finding a dissociation, which means a gap between two measures.

A dissociation occurs when a person shows an effect on one measure, such as behaving as if they learned something, while showing nothing on another measure, such as being unable to report or explain what they learned.

A well-known example comes from amnesia, where patients with severe memory loss can improve on a skill or show priming from earlier exposure while sincerely denying any memory of the training, revealing that the influence is real but the awareness of it is absent.

Similar dissociations appear in healthy people in tasks where they pick up on a hidden regularity and use it to respond faster while being unable to state what the regularity was.

These dissociations are the central evidence that memory and learning are not single conscious things but include processes that operate below awareness.

A fair caution, echoing the previous sub-section, is that a dissociation is only convincing if the awareness measure is sensitive enough, because a weak test of awareness can make ordinary conscious knowledge look unconscious, so the strength of these claims depends heavily on how carefully awareness is assessed.


43.3 The measurement of awareness

Everything in this chapter depends on being able to tell what someone is and is not aware of, and that turns out to be one of the thorniest problems in the field, which this section confronts directly.


43.3.1 Objective and subjective thresholds

To claim that something was processed unconsciously, you must define the line below which a stimulus counts as unseen, and there are two very different ways to draw that line.

An objective threshold is defined by performance: a stimulus is treated as unconscious only if the person cannot do better than chance at any forced choice about it, for example cannot guess above chance whether a word was present.

A subjective threshold is defined by report: a stimulus is treated as unconscious if the person says they did not see it and reports no experience of it, even if their behaviour shows some sensitivity.

These two thresholds usually do not sit in the same place, and the gap between them is scientifically revealing.

People often can make above-chance forced-choice guesses about stimuli they sincerely report not seeing, which means that by the subjective criterion the stimulus is unconscious while by the objective criterion it is not.

Which threshold you choose changes your conclusions dramatically, because the loose subjective criterion makes unconscious perception look powerful and common, while the strict objective criterion makes it look rarer and weaker.

There is no fully agreed answer about which threshold is correct, and this choice is one of the main reasons that estimates of how much the unconscious can do vary so widely between researchers.


43.3.2 The process-dissociation procedure and the no-report paradigms

Because simple awareness measures are so slippery, researchers have developed cleverer methods to separate conscious from unconscious influences, and two are especially important.

The first is the process-dissociation procedure, introduced by Larry Jacoby in 1991.

Its clever idea is to set conscious and unconscious influences against each other by giving people two kinds of instruction: sometimes to use a memory and sometimes deliberately to avoid using it.

If a memory keeps influencing behaviour even when the person is trying hard not to use it, that influence must be automatic and unconscious rather than deliberately controlled, and by comparing the two conditions the method estimates the size of the conscious and the unconscious contributions separately rather than assuming a task is purely one or the other.

The second development is the family of no-report paradigms, which come mostly from consciousness research.

The problem they solve is that asking someone to report what they experienced adds extra mental steps, such as making a decision and pressing a button, and those steps have their own brain activity that can be mistaken for the brain activity of consciousness itself.

No-report paradigms try to infer what a person is experiencing without asking them to report it, for instance by using eye movements or physiological signals that naturally track perception, so that the measured brain activity reflects the experience more purely.

This matters because some brain activity once thought to be the signature of consciousness, particularly in the prefrontal cortex, turned out to shrink when the report requirement was removed, suggesting it reflected the act of reporting rather than the experience.

At the same time, this fix is not perfect, since a completely report-free method makes it harder to be sure what the person actually experienced, so the field is still working out how to have it both ways, which leads naturally into the study of consciousness itself.


CHAPTER 44. CONSCIOUSNESS: CONCEPTS, MEASURES, AND THEORIES (CONTEXT)

This chapter is about consciousness itself, the fact that there is something it is like to be you, to see red, to feel pain, to have an inner life.

It is placed as context because consciousness is the deepest and least settled topic in the science of mind, where careful researchers still disagree about basic questions, and honesty about that disagreement is part of the lesson.

Consciousness matters here for a very practical reason too: as machines grow more capable, questions about what could be conscious, and how we would ever tell, stop being purely philosophical.

We will separate the key concepts, survey the main scientific theories, look at how the field tries to test them, including a remarkable experiment where rival camps agreed in advance how to be proven wrong, and consider what consciousness might actually be for.


44.1 The concepts

Before theorising, we need to carve the vague word consciousness into sharper pieces, because much confusion comes from people using the one word for several different things.


44.1.1 Access and phenomenal consciousness

The philosopher Ned Block drew a distinction in the 1990s that has organised much of the field, between access consciousness and phenomenal consciousness.

Access consciousness is information being available to the rest of the mind, meaning it can be used to guide reasoning, speech, memory, and action.

Something is access-conscious if you can report it, think about it, and act on it, so access consciousness is defined by what information does for the wider system.

Phenomenal consciousness is the raw felt quality of experience itself, the what-it-is-likeness, such as the actual redness of red or the actual hurt of pain.

The distinction matters because it is at least conceivable that these two come apart, for instance that there could be felt experience that is not fully available for report, or availability without any accompanying feel.

Some thinkers argue the two always go together in practice, and others insist they are genuinely separate, and this disagreement is not merely verbal, because it shapes what one thinks a theory of consciousness even has to explain.

A useful way for a newcomer to hold it is that access consciousness is about function, what the information can be used for, while phenomenal consciousness is about feeling, what the experience is like from the inside.


44.1.2 The hard problem

The hard problem of consciousness is a phrase coined by the philosopher David Chalmers in 1995, and it names why consciousness is uniquely difficult to explain.

Chalmers separated the easy problems from the hard problem.

The easy problems, which are not really easy but are tractable, are about explaining functions and behaviours, such as how the brain integrates information, focuses attention, controls behaviour, or reports its own states.

The hard problem is the question of why any of that physical processing is accompanied by subjective experience at all, rather than going on in the dark with no inner feel.

Put simply, even if we fully explained every function the brain performs, it seems we could still ask why all that functioning feels like something, and that leftover question is the hard problem.

This is genuinely contested territory.

Some researchers think the hard problem is a real and possibly permanent limit on scientific explanation, some think it will dissolve as the easy problems are solved, and some think it rests on a confusion, so a beginner should understand it as a live and respectable dispute rather than a settled truth.

The main practical effect of the hard problem is that it divides theories of consciousness into those that try to confront felt experience head-on and those that focus on the functions and set the felt quality aside.


44.1.3 Level against content of consciousness

A third useful distinction separates two different questions that the word consciousness runs together.

The level of consciousness is how conscious a creature is overall, its global state, ranging from full alert wakefulness down through drowsiness, dreaming sleep, dreamless sleep, general anaesthesia, and coma.

The content of consciousness is what a conscious creature is conscious of at a given moment, that is, the particular experiences filling awareness right now, such as this page, a background hum, or a passing thought.

Keeping these apart is important because they can vary somewhat independently and involve different brain mechanisms.

Studying level asks what makes the difference between being awake and being under anaesthesia, which is largely about broad brain states and arousal systems.

Studying content asks why, at a fixed level of wakefulness, you become aware of one thing rather than another, which is the question behind many perception experiments.

Much of the experimental work on consciousness holds the level fixed at ordinary wakefulness and manipulates content, for instance by making a stimulus sometimes seen and sometimes not, in order to isolate what changes in the brain when something enters awareness.


44.2 The theories

This section surveys the leading scientific theories of consciousness, which disagree not only on the answers but on what the central question is, and it presents them plainly without pretending one has won.


44.2.1 Global workspace and global neuronal workspace

Global workspace theory begins with a simple and appealing metaphor.

The mind is pictured as a theatre in which many unconscious processes work in the dark, and consciousness is like a spotlight on a stage that makes selected information available to the whole audience of other processes.

The original version was proposed by Bernard Baars, and the idea is that a piece of information becomes conscious when it is broadcast widely across the mind so that many separate systems can use it at once.

Stanislas Dehaene and Jean-Pierre Changeux developed a brain-based version called the global neuronal workspace theory.

In their account, information becomes conscious when it is amplified and broadcast across a network of long-range connections, especially involving the prefrontal and parietal regions, in a sudden nonlinear surge they call ignition.

Before ignition, a stimulus can be processed locally and unconsciously, but once it triggers this global broadcast it becomes consciously accessible and reportable.

The great strength of this theory is that it directly explains access consciousness and connects neatly to experiments on report, attention, and the sudden all-or-none way stimuli often pop into awareness.

Its main perceived weakness is that critics say it explains the functional access to information but says little about phenomenal feel, so it is often accused of setting the hard problem aside rather than answering it.


44.2.2 Higher-order theories

Higher-order theories start from a different intuition: that a mental state becomes conscious only when the mind represents itself as being in that state.

In plainer words, seeing red is not enough to be conscious of red; there must also be a higher-order representation, a kind of inner awareness that you are seeing red.

The lower-order state is the ordinary perception, and the higher-order state is a representation of that perception, and consciousness on this view lives in the relationship between them.

This is why these are called higher-order theories, because the crucial ingredient is a thought or representation about another mental state, one level up.

A strength of this approach is that it takes seriously the introspective sense that being conscious involves a kind of self-awareness, and it fits evidence that the prefrontal cortex, associated with such self-monitoring, is involved in consciousness.

A common objection is that it seems to demand a lot of sophisticated self-representation for what feels like simple sensory experience, and critics ask whether a creature must really represent its own mind in order to simply feel pain.

Higher-order theories also connect closely to the metacognition of the previous chapters, since the higher-order representation is a kind of monitoring of one's own states.


44.2.3 Integrated information theory

Integrated information theory, developed by Giulio Tononi starting around 2004, takes the boldest and most unusual approach, and it is worth explaining slowly.

Rather than starting from the brain, it starts from the felt properties of experience itself and asks what any physical system would need to have those properties.

Its central claim is that consciousness just is integrated information, meaning the extent to which a system's parts form a unified whole that is more than the sum of the parts and cannot be cleanly divided without loss.

It proposes a quantity, written with the Greek letter phi, that is meant to measure how much integrated information a system has, and it holds that the amount of consciousness corresponds to phi.

A striking consequence is that consciousness becomes a matter of degree and of a system's causal structure, so that any sufficiently integrated system could have some consciousness, a view with panpsychist leanings that many find either profound or troubling.

The theory tries to face the hard problem directly by tying phenomenal experience to a precise structural property, which its supporters see as its great ambition.

It is also heavily criticised, however.

Some critics argue that phi is effectively impossible to calculate for real brains, that the theory makes few testable predictions, and that its claim about which systems are conscious can seem counterintuitive, and in 2023 a large group of researchers publicly argued that the theory was, in their words, unproven and possibly untestable, a charge its defenders dispute.

For a newcomer, the key point is that integrated information theory is genuinely radical, taken seriously by many, and sharply contested by many others.


44.2.4 Recurrent processing and predictive-self accounts

A further family of theories locates consciousness not in a global broadcast or a higher-order thought but in a particular style of local brain activity.

The recurrent processing theory, associated with Victor Lamme, proposes that consciousness arises when signals do not merely flow forward through the sensory system but loop back, with higher areas sending activity back down to lower ones in sustained back-and-forth exchanges.

The idea is that a fast, purely forward sweep of processing can occur unconsciously, and that it is the recurrent, looping activity that turns processing into experience, even without any global broadcast to the front of the brain.

A related and broader family are the predictive-self accounts, which grow out of the idea that the brain is fundamentally a prediction machine constantly generating a model of the world and of the body.

On these views, consciousness is bound up with the brain's best current model, and in particular with its model of itself as an embodied agent, so that the felt self is a kind of controlled construction the brain builds to make sense of its own states.

These accounts are attractive because they connect consciousness to the wider predictive-processing framework used elsewhere in cognitive science, and because they naturally include the body and the emotions in the story.

They remain, like all the theories here, incomplete and debated, and part of their value is in widening the range of serious options beyond the two or three most famous theories.


44.3 The empirical programme

Theories are only science if they can be tested against evidence, and this section describes how researchers hunt for the fingerprints of consciousness in the brain and how they have tried to referee the disputes between theories fairly.


44.3.1 The search for the neural correlates of consciousness

A neural correlate of consciousness is the minimal brain activity that is sufficient for a specific conscious experience.

The research strategy, pioneered in part by Francis Crick and Christof Koch in the 1990s, is to hold everything else fixed and find just the brain events that differ when a person is aware of something versus not aware of it.

A favourite tool is to use a stimulus that stays physically constant but is sometimes seen and sometimes not, such as an image shown so briefly it is caught only on some trials, or rivalrous images that flip in and out of awareness, and then to compare brain activity between the aware and unaware cases.

The goal is to subtract away everything that is the same and leave only the neural signature of the experience itself.

This programme has been productive but also harder than it first looked, and a major complication is exactly the report problem discussed in the previous chapter: some of the brain activity that seemed to mark consciousness turned out to reflect the act of reporting or attending rather than the experience, which is why no-report methods became so important.

As a result, researchers now try hard to distinguish the true correlates of an experience from its mere preconditions, such as attention, and its consequences, such as thinking about it and reporting it, and this refinement is a real advance even though a definitive neural correlate has not been pinned down.


44.3.2 Adversarial collaboration as a method for a contested field

When a field is full of committed rival camps, ordinary studies rarely change anyone's mind, because each side interprets ambiguous results in its own favour.

Adversarial collaboration is a method designed to break that deadlock, and it is a genuinely admirable piece of scientific practice worth understanding.

In an adversarial collaboration, the proponents of competing theories sit down together, in advance, and agree on exactly what experiment to run and, crucially, on what results would count as a point for each theory and what results would embarrass it.

Because the predictions and their interpretation are locked in before any data are collected, in a public preregistration, neither side can move the goalposts afterward.

A large effort of this kind, run by a consortium called Cogitate, pitted global neuronal workspace theory against integrated information theory, with the theories' own leading advocates helping design the test.

Around two hundred and fifty six participants viewed images while their brain activity was recorded with several methods at once, and the results, published in the journal Nature in 2025, were mixed for both theories rather than a clean victory for either.

The findings included evidence that information about what a person was consciously seeing could be decoded from the back of the brain, and a relative lack of the sustained prefrontal ignition that the global workspace theory had predicted, which was awkward for that theory, while integrated information theory was challenged by the absence of the sustained posterior synchronisation it had predicted.

Neither theory was confirmed or refuted outright, and that ambiguous outcome is itself instructive, because it shows how genuinely unsettled the science of consciousness remains.

The deeper lesson for a beginner is about method: when a question is hard and opinions are entrenched, agreeing in advance on how you could be proven wrong is one of the most honest things science can do.


44.4 The functions of consciousness

Having asked what consciousness is and how to study it, this final section asks what it is good for, that is, what jobs awareness might do that unconscious processing cannot, while remembering that even this is debated.


44.4.1 Access, flexible control, and integration

The most widely supported view of what consciousness does is that it makes information globally available so the whole mind can use it flexibly.

Unconscious processes, as earlier chapters showed, tend to be specialised, fast, and rigid, each doing its own narrow job, whereas consciousness seems to pool information from many sources into a common form that any system can draw on.

This pooling is thought to support flexible, novel, and deliberate behaviour, the kind that cannot run on a fixed habit, which fits the global workspace idea that broadcasting is the core function.

Consciousness is also linked to integration, the binding together of many separate features, such as a colour, a shape, a sound, and a meaning, into a single unified experience of one object or scene rather than a jumble of disconnected parts.

On this account, the value of being conscious of something is that it becomes usable by reasoning, language, memory, and planning together, so awareness is the shared workspace where otherwise isolated processes meet.

An important honesty check remains, though, because so much turns out to be doable unconsciously that some researchers question how much extra work consciousness really performs, and pinning down its unique contribution is still an open problem rather than a solved one.


44.4.2 Volition and the sense of agency

The last topic is the feeling that you are the author of your own actions, which is one of the most personally important aspects of conscious life.

The sense of agency is the experience that you are the one causing your actions, that it is you who decides to raise your hand and you who moves it.

This feeling became scientifically famous through experiments by Benjamin Libet in the 1980s.

Libet asked people to make a simple spontaneous movement whenever they felt like it and to note the moment they were first aware of the urge, while he recorded a slow build-up of brain activity called the readiness potential.

His striking result was that the readiness potential seemed to begin before the reported moment of conscious intention, which many took to mean the brain had already started the action before the person consciously decided, appearing to threaten the idea of conscious free will.

These experiments provoked decades of argument, and the modern verdict is much more cautious than the original headlines.

Later work questioned what the readiness potential actually is, with some evidence suggesting it may partly reflect ordinary background fluctuations in brain activity rather than a specific decision command, and questioned whether the timing of a fuzzy inner urge can be measured accurately at all.

Some studies also found that the readiness potential appears before arbitrary, unimportant choices but not clearly before deliberate, considered decisions, which weakens the leap from Libet's simple finger movements to meaningful human choice.

The careful conclusion today is that Libet's experiments revealed something real and interesting about the timing of awareness and action, but they did not settle the deep questions of free will, and the confident early claim that they disproved conscious agency has not held up.

It is fitting that this outline of cognition ends here, at the sense of agency, because the feeling of being a self who chooses is where the machinery of the mind and the mystery of the person meet, and it is exactly the frontier where the science of human cognition begins to matter for how we think about minds we might one day build.

PART ELEVEN. HOT COGNITION: EMOTION, MOTIVATION, AND THE SOCIAL MIND

================================================================================

CHAPTER 45. EMOTION AND AFFECTIVE SCIENCE (PROCESS)

This chapter is about feelings, and about the surprising fact that scientists still argue over what a feeling actually is.

Emotions are the states we all know from the inside: fear, joy, anger, sadness, disgust, love, and the many shades between them.

They matter for a science of the mind because they are not separate from thinking; they steer what we notice, what we remember, and what we decide.

Affective science is simply the organised study of emotion, mood, and feeling, and the word "affective" just means "having to do with feelings".

In this chapter we will look at the main theories of where an emotion comes from, and then at the parts an emotion is made of.


45.1 The theories of emotion

The central puzzle here is the order of events inside an emotion.

When something frightening happens, does your body react first and your feeling follow, or does your mind judge the situation first and your body follow?

Different theories give different answers, and each answer has shaped decades of research.

This section lays out the main contenders so you can see what each one claims.


45.1.1 Appraisal theories

An appraisal theory says that an emotion begins with an evaluation, a quick mental sizing-up of what a situation means for you.

The word "appraisal" here simply means a judgment of significance: is this good or bad for me, and can I cope with it?

The key idea is that the event itself does not fix the emotion; your interpretation of the event does.

The same loud knock at the door can bring joy if you expect a friend or terror if you fear an intruder, and appraisal theory says the difference lives entirely in the interpretation.

Richard Lazarus, an American psychologist who developed this view through the second half of the twentieth century, proposed that appraisal happens in stages.

In what he called primary appraisal, you judge whether a situation touches your goals and wellbeing at all.

In what he called secondary appraisal, you judge whether you have the resources to cope with it.

A looming deadline you believe you can meet produces a very different emotion from the same deadline you believe you cannot meet, and that difference is a difference in secondary appraisal.

Later appraisal theorists, notably Klaus Scherer, a Swiss researcher, broke the evaluation into a longer checklist of dimensions, such as novelty, pleasantness, goal relevance, who or what is to blame, and how much control you have.

The attraction of appraisal theory is that it explains why the same event yields many different emotions in different people, and why an emotion can change the instant your interpretation changes.

The main criticism is that a full, deliberate evaluation seems too slow to explain how fast some emotions arrive, though appraisal theorists reply that appraisal can be rapid and automatic rather than conscious and effortful.


45.1.2 The two-factor theory

The two-factor theory, proposed by Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer in 1962, says that an emotion is built from two ingredients combined.

The first ingredient is physiological arousal, meaning a general bodily stirring such as a racing heart, faster breathing, or a jolt of energy.

The second ingredient is a cognitive label, meaning the name your mind gives to that arousal based on what is happening around you.

The striking claim is that the bodily arousal by itself is vague and undirected; it does not come pre-labelled as fear or excitement.

Your mind looks around for a cause, and the cause it settles on determines which emotion you feel.

In their famous experiment, participants were given an injection of adrenaline, a hormone that produces arousal, and those who did not know it would stir them up caught the mood of a nearby actor, feeling either euphoric or annoyed depending on how that actor behaved.

This is why the theory is sometimes summarised as arousal plus a label equals emotion.

The two-factor theory built directly on an older insight from William James and Carl Lange, who argued in the late nineteenth century that we feel afraid because we tremble, rather than trembling because we feel afraid.

Schachter and Singer added the crucial second step: the same trembling can become different emotions depending on the interpretation.

The theory has not held up cleanly in every replication, and modern researchers see it as an important early move rather than the final word, but its core lesson survives.

That lesson is that a bodily state and a mental interpretation work together to produce what we call a feeling.


45.1.3 Basic-emotion against dimensional and constructionist accounts

Here the field splits into three large camps over the most basic question of all: how many emotions are there, and are they built into us?

The basic-emotion view, associated above all with Paul Ekman, holds that there is a small set of biologically wired emotions that all humans share.

Ekman's classic list has six: happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, and disgust, each with its own signature facial expression.

His evidence famously included a 1971 study among the Fore people of Papua New Guinea, a group with little contact with the outside world, who nonetheless matched the same expressions to the same situations as Westerners did.

On this view each basic emotion is like a distinct, inherited program that fires as a whole.

The dimensional view, developed by James Russell and others, rejects the idea of a few discrete kinds and instead places every emotion on a map with two axes.

One axis is valence, meaning how pleasant or unpleasant the feeling is, and the other is arousal, meaning how activated or calm you are.

This map is called the circumplex model, because the emotions arrange themselves in a rough circle around the two axes, with excitement in the pleasant-and-activated quarter and depression in the unpleasant-and-calm quarter.

On this view fear and anger are not separate species; they are nearby points that share high arousal and unpleasant valence.

The constructionist view, argued most forcefully by Lisa Feldman Barrett in her theory of constructed emotion, goes further still.

It says the brain starts with only general raw ingredients, chiefly a body-based sense of pleasantness and arousal, and then constructs a specific emotion on the spot using concepts learned from your culture and language.

On this account there is no fixed fear circuit waiting in the brain; "fear" is a category your mind assembles, much as it assembles the category "chair" from many different objects.

The debate is genuinely unsettled, and it is fair to say the tide has moved against the strongest form of the basic-emotion claim.

Barrett's large reviews of the evidence concluded that you cannot reliably read a specific emotion off a facial expression, because people scowl when angry only some of the time and scowl for many other reasons too.

Defenders of basic emotions reply that the wiring shows up more in the body and brain than on the face, so the argument continues.

For a builder of thinking machines the practical takeaway is caution: treating the six-expression list as settled fact would be building on contested ground.


45.2 The components of an emotion

Whatever their disagreements, most researchers agree that a full-blown emotion is not a single thing but a bundle of parts that usually move together.

This section names those parts and then looks closely at one of them, the felt sense of the body, which has become a hot topic in recent science.

Seeing an emotion as a bundle helps explain why the parts can sometimes come apart, for example when your heart pounds but you do not feel afraid.


45.2.1 Physiology, expression, feeling, and action tendency

An emotion is usually described as having four loosely coupled components, and it helps to take them one at a time.

The first is physiology, meaning the changes in your body, such as heart rate, sweating, hormone release, and muscle tension, driven largely by the part of the nervous system that runs automatic functions.

The second is expression, meaning the outward signs others can read, chiefly in the face and voice but also in posture.

The third is feeling, meaning the subjective experience, the "what it is like" from the inside that only you have direct access to.

The fourth is action tendency, a term from the Dutch psychologist Nico Frijda, meaning the urge to do something particular, so that fear carries a pull toward escape and anger carries a pull toward confrontation.

Frijda captured this with the memorable idea that emotions are states of action readiness, poised urges to approach, avoid, attack, or attend.

The reason to break an emotion into these four components is that they do not always agree.

You can hide the expression while the feeling rages, or your body can show arousal that you do not consciously feel, and these mismatches are exactly what different theories try to explain.

Thinking of emotion as a coordinated bundle rather than one indivisible thing is one of the most useful ideas in the whole field.


45.2.2 Interoception and the construction of feeling

Interoception is your sense of the internal state of your own body, the perception of signals such as your heartbeat, your breathing, the fullness of your stomach, and the tension in your gut.

The word is built to parallel "exteroception", which is perception of the outside world; interoception is perception turned inward.

The reason it matters for emotion is a growing belief that the felt part of an emotion is largely built out of these bodily signals.

The neuroscientist Arthur Craig, often called Bud Craig, traced a pathway carrying signals about the body's condition up into a brain region called the insula, a patch of cortex folded deep in the side of the brain.

He proposed that these signals are refined along the insula from back to front, and that the front tip, the anterior insula, produces a unified feeling of the sentient self, a "global emotional moment".

More recent accounts, associated with Lisa Feldman Barrett and Sahib Khalsa among others, add a predictive twist.

On this view the brain does not passively wait for bodily signals; it constantly predicts what the body's state should be and compares that prediction against the incoming signals.

A feeling, on this account, is largely the brain's best guess about the state of the body, corrected by the actual sensations arriving from it.

This fits neatly with the constructionist theory of emotion from the previous section, because it supplies the raw bodily ingredient that a specific emotion is then constructed from.

There is real evidence that people who are better at sensing their own heartbeat also tend to report more intense emotions, which supports a link between interoception and feeling.

At the same time the details are still debated, and no one claims that every emotion is only a story the brain tells about the gut, so the honest summary is that the body is now seen as a central author of feeling rather than a mere bystander.


CHAPTER 46. EMOTION-COGNITION INTERACTION AND MOTIVATION (PROCESS)

This chapter is about the traffic that runs both ways between feeling and thinking, and about what makes us want things in the first place.

For a long time emotion and reason were treated as opposites, with feeling seen as the enemy of clear thought.

The modern picture is very different: emotion and motivation are woven through attention, memory, and judgment at every step.

Here we look first at how emotion shapes cognition, then at how wanting and curiosity drive us, and finally at how people manage their own feelings.


46.1 The influence of emotion on cognition

This section is about the many ways a feeling changes how the mind works.

An emotion can decide what you look at, what you remember, and how you judge a stranger, often without your noticing.

Understanding these effects is the first step to seeing why a purely cold, feelingless reasoner would not think the way people do.


46.1.1 Emotional capture of attention

Emotional capture of attention means that emotionally charged things grab our focus automatically, before we choose to look.

A snarling face in a crowd, a spider on the wall, or our own name across a noisy room tends to pull attention whether we want it to or not.

Researchers study this with a task called the dot-probe task, in which two pictures flash briefly and then a small target appears where one of them was.

People are reliably faster to respond to the target when it appears where a threatening picture had been, which shows their attention was already parked there.

This makes good sense from a survival standpoint, because a mind that ignored threats would not last long.

The effect is especially strong for signals of danger, and it is exaggerated in anxiety, where threatening information captures attention more powerfully and holds it longer.

The lesson is that attention is not a neutral spotlight we aim at will; emotion is constantly nudging the spotlight toward what matters for our wellbeing.


46.1.2 Mood-congruent and arousal-enhanced memory

This sub-section covers two related ways that emotion strengthens and colours memory.

Mood-congruent memory is the tendency to remember material that matches your current mood.

The psychologist Gordon Bower showed in the 1980s that a person in a sad mood more easily recalls sad events, and a person in a happy mood more easily recalls happy ones.

His explanation was that a mood activates a web of related memories, so information that fits the mood receives more attention and richer processing and is later easier to retrieve.

Arousal-enhanced memory is different: it is the finding that emotionally arousing events, whether pleasant or unpleasant, are usually remembered better than dull ones.

A frightening or thrilling experience tends to be encoded more deeply and to survive longer, an effect linked to stress hormones acting on memory circuits during and just after the event.

A famous special case is the flashbulb memory, the vivid, confident recollection people have of where they were when they heard shocking news.

Here the science carries an important warning: these memories feel photographic and certain, but studies that checked them against the facts found they drift and distort over time just like ordinary memories, even while confidence stays high.

So the honest summary is that arousal makes memories feel stronger and more vivid, but vividness and confidence are not the same as accuracy.


46.1.3 Affect as information in judgment

The affect-as-information idea says that people often use their current feeling as a quick piece of evidence when making a judgment.

Put simply, we ask ourselves, without noticing we are doing it, "How do I feel about this?", and we read the answer as if it were information about the thing we are judging.

The classic demonstration comes from Norbert Schwarz and Gerald Clore, who found that people report being more satisfied with their lives as a whole on sunny days than on rainy ones.

The twist is that when the good or bad mood was pointed out and explained away, for instance by mentioning the weather, the effect vanished.

That is the tell-tale sign that people were misreading a passing mood as a verdict on their whole life.

This matters because it shows feelings are not just noise inside judgment; they are treated by the mind as a source of data, useful when the feeling really is about the matter at hand and misleading when it is not.

It also explains a lot of everyday error, from shopping decisions made while hungry to harsh judgments made while irritated.


46.2 Motivation and cognition

Motivation is what gets a mind moving toward some things and away from others.

Without it, all the perceiving and remembering in the world would sit idle, because nothing would be worth doing.

This section looks at how value pulls our thinking around, and at curiosity, the special hunger for information itself.


46.2.1 Incentive value and motivated cognition

Incentive value is the pull that a possible reward or punishment exerts on behaviour and thought.

A useful distinction from the neuroscientist Kent Berridge is between "liking" and "wanting", which he showed are separate processes in the brain.

Liking is the pleasure you actually get from something, while wanting, which he calls incentive salience, is the craving or pull toward it, and the two can come apart, as when an addict wants a drug intensely without liking it much.

Motivated cognition is the broad finding that what we want shapes what we think, not just what we do.

The psychologist Ziva Kunda described motivated reasoning as the way our goals bias the whole process of thinking, so that we search harder for evidence supporting conclusions we prefer and scrutinise unwelcome evidence more critically.

Importantly, this is not simple lying to oneself; people still feel they are being fair, because the bias operates quietly inside the reasoning.

This is why a fan and a rival can watch the same match and honestly see different fouls.

For a science of mind the key point is that thinking is never fully separate from wanting; goals reach in and tilt the machinery of reason.


46.2.2 Curiosity and information-seeking

Curiosity is the desire to know, the drive that makes information itself feel rewarding.

A leading account comes from George Loewenstein, whose information-gap theory says curiosity arises when we notice a gap between what we know and what we want to know.

On this view the gap feels like a small deprivation, an itch, and closing it by learning the answer brings relief, which is why an unanswered question or an unfinished story can nag at us.

This explains everyday experiences such as needing to know how a film ends or being unable to leave a riddle alone.

Newer work treats curiosity as partly a form of reward-seeking, in which the brain assigns value to the prospect of learning, using some of the same machinery it uses for food or money.

Researchers also distinguish curiosity that is driven by the pleasure of discovery from curiosity that is driven by discomfort at not knowing, and integrative models try to combine the information-gap idea with these reward and appraisal accounts.

The reason this matters for building intelligent systems is that a purely goal-driven agent that never explored for its own sake would learn poorly; curiosity is, in effect, a built-in motive to gather information before you strictly need it.


46.3 Emotion regulation

Emotion regulation is the set of things people do to influence which emotions they have, when they have them, and how strongly they feel and show them.

It is one of the most practical topics in the whole field, because the ability to manage feeling underlies mental health, self-control, and getting along with others.

This section describes the main strategies and then zooms in on the one that has been studied most.


46.3.1 The strategies of regulation

The most influential map of these strategies comes from James Gross, whose process model arranges them by where they act in the timeline of an emotion.

The core insight is that an emotion unfolds over time, from encountering a situation, to attending to it, to interpreting it, to responding, and you can step in at any of these points.

The first strategy is situation selection, meaning you choose which situations to enter or avoid, as when you skip a party you know will upset you.

The second is situation modification, meaning you change the situation you are in, as when you steer a tense conversation to safer ground.

The third is attentional deployment, meaning you shift what you focus on, as when you distract yourself from a needle at the doctor.

The fourth is cognitive change, meaning you change how you interpret the situation, which is the strategy called reappraisal that the next sub-section covers.

The fifth is response modulation, meaning you act on the emotion after it has arisen, as when you take slow breaths to calm down or hide your expression.

A repeated finding is that strategies that act early, before the emotion has fully formed, tend to work better and cost less than strategies that try to wrestle the emotion down once it is in full flow.

In particular, simply suppressing the outward expression of an emotion often fails to reduce the inner feeling and can even leave the body more stirred up.


46.3.2 Cognitive reappraisal

Cognitive reappraisal means changing how you interpret a situation in order to change how it makes you feel.

It sits in the "cognitive change" family of Gross's model, and it is powerful because it works on the appraisal that, as chapter 45 explained, largely creates the emotion in the first place.

A simple example: if you reframe a pounding heart before a speech as excitement and readiness rather than as dread, the fear can genuinely ease.

Another example: reminding yourself that a rude driver may be rushing to a hospital can dissolve anger that a moment ago felt fully justified.

Because reappraisal steps in early, before the emotion has crested, it tends to reduce the feeling and the bodily arousal together, unlike late suppression which mostly hides the outside while the inside churns on.

Studies of the brain link reappraisal to increased activity in the prefrontal cortex, the front region involved in deliberate control, working to turn down activity in emotion-related regions such as the amygdala.

Reappraisal is not a cure-all; it takes effort, it is harder when emotions are intense, and constantly explaining away every feeling would be its own kind of problem.

Still, the ability to re-see a situation in a better light is one of the most reliable tools people have for governing their own emotional lives, and it is a cornerstone of several effective talking therapies.


CHAPTER 47. SOCIAL COGNITION AND THEORY OF MIND (PROCESS)

This chapter is about the mind's most demanding job: understanding other minds.

Other people are the most complicated objects we ever deal with, because they have hidden thoughts, beliefs, and intentions that we cannot see directly.

Social cognition is the study of how we make sense of other people and of ourselves in relation to them.

Here we look at how we read what others are thinking, how we form impressions of them, and how minds coordinate to act and communicate together.


47.1 Theory of mind

Theory of mind is the everyday ability to attribute mental states to others, to grasp that other people have beliefs, desires, and intentions that may differ from your own and from reality.

The phrase can mislead a newcomer, because it does not refer to a scientist's theory but to the ordinary skill each of us uses to guess what is going on in someone else's head.

It is sometimes called mentalising, and it is the invisible engine behind cooperation, deception, teaching, and simple conversation.

This section looks at how it is tested, at rival explanations of how it works, and at a modern computational account.


47.1.1 The false-belief task and its development

The false-belief task is the classic test of whether someone understands that another person can hold a belief that is wrong.

The most famous version is the Sally-Anne task, introduced by Heinz Wimmer and Josef Perner in 1983 and later used with autistic children by Simon Baron-Cohen and colleagues.

In it, a character named Sally puts a marble in a basket and leaves the room, and while she is gone another character, Anne, moves the marble to a box.

The child is then asked where Sally will look for her marble when she returns.

The correct answer is the basket, because that is where Sally still believes it to be, even though the child watching knows it is really in the box.

To pass, the child must hold two pictures of the world at once: reality, and Sally's false belief about reality.

The robust developmental finding is that most children begin to pass this test around the age of four, while younger children tend to answer with the true location, seemingly unable yet to separate what they know from what Sally knows.

This age shift is one of the most replicated results in developmental psychology, though researchers debate what changes at four, and some newer studies using looking-time measures suggest that infants show a hint of belief understanding far earlier, before they can talk.

The task also became central to autism research, where difficulties with false-belief reasoning were taken as evidence of differences in mentalising, a view that has since been refined and made less absolute.


47.1.2 Theory-theory against simulation accounts

This sub-section is about two rival explanations of how we actually read other minds.

The first, called the theory-theory, says we understand others by using something like an informal theory of how minds work.

On this account you carry around a set of rules linking situations, beliefs, desires, and actions, and you apply them to predict what someone will do, rather as a scientist applies a theory to predict an experiment.

The second, called the simulation theory, says we understand others not by consulting rules but by imagining ourselves in their shoes.

On this account you run your own mind as a model of theirs, pretending to have their beliefs and desires and seeing what decision your own mind would then produce.

A quick way to feel the difference: to predict a frightened friend's next move, the theory-theory says you apply a rule about fear and flight, while the simulation theory says you imagine being frightened yourself and notice the urge to flee.

Both accounts have support, and many researchers now think the truth is a blend, with simple, fast mind-reading leaning on simulation and complex, unusual cases leaning on theory-like reasoning.

The debate matters for artificial intelligence because it asks whether a machine needs an explicit model of human psychology or whether it could read people by running a copy of a mind.


47.1.3 Mentalising as inverse planning

Inverse planning is a modern, mathematical way of describing what mind-reading does.

The core idea starts from a simple assumption: people usually act to achieve their goals, given their beliefs, in a roughly sensible way.

Ordinary planning goes forward, from a goal to the actions that would reach it.

Inverse planning runs that arrow backward: it starts from the actions you observe and works out which goals and beliefs would best explain them.

If you see someone take a long detour around a fence to reach a spot, you infer they wanted that spot and believed the fence was in the way, because that pairing of desire and belief best explains the path.

Researchers such as Chris Baker, Joshua Tenenbaum, and Rebecca Saxe built formal models that treat this as probabilistic inference, using the mathematics of Bayesian reasoning, which is a principled way of updating beliefs from evidence.

These models predict people's moment-to-moment guesses about others' goals with real accuracy, which is impressive support for the idea.

This connects theory of mind to the broader theme of the mind as a model-builder, because reading another person becomes a matter of inferring the hidden causes, their goals and beliefs, behind the visible behaviour.

It also gives engineers a concrete recipe, since inverse planning can be programmed, and it is one of the more promising bridges between human social cognition and machine social intelligence.


47.2 Person perception

Person perception is how we form impressions of what other people are like.

Unlike the false-belief task, which is about reading a single hidden thought, this is about building a lasting picture of someone's character.

This section looks at how those impressions form and at the biases, often invisible to us, that shape them.


47.2.1 Impression formation and attribution

Impression formation is the process of combining scraps of information about a person into an overall sense of who they are.

The pioneering work came from Solomon Asch in the 1940s, who showed that we do not simply add up a person's traits like items on a list.

Instead the traits interact, and some traits are central, colouring how we read everything else.

In his famous demonstration, describing a person as "warm" versus "cold", while keeping every other word the same, dramatically changed the whole impression, whereas swapping "polite" for "blunt" changed it far less.

So "warm" and "cold" are central traits that reorganise the entire picture, while others are peripheral.

Attribution is the closely related process of explaining why a person did something, in particular whether we credit it to their character or to their circumstances.

A large and reliable bias here is the fundamental attribution error, our tendency, as observers, to over-explain other people's behaviour by their personality and to under-weight the situation they were in.

When a stranger snaps at a waiter we tend to think "what a rude person", giving little thought to the terrible day that might explain it, yet we readily excuse our own snapping by pointing to our circumstances.

This asymmetry is worth remembering because it quietly distorts everyday judgments of blame and praise, though its strength varies across cultures, being generally weaker in societies that emphasise the group and the situation.


47.2.2 Implicit social cognition and stereotyping

Implicit social cognition is the part of our thinking about people that runs automatically and outside awareness.

The important and sometimes uncomfortable idea is that we can hold attitudes and associations we would sincerely disavow if asked directly.

A stereotype is a generalised belief about the members of a group, a mental shortcut that saves effort but flattens individuals into a category.

Such shortcuts form easily because grouping is a basic feature of how the mind organises the world, but applied to people they can be inaccurate and unfair.

Researchers measure the automatic side of these associations with tools such as the Implicit Association Test (IAT), developed by Anthony Greenwald, Mahzarin Banaji, and colleagues in the late 1990s.

The test measures how quickly a person pairs, for example, faces from a group with pleasant or unpleasant words, on the logic that we are faster to link things that already feel associated in our minds.

It is important to be careful and honest here, because the science is contested: the test reliably detects average automatic associations across groups of people, but it predicts any single individual's behaviour only weakly, and experts disagree about exactly what it measures.

So the responsible summary is that automatic biases are real and widespread, that they can influence behaviour in ways their holders do not intend, but that no single test reads a person's prejudice off a screen.

For designers of automated systems the deeper lesson is sobering, because machines that learn from human data readily absorb the very stereotypes buried in that data.


47.3 Shared cognition

Shared cognition is about minds working together, coordinating their thoughts and actions toward a common end.

Much of what makes humans distinctive is not what one mind can do alone but what two or more minds can do together.

This section looks at how people share goals and act jointly, and at communication as a cooperative meeting of minds.


47.3.1 Shared intentionality and joint action

Shared intentionality is the capacity to share a goal and a plan with another person, to hold a "we" intention rather than only an "I" intention.

The developmental psychologist Michael Tomasello has argued that this ability is a deep dividing line between humans and other great apes.

His research suggests that even young children readily do things together for a shared purpose, taking turns, sharing attention, and helping a partner meet a joint goal, in ways that chimpanzees largely do not.

A simple example is two people carrying a table that neither could carry alone, each adjusting to the other, each understanding that they are doing this together.

The foundation Tomasello points to is joint attention, the early achievement of an infant and a caregiver both attending to the same thing and each knowing that they are sharing it.

From this shared "we" grows the ability to build common ground, the pool of things two people know that they both know, which turns out to be the bedrock of cooperation and culture.

Joint action, the coordinated activity that shared intentionality makes possible, is studied in tasks where two people must synchronise, and it shows the mind constantly predicting a partner's moves and adjusting to mesh with them.

Tomasello's larger claim is that this cooperative infrastructure, more than raw brainpower alone, is what let humans accumulate culture across generations.


47.3.2 Communication as a cognitive act

This sub-section makes a deceptively simple point: communicating is not just transmitting signals, it is a cooperative act of getting into another mind and being let in.

The philosopher Paul Grice argued that ordinary communication rests on the listener recognising the speaker's intention to be understood, not merely decoding the words.

When a friend says "it is cold in here", they may intend you to close the window, and you grasp the real meaning by inferring their intention rather than by translating the sentence literally.

This is why understanding language leans so heavily on theory of mind, the mind-reading of the earlier sections, because to catch what someone means you must model what they intend.

Tomasello built on Grice to argue that human communication is unusually cooperative at its root, aimed at genuinely sharing attention and helping the listener, and that it grew out of the same shared intentionality described just above.

Communication also uses ostensive cues, meaning signals such as eye contact, pointing, and a special tone of voice that announce "I have something to tell you, and it is for you".

Infants are especially tuned to these cues and treat information offered with them as general and trustworthy, which makes such signalling a powerful engine of early learning.

The overall lesson is that a message is not a package handed over intact; it is a hint that two cooperating minds use to converge on a shared meaning, which is why truly humanlike communication is such a demanding target for machines.


CHAPTER 48. MORAL COGNITION AND SELF (PROCESS)

This chapter is about two of the most personal parts of the mind: our sense of right and wrong, and our sense of who we are.

Moral cognition is the study of how people judge actions as good or bad and decide what they ought to do.

The self is the study of how a mind represents itself, holds a picture of its own character, and stitches its life into a single continuing story.

Both topics touch on what feels most essentially human, and both turn out to be built from ordinary cognitive parts working in concert.


48.1 Moral cognition

Moral cognition asks how we arrive at judgments like "that was wrong" or "she did the right thing".

For centuries the assumption was that moral judgment is the work of careful reasoning, but recent science has complicated that picture considerably.

This section looks at the influential idea that morality runs on two systems, and at the powerful role of feeling and intuition.


48.1.1 The dual-process account of moral judgment

The dual-process account, developed most prominently by the psychologist and neuroscientist Joshua Greene, says moral judgment draws on two different systems in the mind.

The first is fast, automatic, and emotional, producing gut reactions about what is acceptable.

The second is slow, effortful, and deliberate, producing reasoned calculations about outcomes.

Greene studied this using the trolley problem, a thought experiment in which a runaway trolley will kill five people unless it is diverted or stopped in a way that kills one.

People generally accept flipping a switch to divert the trolley onto a track where it kills one instead of five, a calculation of outcomes.

Yet most people refuse to push a large stranger off a footbridge to stop the trolley, even though the arithmetic of one death versus five is identical.

Greene's proposal is that the up-close, personal act of pushing someone triggers a strong emotional alarm from the fast system, which vetoes it, while the impersonal switch leaves the slow, calculating system free to favour the greater good.

Brain imaging supported this by showing that the personal version stirs more activity in emotion-related regions, and that people who override the alarm to give the calculating answer take longer and engage more of the brain's deliberate-control machinery.

The account remains debated, and some researchers question whether emotion and reason divide up so neatly, but it reshaped the field by showing that feeling is not a contaminant of moral judgment; it is a central part of how moral judgment is made.


48.1.2 Moral emotions and moral intuition

This sub-section deepens the point that much of morality begins with feeling rather than argument.

Moral emotions are feelings tied to right and wrong, including guilt and shame about one's own conduct, anger or indignation at others' wrongs, disgust at what seems degrading, and elevation or gratitude at moral beauty.

These emotions are not side effects of moral thinking; they often are the moral response, arriving fast and pushing us toward blame or praise before we can explain ourselves.

The psychologist Jonathan Haidt captured this with his social intuitionist model, which argues that moral judgments usually come first, as quick intuitions, and that our reasoning mostly follows afterward to justify what we already felt.

He illustrated it with "moral dumbfounding", the state in which people feel sure that some act is wrong yet cannot produce any reason for it, insisting on the wrongness even after every argument they offer is answered.

The word "intuitionist" here just means the model puts intuition, the fast automatic feeling, in the driver's seat, with conscious reasoning acting more like a press secretary than a judge.

Haidt and Greene broadly agree that emotion and intuition do much of the heavy lifting in moral judgment, though they differ on how much room is left for reasoning to change our minds.

This does not mean morality is merely irrational; it means our moral sense grows from a deep well of social emotions, and reasoning works best as a slower partner that can, with effort, revise the intuitions rather than replace them.


48.2 The self

The self is the mind's model of itself, the answer each of us carries to the question "who am I?".

It is easy to assume the self is a single thing sitting at the centre of the mind, but the science suggests it is more like a construction, assembled and maintained by many processes.

This section looks at how we know ourselves and at how we hold ourselves together across time.


48.2.1 Self-knowledge and self-representation

Self-knowledge is what we know about our own traits, feelings, abilities, and preferences, and self-representation is the mental picture in which that knowledge is stored.

A natural assumption is that we know ourselves directly and infallibly, by simply looking inward, but psychology has found this is only partly true.

Daryl Bem's self-perception theory made the surprising proposal that we often learn our own attitudes and feelings the same way an outside observer would, by watching our own behaviour.

On this view, when our inner signals are weak or unclear, we infer "I must like this, because I keep choosing it", reading ourselves off our actions rather than reading our actions off a clearly felt preference.

This does not mean we are strangers to ourselves, but it does mean self-knowledge is partly inferred and constructed, not simply perceived.

The self-representation we build is also organised and selective, tending to be more positive than the plain facts warrant, a gentle bias that generally supports wellbeing.

The picture that emerges is of a self-model that is genuinely useful and mostly stable, yet assembled from inference and open to error, much like our models of other people.


48.2.2 The self across time and the narrative self

This final sub-section is about what makes you feel like the same person today that you were as a child and will be in old age.

Our bodies and even most of our memories change enormously across a life, so the sense of being one continuous self is a real achievement rather than a given.

A leading answer is the narrative self, the idea that we hold ourselves together by telling an ongoing life story that links our past, present, and imagined future into a single character.

The philosopher Daniel Dennett described the self as a "center of narrative gravity", not a thing you could find in the brain but a useful fiction, the main character of the story the mind keeps telling about itself.

Support for the constructed nature of this narrative comes from studies by Michael Gazzaniga of patients whose two brain hemispheres had been surgically separated.

He found that when one half of the brain acted on information the other half could not see, the speaking half would smoothly invent a plausible reason for the action, confident it was reporting the truth.

Gazzaniga called the mechanism behind this the interpreter, a process in the mind that continually weaves our actions and feelings into a coherent, sensible story, even when it has to make parts of that story up.

None of this means the self is a mere illusion with nothing behind it; it means the unified self is something the mind actively builds and maintains, moment by moment and year by year.

This connects back to the whole chapter, for the same mind that constructs its emotions, reads other minds, and feels its way to moral judgments also constructs, out of all these materials, the ongoing sense of being someone.


================================================================================

PART TWELVE. THE VARIETIES AND ORIGINS OF COGNITION

================================================================================

CHAPTER 49. COGNITIVE DEVELOPMENT (PROCESS)

This chapter is about how a human mind grows from the simple starting point of a newborn into the rich thinking of an adult.

Cognitive development is the study of that growth: how knowing, remembering, reasoning, and understanding change across the early years of life.

It matters because every adult ability the rest of this outline describes had to be built, and watching it being built tells us what the finished machine is really made of.

A newborn cannot talk, plan, or do arithmetic, yet within a few years a child does all three, and the question of how that happens is one of the oldest and deepest in the science of mind.

This chapter walks through the main answers, from the classic stage theories to the modern view of the child as a kind of young scientist.


49.1 The stage and constructivist theories

This section covers the first great theory of how the mind grows, and the theories that grew up to correct it.

The word constructivist here means a view in which the child actively builds their own understanding, rather than simply having knowledge poured in from outside.

The central figure is Jean Piaget, a Swiss thinker whose ideas dominated the field for most of the twentieth century, and whose picture is still the starting point for almost every discussion.


49.1.1 Piaget's stages and the mechanisms of assimilation and accommodation

Jean Piaget, who worked from the 1920s to the 1970s, proposed that children think in ways that are not just simpler than adult thought but different in kind, and that they pass through a fixed series of stages on the way to maturity.

A stage, in his sense, is a whole way of thinking that colours everything the child does at that age, not just a single skill.

Piaget described four main stages.

The first is the sensorimotor stage, from birth to about two years, in which the baby knows the world only through the senses and through actions such as grasping, sucking, and looking.

The second is the preoperational stage, from about two to seven years, in which the child can use words and images but still reasons in a way tied to how things look.

The third is the concrete operational stage, from about seven to eleven years, in which the child can reason logically about real, concrete objects.

The fourth is the formal operational stage, from about twelve years onward, in which the young person can reason about abstract ideas and hypothetical possibilities.

To explain how a child moves through these stages, Piaget used two key ideas.

The first is a scheme, sometimes written schema, which is a mental pattern or rule for dealing with the world, such as a baby's built-in pattern for grasping anything placed in the hand.

Assimilation is the process of fitting a new experience into an existing scheme, the way a baby who knows how to grasp a rattle will also grasp a spoon by treating it as one more graspable thing.

Accommodation is the opposite and complementary process of changing the scheme to fit a new experience that will not fit as it is, the way the baby must adjust the grip for a large ball that cannot be seized like a rattle.

Piaget believed learning is a constant back and forth between these two, driven by a drive he called equilibration, which is the mind's push to resolve the discomfort it feels when the world does not match its expectations.

That felt mismatch he called disequilibrium, and the resolving of it is what moves the child forward.

One of Piaget's most famous demonstrations was conservation, the understanding that a quantity stays the same when its appearance changes but nothing is added or taken away.

In the classic task, a child watches water poured from a short wide glass into a tall thin one, and a preoperational child typically says the tall glass now has more, because it looks like more, while an older child knows the amount is unchanged.

Piaget read this as showing that the younger child's thinking is captured by appearances in a way the older child's is not.


49.1.2 The neo-Piagetian and information-processing accounts

Piaget's picture was hugely influential, but later research showed that some of it was wrong, and this sub-section covers the theories built to keep what was right while fixing what was not.

The word neo-Piagetian simply means the newer theories that came after Piaget and revised him, mostly in the 1970s and 1980s.

The main problem these theories addressed is that Piaget consistently underestimated young children.

His tasks often demanded that a child give a spoken answer or perform a fiddly action, and when researchers used simpler tests, children turned out to understand things such as number and hidden objects far earlier than Piaget had claimed.

Development also looked less like a sudden jump between whole stages and more gradual and uneven, so that a child might grasp conservation of number before conservation of liquid rather than switching over all at once.

The neo-Piagetian theorists kept Piaget's core idea that children build their own understanding, but they explained the changes using the language of information processing, which is the approach that treats the mind like a system that takes in, stores, and works on information, much as a computer does.

A leading example is the work of Juan Pascual-Leone, who proposed that what grows with age is the amount of information a child can hold in mind and juggle at once, a kind of mental workspace.

On this view a five-year-old fails the conservation task not because their whole way of thinking is different, but because the task demands holding more pieces of information at once than their still-small working memory can manage.

Working memory here means the small store that holds the handful of things you are actively thinking about right now.

Other neo-Piagetians such as Robbie Case and Kurt Fischer built detailed accounts in which growing processing capacity, faster mental operations, and practice together explain the orderly march of development.

The lasting lesson is that the broad sequence Piaget saw is real, but its engine is better described as the gradual growth of memory, speed, and control than as the replacement of one whole logic by another.


49.2 Core knowledge and nativism

This section covers a different and more recent tradition that asks what, if anything, a baby knows before experience has had a chance to teach it.

Nativism is the view that some knowledge or ability is built in from birth rather than learned, and it stands opposite to the older idea of the infant mind as a blank slate.

The modern evidence, gathered by carefully watching where babies look and how long they look, suggests that the newborn mind is far from blank.


49.2.1 The core systems of object, agent, number, and space

The core knowledge view, developed above all by the psychologist Elizabeth Spelke and her colleagues from the 1990s onward, holds that human thought is founded on a small set of ancient, built-in systems that are present in early infancy and shared with other animals.

A core system is a specialised bit of mental machinery dedicated to one kind of information, that works automatically and is present long before language.

Researchers usually name four such systems.

The first is a system for objects, which lets even young babies expect that a solid thing moves as a connected whole, does not pass through other solid things, and continues to exist when it goes out of sight.

Babies reveal this by looking longer at an event that violates these expectations, such as one solid object appearing to pass through another, and longer looking is taken to mean the baby found the event surprising.

The second is a system for agents, which lets babies treat some things as goal-directed actors that move on their own and respond to others, and to expect such agents to act efficiently toward their goals.

The third is a system for number, which gives babies a rough, wordless sense of quantity, so that they can tell a small set of items from a clearly larger one without counting.

The fourth is a system for space and geometry, which lets babies and young children find their way using the shape of their surroundings.

Some researchers add a fifth system for social partners, dealing with who belongs to one's own group.

The claim is not that babies are born knowing facts, but that they are born with these narrow, reliable ways of parsing the world that give learning something to build on.


49.2.2 Conceptual change and bootstrapping

If the mind starts with only a few narrow core systems, a hard question follows: how does it ever reach the rich, abstract concepts of an adult, such as the exact counting numbers, that the core systems alone cannot supply.

This sub-section covers the leading answer, developed above all by the psychologist Susan Carey.

Conceptual change means a genuine reorganisation of what a person knows, in which new concepts appear that could not simply be assembled from the old ones, rather than just more facts being added.

Carey argued that human development includes several such deep reorganisations, so that a child's early theory of the world is sometimes replaced, not merely extended, much as science itself sometimes overturns an old picture.

Her key mechanism is bootstrapping, named for the image of pulling oneself up by one's own bootstraps, which is the idea that a learner can use structures they already have, together with a system of external symbols such as the count words, to build a genuinely new concept that goes beyond the starting materials.

The favourite example is learning to count.

Carey proposed that a child first learns the count words as a meaningless ordered list, like a rhyme, then slowly maps the first few words onto their built-in sense of small quantities, and finally makes a leap to grasp the rule that each next word means exactly one more, which is a concept neither core system contained on its own.

Spelke and others agree that language, by letting the child combine the outputs of separate core systems, plays a central role in creating these new concepts.

There is real and ongoing debate here: some theorists see the counting concept as truly new, built by bootstrapping, while others argue it was latent in the child's innate resources all along, and the field has not fully settled the question.


49.3 The child as scientist

This section covers a modern framework that captures how children learn about the causal structure of the world, the hidden ways in which one thing makes another happen.

The guiding image is that a young child behaves rather like a scientist, forming ideas about how things work, running little experiments through play, and revising those ideas in light of the evidence.

The framework brings together developmental psychology with the mathematics of probability, and its leading figure is the psychologist Alison Gopnik.
