49.3.1 Children's causal learning

Causal learning means figuring out what causes what, for example that flipping a switch is what makes a light come on rather than the two events just happening together by chance.

Research from the 1990s onward showed that even toddlers are surprisingly good at this, and do not simply notice that two things occur together but work out the underlying cause.

In a well-known style of study, children watch which objects, when placed on a special machine, make it light up and play music, and they use the pattern of what happens to infer which object is the true cause, even distinguishing a real cause from a mere coincidence.

Children learn causes in several ways: by watching how events line up over time, by acting on the world themselves and seeing what changes, and by observing and imitating what other people do.

Their spontaneous play turns out to be full of informal experiments, and children tend to explore an object more when its workings are surprising or unclear, exactly as someone gathering evidence would.

These findings have been demonstrated in children from around sixteen months to four years of age.


49.3.2 Rational constructivism and development as inference

Rational constructivism is the name Gopnik and colleagues gave to their overall theory, and this sub-section explains it.

The word rational here signals that the child's learning follows the sound logic of probability, and constructivism, as before, signals that the child actively builds their own understanding.

The framework uses Bayesian inference, which is the mathematically correct way to update your beliefs when new evidence arrives, weighing how likely the evidence would be under each of the possibilities you are considering.

The claim is that a child faced with the buzzing confusion of experience behaves, in effect, as a good Bayesian: they start with some hypotheses about how the world works, see how well the incoming evidence fits each one, and shift their confidence toward the hypotheses the evidence favours.

Over time this process lets the child build abstract models of the causal structure of the world out of the concrete particulars of what they see and do.

This view is sometimes called the theory theory, the somewhat awkward name for the idea that children hold something like informal scientific theories and revise them as a scientist revises a theory.

Rational constructivism is attractive because it is at once constructivist, in Piaget's spirit, and mathematically precise, and because the same Bayesian tools describe adult learning, tying development to the rest of cognitive science.

It is not without critics, who question whether children really carry out anything like the heavy computation the models assume, but it is one of the most active and productive frameworks in the field today.


49.4 The development of the particular faculties

The earlier sections looked at development in general, but each specific mental faculty also has its own developmental story, and this section samples two of the most important.

The point is that the growth of the mind is not one single process but many overlapping ones, each with its own timetable.

The two chosen here, control of attention and understanding of other minds, are chosen because they are pillars on which much later thinking rests.


49.4.1 The development of attention and executive control

This sub-section is about how children gain command over their own minds, the ability to hold a goal, resist distraction, and switch flexibly between tasks.

Executive control, also called executive function, is the umbrella term for these self-directing abilities, the mental manager that keeps behaviour aimed at a goal.

Researchers commonly split it into three related parts.

Inhibition is the ability to stop an automatic or tempting response, such as not blurting out an answer or not grabbing a treat.

Working memory, met earlier, is the holding and updating of goal-relevant information in mind.

Shifting, also called cognitive flexibility, is the ability to switch between tasks or rules rather than getting stuck on one.

These abilities begin to appear in infancy and grow most dramatically during the preschool years, from about three to five, which is why a two-year-old struggles mightily to wait while a five-year-old manages far better.

A classic demonstration is a card-sorting game in which young children are asked first to sort cards by colour and then by shape: three-year-olds typically keep sorting by the old rule even when told the new one, while by around age five children switch smoothly, revealing the growth of shifting.

Attention and executive control are closely linked, because holding attention on what matters and away from distraction is much of what the executive does, though careful studies show the two are related yet not identical.

This development continues well beyond childhood, with the executive abilities reaching their peak only in early adulthood, which is part of why teenagers can reason well yet still act impulsively.


49.4.2 The development of theory of mind

This sub-section is about how children come to understand that other people have minds of their own, with beliefs, wishes, and views that may differ from the child's own and from reality.

Theory of mind is the everyday but remarkable ability to attribute mental states to others and to use them to explain and predict what people do.

The most famous test is the false-belief task, which checks whether a child understands that someone can hold a belief that is false.

In one version a child watches a puppet put a marble in a basket and leave, then sees the marble moved to a box while the puppet is away, and is asked where the puppet will look for it on returning.

To pass, the child must say the basket, the place the puppet still wrongly believes the marble to be, rather than the box where it truly is.

Most children begin to pass this test between about three and five years of age, with a fairly reliable shift around age four.

Development follows an orderly sequence: children first grasp that people can want different things, then that people can know or not know things, and only later that people can hold beliefs that are outright false.

There is an important and unresolved wrinkle, however, for some studies using looking-time measures suggest that infants as young as fifteen months already show a hint of sensitivity to others' false beliefs, long before they can pass the spoken test.

Whether this early sensitivity is genuine understanding or something simpler is debated, and the honest position is that the timing of when true theory of mind arrives is still contested.

Later in childhood the ability deepens into second-order reasoning, thinking about what one person believes about another person's beliefs, which underlies the understanding of complex social situations.


CHAPTER 50. INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES, INTELLIGENCE, AND AGING (CONTEXT)

This chapter is about the ways in which minds differ from one another, and how a single mind changes across the span of an adult life.

Everywhere else this outline describes cognition as if all minds were the same, but of course they are not: some people reason faster, remember more, or learn more easily than others.

The study of these differences, and especially of what we call intelligence, is one of the oldest and most controversial parts of the field, and this chapter treats it plainly.

It also covers what happens to thinking as we grow old, which is a question every reader has a personal stake in.


50.1 The structure of intelligence

This section asks a basic question: when we say one person is more intelligent than another, is there one thing we are measuring, or many.

The answer that emerged over a century of research is subtle: there seems to be both a single broad factor and many separate abilities, layered together.

This section lays out the layered picture that most researchers now accept.


50.1.1 General intelligence and the positive manifold

The starting fact that every theory of intelligence must explain is called the positive manifold, and this sub-section explains it.

The positive manifold is the well-established observation that people who do well on almost any one mental test tend also to do well on almost any other, whether the tests involve words, numbers, shapes, or memory.

The word manifold here just means the whole web of positive relationships among the tests.

The British psychologist Charles Spearman first noticed this pattern in 1904 and proposed that it points to a single underlying general ability, which he labelled g, short for general intelligence.

General intelligence, or g, is the idea of one broad mental power that contributes to performance on every kind of cognitive task, so that having more of it helps with everything at once.

It is important to be careful here: g is a statistical summary of the fact that abilities go together, and saying it exists does not by itself tell us what in the brain or mind produces it, which remains an open question.

Still, g is one of the most reliable and replicable findings in all of psychology, and it predicts real outcomes such as school and job performance to a modest but genuine degree.


50.1.2 Fluid and crystallised intelligence and the Cattell-Horn-Carroll synthesis

While g captures what all mental abilities share, researchers also found that intelligence is not entirely uniform, and this sub-section covers the most important division within it.

The psychologists Raymond Cattell and his student John Horn, working from the 1940s through the 1960s, argued that general intelligence splits into two broad kinds.

Fluid intelligence, written Gf, is the ability to reason, solve novel problems, and see patterns in unfamiliar material, without relying on stored knowledge, the kind of raw thinking you use on a puzzle you have never seen.

Crystallised intelligence, written Gc, is the store of knowledge, facts, and skills you have built up over a lifetime, such as vocabulary and general information.

The two behave very differently across life: fluid intelligence tends to peak in early adulthood and slowly decline, while crystallised intelligence keeps growing well into middle age and beyond, which is why an older person may reason a little slower yet know far more.

Decades later this Cattell and Horn picture was merged with the work of John Carroll, who in 1993 analysed hundreds of data sets and mapped out the abilities in careful detail.

The merger, credited largely to the psychologist Kevin McGrew in the 1990s, is called Cattell-Horn-Carroll theory, or CHC theory, and it is now the most widely accepted account of the structure of human abilities and the basis of most modern intelligence tests.


50.1.3 The three-stratum model and its rivals

This sub-section covers the shape that the CHC picture takes, and the main disagreement inside it.

A stratum here means a layer, and the model is called three-stratum because it arranges abilities into three layers of a pyramid.

At the top, the third stratum, sits general intelligence g, the single broad factor.

In the middle, the second stratum, sit about ten broad abilities, including fluid reasoning, comprehension and knowledge, visual processing, working memory, and processing speed, which is simply how quickly a person can carry out basic mental operations.

At the base, the first stratum, sit more than seventy narrow, specific abilities, such as vocabulary knowledge or memory span, each feeding into the broad ability above it.

The chief disagreement among the theory's founders was about the very top layer.

Carroll placed g firmly at the apex, holding that a single overarching ability is real, while Cattell and Horn doubted this and preferred to see the broad abilities, especially fluid and crystallised intelligence, as the highest real level, with no single g above them.

This is not a settled matter, and some current researchers argue that treating g as a real thing rather than a statistical convenience overstates what the data show, which leads directly to the rival accounts in the next section.


50.2 The mechanisms behind the differences

The previous section described the pattern of intelligence differences, but a description is not an explanation, and this section asks what actually produces those differences.

The question is what, in the workings of the mind, makes one person score higher than another, and why the abilities hang together in a positive manifold at all.

Two broad kinds of answer are covered, one pointing to a specific bottleneck ability and one denying that any single thing is responsible.


50.2.1 Working memory, attention control, and their link to fluid intelligence

This sub-section covers the influential idea that the engine behind fluid intelligence is the control of attention and working memory.

Recall that working memory is the small store holding what you are actively thinking about, and that attention control is the ability to keep the mind focused on what matters and away from distraction.

Beginning in the 1990s, researchers such as Randall Engle and colleagues found that how much a person can hold and manage in working memory correlates strongly with their fluid intelligence, the ability to reason about novel problems.

Their proposal is that the crucial ingredient is not raw storage but executive attention, the ability to keep goal-relevant information active and shielded from interference, especially when distractions push against it.

On this view, the reason some people reason better is partly that they can hold the pieces of a problem steady in mind while working on it, without losing the thread.

The link between working memory and fluid intelligence is one of the most robust findings in this area, though researchers debate exactly which part of working memory, storage or attention or speed, is doing the most work.


50.2.2 The process-overlap and mutualism accounts of the positive manifold

This sub-section covers two modern theories that try to explain the positive manifold without assuming a single real g sitting behind everything.

Both start from unease with the idea that g is a genuine mental power rather than a statistical shadow, and both offer a way for abilities to correlate without a common cause.

The process-overlap theory, developed by Kristof Kovacs and Andrew Conway around 2016, proposes that any given mental task calls on several different processes at once, and that certain domain-general processes, especially those of executive attention, are tapped by nearly every task.

Because these shared processes are involved everywhere, tests come out correlated, producing the positive manifold, without there needing to be a single underlying substance called g; the overlap of many processes, not one thing, creates the appearance of one thing.

The mutualism theory, proposed by Han van der Maas and colleagues in 2006, offers a different route.

It suggests that the separate abilities start out largely independent in early childhood but help one another grow over time, so that being good at reading helps you learn, which helps your vocabulary, which helps your reasoning, and so on.

Through these mutually beneficial interactions during development, the abilities become positively correlated even though there was no common g to begin with.

Both accounts remain live options, and together with the traditional g view they show that a finding as solid as the positive manifold can still be explained in strikingly different ways.


50.3 Biology and change

This section turns to where intelligence differences come from in the deeper sense of nature and nurture, and to how cognition changes as a person ages.

These are questions loaded with strong feelings and a long history of misuse, so they call for special care and plain honesty about what is and is not known.

The section covers the roles of genes and environment, a puzzling rise in test scores over the generations, and the changes that come with old age.


50.3.1 Heritability, the gene-environment interplay, and the Flynn effect

This sub-section covers how much of the difference in intelligence between people traces to their genes, how genes and environment work together, and a famous historical trend.

Heritability is a technical term that is very easy to misread, so it must be defined carefully.

Heritability is the proportion of the differences among people in a particular group and setting that can be statistically traced to genetic differences among them; it is a statement about variation in a population, not about how much of any one person's intelligence is fixed by their genes.

For intelligence, estimates of heritability commonly range from about 30 percent to about 75 percent, and a striking finding is that heritability rises with age, from roughly 20 percent in early childhood to perhaps 60 to 80 percent in adulthood.

That rise seems strange until you learn about gene-environment correlation, the tendency for people to seek out and create environments that suit their genetic leanings, so that a child inclined toward reading finds more books and reads more, amplifying the original small difference over time.

This means genes and environment are not two separate forces to be added up but are woven together throughout development.

The Flynn effect, named for the researcher James Flynn who documented it, is the observation that raw scores on intelligence tests rose steadily across the twentieth century in many countries, by roughly three points per decade.

Because this rise happened far too fast to be caused by changes in genes, it must be environmental, reflecting things such as better nutrition, more schooling, and more cognitively demanding daily life.

The Flynn effect is a powerful reminder that high heritability within a generation does not mean intelligence is fixed, since the whole population's scores can shift a great deal in a single lifetime; in some places the rise has recently stalled or reversed, and that too appears to be environmental.


50.3.2 Cognitive aging: processing speed, inhibition, and reserve

This sub-section covers what happens to thinking in the second half of life, which is a mix of real decline and real preservation.

The most consistent finding is that fluid abilities decline with age while crystallised abilities are largely preserved, so an older adult typically reasons and processes new information more slowly but retains, and even keeps adding to, their store of knowledge and vocabulary.

A leading explanation, associated with the psychologist Timothy Salthouse, points to processing speed: as we age the basic speed of mental operations slows, and because so many tasks depend on doing several steps quickly before information is lost, a general slowing drags down performance across the board.

A second proposed factor is a weakening of inhibition, the ability to keep irrelevant thoughts and distractions out of mind, so that older adults may be more easily sidetracked by interfering information.

Not everyone declines at the same rate, and this is where the idea of reserve comes in.

Cognitive reserve is the notion that a lifetime of education, mentally demanding work, and engagement builds up a buffer that lets some people sustain more brain change before it shows as a loss of function, rather like a stronger engine coping with more wear before it stumbles.

Reserve helps explain why two people with similar brain aging can differ greatly in how sharp they remain, and it offers a hopeful message, since the activities that build reserve are partly within a person's control.

It is worth stating plainly that normal aging is not the same as dementia, which is a disease process, and that much of the mind's most valuable capacity, its accumulated knowledge and judgment, holds up well into late life.


CHAPTER 51. COMPARATIVE AND EVOLUTIONARY COGNITION (CONTEXT)

This chapter widens the lens from the human mind to minds in general, asking what other animals can think and why human thinking took the shape it did.

Comparative cognition studies the mental abilities of non-human animals and compares them across species, while evolutionary cognition asks how and why the human mind was shaped by natural selection.

The two together give perspective: they show which of our abilities are shared with our animal relatives and which, if any, are truly special, and they remind us that the mind is a biological organ with a history.

This matters for a project like konnectome because understanding what is general to minds and what is particular to ours helps set the target for a humanlike machine.


51.1 Comparative cognition

This section is about the minds of other animals, studied carefully and without either flattering or dismissing them.

The great challenge of the field is that animals cannot tell us what they think, so everything must be inferred from behaviour, which makes it easy to read in too much or too little.

This section samples what animals can do and then covers the rule of caution that keeps the inferences honest.


51.1.1 Learning, number, and space across species

This sub-section surveys some of the impressive cognitive abilities found across the animal kingdom.

The lesson of a century of research is that many capacities once thought uniquely human turn out, in simpler forms, to be widespread.

Many animals show a rough sense of number, an ability to tell more from less without counting in words, which has been demonstrated in creatures as different as monkeys, birds, fish, and even some insects.

This wordless number sense closely resembles the core number system found in human infants, suggesting a deep and ancient shared ability.

Animals also navigate space with great skill, and some, such as certain birds that store thousands of seeds and later recover them, have spatial memories that put humans to shame.

Learning itself, in the forms of forming associations and adjusting behaviour by its consequences, is universal across animals with nervous systems and is the foundation on which the more elaborate abilities are built.

Some species show remarkable feats: certain crows and other corvids make and use tools and solve multi-step puzzles, and great apes can learn to use symbols to communicate to a limited degree.

The overall picture is of a continuum, with human abilities often being sharper or more general versions of capacities that exist, in seed form, across many species.


51.1.2 Animal theory of mind and metacognition

This sub-section covers two of the most contested questions in the field: whether animals understand other minds, and whether they can reflect on their own knowledge.

Theory of mind, as in the human chapter, means understanding that others have mental states such as beliefs and intentions.

Whether any animal has it is fiercely debated: chimpanzees clearly track what others can see and know, and act on it, but whether they grasp that another can hold a false belief, the human benchmark, remains uncertain, with some recent studies offering suggestive but not decisive evidence.

Metacognition means thinking about one's own thinking, and in animals the question is usually whether an animal can sense its own uncertainty, whether it knows when it does not know.

In clever studies, animals such as monkeys and dolphins are given a hard perception task plus the option to decline a trial for a smaller but sure reward, and some animals decline more often exactly on the hardest trials, as if aware they are unsure.

This looks like metacognition, but there is a serious alternative reading, since a simple learned association between hard stimuli and the escape response could produce the same behaviour without any real self-awareness.

The debate is genuinely unsettled, and careful researchers hold that the behaviour is real and interesting while the interpretation remains open, which is exactly the kind of caution the next sub-section is about.


51.1.3 Morgan's canon and the control of anthropomorphism

This sub-section covers the guiding rule of caution that has shaped the whole field, and its limits.

Anthropomorphism is the tendency to project human thoughts and feelings onto animals, seeing a guilty conscience in a dog or a grudge in a cat where simpler explanations may do.

To guard against this, the British psychologist Conwy Lloyd Morgan proposed in 1894 a principle now called Morgan's canon, which says we should not explain an animal's behaviour as the product of a higher mental power if it can be explained by a lower and simpler one.

In practice this makes the simpler explanation the default, and puts the burden of proof on anyone claiming a richer mental ability, which has kept the field disciplined for over a century.

But the canon has its own critics, who warn that it can be pushed too far and load the deck against animal minds.

One such worry has been named anthropofabulation, the mistake of setting the bar for crediting an animal with some ability at an inflated picture of how well humans do that same thing, so that animals are denied an ability that, measured fairly, they actually share with us.

The mature position is to use Morgan's canon as a check against wishful thinking while remembering that the simplest explanation is not automatically the correct one, and that being unfairly stingy is as much an error as being unfairly generous.


51.2 Evolutionary cognition

This section asks why the human mind has the particular shape it does, by looking at the evolutionary pressures that built it.

The core idea is that the mind, like the body, is a product of natural selection, and that its features are there because they helped our ancestors survive and reproduce.

The section covers the claim that the mind is a bundle of special-purpose tools, the idea that its growth was driven by social life, and the notion of a distinctively human way of making a living.


51.2.1 The adapted mind and domain-specific mechanisms

This sub-section covers the central proposal of evolutionary psychology, associated with Leda Cosmides, John Tooby, and the 1992 book The Adapted Mind.

The main claim is that the mind is not a single general-purpose problem solver but a large collection of specialised mechanisms, each shaped by evolution to solve a particular problem our ancestors repeatedly faced.

A domain-specific mechanism is a piece of mental machinery dedicated to one kind of problem, such as choosing a mate, avoiding spoiled food, detecting cheaters in an exchange, or reading facial expressions.

The argument for this view is that narrow, specialised problems are usually easier to solve well than broad general ones, so evolution would favour many dedicated tools over one all-purpose one, much as a kitchen holds many specialised utensils rather than one universal gadget.

On this picture the mind resembles a Swiss Army knife or a set of many small computers, each tuned to its own ancestral task, rather than a single blank general processor.

This framework is influential but also criticised, with opponents arguing that it can overstate how modular and how fixed the mind really is, and that much human ability seems flexible and general rather than carved into fixed special purposes.

The honest summary is that some degree of specialisation is widely accepted, while the claim that the mind is mostly a bundle of narrow innate modules remains contested.


51.2.2 The social-brain hypothesis

This sub-section covers a leading explanation for why humans and their relatives evolved such large and powerful brains.

The social-brain hypothesis, associated especially with the anthropologist Robin Dunbar in the 1990s, proposes that the main driver of big brains was not the physical world but the social one.

The idea is that living in large, stable groups full of shifting alliances, rivalries, and relationships is cognitively demanding, and that keeping track of who is friends with whom, who owes whom, and who can be trusted required ever more brainpower.

In support, Dunbar found that across primate species the size of the social group an animal lives in tends to track the relative size of its neocortex, the outer, thinking part of the brain.

Extending this to humans yields the well-known estimate, sometimes called Dunbar's number, of roughly 150 as the number of stable relationships a person can comfortably maintain, though this figure is a rough average and is itself debated.

The broader claim, that the challenges of social life were a major engine of human intelligence, is widely taken seriously, even as researchers argue over how much of the story it explains.


51.2.3 The cognitive niche

This sub-section covers a complementary idea about what makes the human way of life distinctive.

A niche, in biology, is the particular way a species makes its living, the set of resources and strategies it depends on.

The cognitive niche, a term from John Tooby and Irven DeVore, is the proposal that humans survive above all by reasoning, planning, and knowledge, using intelligence to outwit problems that other animals meet with fixed instincts or physical adaptations.

Rather than growing thicker fur or sharper claws, humans work out how to make clothing and weapons, and rather than each generation starting from scratch, they pass hard-won knowledge to the next through language.

A closely related idea, sometimes called the cultural niche, stresses that no single human is smart enough to invent all this alone, and that our real advantage is the ability to learn from one another and accumulate know-how over generations, which links directly to the theme of the next chapter.

Together these ideas say that the human specialisation is flexible intelligence married to social learning, a combination that let one species spread into nearly every environment on Earth.


CHAPTER 52. CULTURAL, SITUATED, AND DISTRIBUTED COGNITION (CONTEXT)

This chapter makes a point that is easy to miss when we study the mind one skull at a time: much of human thinking happens between people and out in the world, not just inside a single head.

Cultural cognition studies how the accumulated knowledge of a group shapes and empowers each individual mind; situated and distributed cognition study how thinking is spread across people, tools, and surroundings.

This matters because the single greatest fact about human intelligence may be that it is collective and cumulative, that we are smart largely because we stand on the shoulders of everyone who came before.

A machine meant to think like a human, then, cannot be understood purely as a solitary reasoner, and that is why this chapter closes the survey of human cognition before the outline turns to architectures and machines.


52.1 Cultural cognition

This section is about the role of culture, the shared body of knowledge, skills, and practices that a group passes down, in making human minds what they are.

The key insight is that humans are set apart less by individual cleverness than by an extraordinary ability to learn from each other and to build on what others have worked out.

This section covers how such shared knowledge accumulates, how it is transmitted, and how culture and biology have shaped each other.


52.1.1 Cumulative culture and the ratchet effect

This sub-section covers what may be the single most important feature of human culture: it accumulates.

Cumulative culture means that human knowledge and technology are not reinvented each generation but are built up over time, each generation inheriting what the last achieved and adding a little more.

The psychologist Michael Tomasello captured this with the image of the ratchet effect, named for the mechanical ratchet that turns one way and then locks, preventing any slipping back.

The ratchet effect is the idea that a useful improvement, once made, is faithfully preserved and passed on, so that gains are locked in and later improvements build on top of them rather than the whole thing sliding back to the start.

Because of this ratchet, human tools and ideas have grown to a sophistication that no single person could ever reach alone, from stone flakes to spacecraft, over countless small steps by many hands.

Other animals show culture in a weak sense, such as local traditions in how to crack nuts, but their traditions rarely ratchet upward in complexity the way human culture does, and explaining that difference is a central goal of the field.


52.1.2 Social learning, imitation, and natural pedagogy

This sub-section covers the mechanisms that make the ratchet possible, the ways humans transmit knowledge faithfully from one person to another.

Social learning simply means learning from others rather than by one's own trial and error, and it comes in weaker and stronger forms.

A weaker form is emulation, in which an animal sees the result another achieved and tries to reach the same result its own way, without copying the exact method.

A stronger form is imitation, in which the learner copies the actual actions the other performed, method and all, which is what allows a technique to be reproduced faithfully even when the learner does not understand why each step works.

Tomasello argued that this high-fidelity imitation, combined with active teaching and a human urge to conform, is what lets improvements be preserved without slipping, powering the ratchet.

Human children are in fact famously prone to overimitation, copying even the obviously unnecessary steps in a demonstration, which looks wasteful but may be a price worth paying for reliably absorbing techniques whose logic is not visible.

Researchers Gergely Csibra and Gyorgy Gergely added the idea of natural pedagogy, the proposal that humans come equipped both to teach and to learn from teaching, with built-in signals such as eye contact, being addressed by name, and a special tone of voice that mark information as important and meant to be generalised and remembered.

Together these mechanisms make humans uniquely good at passing knowledge down the generations intact.


52.1.3 Gene-culture coevolution

This sub-section covers the deep idea that human genes and human culture have shaped each other over evolutionary time, each pulling on the other.

Gene-culture coevolution is the view that culture is not merely a product of our biology but has itself become a force of natural selection acting back on our genes.

The classic example is the ability of many adults to digest milk.

Once some human groups took up dairy farming, a cultural practice, it became advantageous to keep producing the enzyme that digests milk sugar into adulthood, and so genes for that ability spread in exactly those populations, a clear case of a cultural invention reshaping the gene pool.

More broadly, once our ancestors came to depend on learning from one another, there was selective pressure favouring minds good at social learning, teaching, and cooperation, so the very features that make culture possible were themselves sharpened by the presence of culture.

This creates a feedback loop in which biology enables culture and culture in turn reshapes biology, and many researchers see this loop as central to how humans became so different from other animals.


52.2 Sociocultural theory

This section covers an older and highly influential tradition, rooted in the work of one Russian psychologist, that placed social interaction at the very centre of how the mind develops.

Where earlier chapters treated development as something happening inside the individual child, this tradition insists that the child's mind is built through interaction with other people and with the tools of their culture.

The section covers the two ideas from this tradition that have had the widest reach.


52.2.1 The zone of proximal development and mediation

This sub-section covers the best-known idea of the psychologist Lev Vygotsky, who worked in the Soviet Union in the 1920s and 1930s and whose writings became widely influential decades later.

The zone of proximal development is the gap between what a learner can do alone and what the same learner can do with help from a more capable person.

The point is that the most important learning happens in this zone, on tasks a child cannot yet manage by themselves but can accomplish with the guidance of a parent, teacher, or more skilled peer.

A related practical idea, developed by later researchers from Vygotsky's work, is scaffolding, the support a helper provides that is gradually withdrawn as the learner grows able to stand on their own, just as a builder's scaffold is removed once the wall can support itself.

Underlying all this is Vygotsky's concept of mediation, the claim that human thinking is almost always carried out through cultural tools, above all language, that stand between the mind and the world and reshape how we think.

On this view we do not confront the world with a bare mind but always through inherited instruments of thought, which is why learning is so bound up with the culture that supplies those instruments.


52.2.2 Internalisation and private speech

This sub-section covers Vygotsky's account of how something that starts as social interaction becomes part of the individual mind.

Internalisation is the process by which a child takes an activity first carried out with other people and gradually turns it into an inner, private mental process of their own.

Vygotsky's striking claim was that many higher mental functions appear first between people, on the social plane, and only later within the single child, on the psychological plane.

His favourite illustration is private speech, the out-loud self-talk that young children so often produce while playing or solving problems, narrating their own actions to themselves.

Vygotsky argued that this private speech begins as ordinary social speech with a caregiver, is then turned by the child upon themselves to guide their own behaviour, and finally goes underground to become silent inner speech, the wordless verbal thinking that adults use to direct themselves.

In this picture the quiet voice in your head that talks you through a hard task is the grown-up descendant of a conversation you once had out loud with someone else, a social process that moved inside.

This idea, that self-control and reasoning have social roots, remains one of the most influential in developmental psychology.


52.3 Situated and distributed cognition

This section covers a family of modern views holding that thinking cannot be fully understood as something sealed inside the individual head, because it reaches out into the body, the tools, and the social setting.

Where the cultural theories stressed what we inherit from others, these views stress how thinking is spread out, in the moment, across people and the physical world around them.

The section covers the situated view, the distributed view, and the intelligence of groups.


52.3.1 Situated action and situated learning

This sub-section covers the idea that thought and action are always shaped by the concrete situation in which they occur, and cannot be well described as the mere execution of abstract plans in the head.

Situated action, a term associated with the researcher Lucy Suchman in the 1980s, is the view that what people actually do arises moment to moment from their ongoing engagement with a specific setting, rather than from a complete plan worked out in advance.

A plan, on this view, is more like a rough resource or guide for action than a script that dictates each step, because the real situation always throws up particulars that must be handled on the spot.

Situated learning, developed by Jean Lave and Etienne Wenger around 1991, applies the same insight to how people learn.

Their claim is that knowledge is not an abstract thing stored in the head and then applied, but is bound up with the real activities and social settings in which it is used, so that learning a trade is best understood as gradually joining a community of people who practise it.

They introduced the idea of legitimate peripheral participation, the way a newcomer starts at the edge of a working community doing small real tasks and moves inward toward full membership as they gain skill, as an apprentice becomes a master.

The broad message is that to understand thinking we must look at people acting in real settings, not only at minds in isolation.


52.3.2 Cognition in the wild and the distribution of thought across people and tools

This sub-section covers the strong claim that a single act of thinking can be spread across several people and their instruments, so that the thinking unit is larger than one brain.

The anthropologist Edwin Hutchins made this case in his 1995 book Cognition in the Wild, based on close study of how a large naval ship is navigated.

Distributed cognition is the view that a cognitive process can be carried by a system made up of several people together with their tools and representations, no one of whom holds the whole process in their own head.

Hutchins showed that navigating the ship is accomplished by a team in which each person handles one part, information passes between them and through instruments, charts, and written records, and the successful navigation is a property of the whole system rather than of any single mind.

The tools themselves, such as the chart and the compass, carry part of the cognitive load, storing and transforming information that would otherwise have to be held in a head.

The phrase in the wild signals the study of thinking as it really happens in the messy world of work, rather than in the tidy isolation of the laboratory.

This view reframes many everyday achievements, from flying an airliner to running a hospital, as feats of distributed rather than individual cognition, and it suggests that designing good tools and good teamwork is a way of designing intelligence itself.


52.3.3 Collective intelligence

This sub-section covers the question of whether groups, as groups, can be more or less intelligent, in a way that parallels individual intelligence.

Collective intelligence refers to the ability of a group to perform well across a wide range of tasks, considered as a property of the group rather than of any single member.

In an influential 2010 study, the researcher Anita Williams Woolley and colleagues found that groups show a measurable general ability factor, sometimes called a c factor, so that a team that does well on one kind of task tends to do well on others, much as an individual's g predicts across tasks.

Strikingly, this collective ability was not well predicted by the average intelligence of the members or by the smartest member.

Instead it was linked to how the group interacted: to members taking turns rather than a few dominating, to the social sensitivity of the members in reading one another, and, in that study, to the proportion of women in the group, which the authors traced largely to higher average social sensitivity.

The finding suggests that making a group smart is partly a separate problem from making an individual smart, and that how people communicate and share the floor can matter more than raw individual horsepower.

Like much in this young area the results continue to be tested and refined, but the core idea, that intelligence can be a feature of a collective, fits naturally with the distributed view of mind and closes this survey of human cognition on the theme with which it is most concerned: that human thought is, at bottom, a shared and cumulative achievement.

PART THIRTEEN. THE COMPUTATIONAL FRAMEWORKS OF MIND

================================================================================

CHAPTER 53. RATIONAL ANALYSIS AND THE BAYESIAN BRAIN (FRAMEWORK)

This chapter is about a big and hopeful idea: that a great deal of what the mind does can be understood as trying to do the smartest possible thing given the situation it is in.

Instead of starting with the wiring of the brain, this way of thinking starts with the problem the mind is trying to solve, and asks what the best solution to that problem would look like.

The word "framework" in the chapter title means a way of thinking and a set of mathematical tools, rather than a single fact or a single experiment.

The particular tools here come from probability, which is the branch of mathematics that deals with uncertainty, with how strongly we should believe things when we cannot be sure.

By the end of the chapter you should understand what "rational analysis" is, what people mean when they call the brain "Bayesian," and why many researchers find this one of the most powerful lenses we have on thinking, while others remain skeptical.


53.1 Rational analysis

Rational analysis is a recipe for building theories of the mind by asking what a well-designed mind ought to do, and then checking whether real people do that.

The key move is to look outward at the world before looking inward at the head, because a mind that works well is a mind that fits the world it lives in.


53.1.1 The rational-analysis method and the role of the environment

Rational analysis is a method introduced by the psychologist John Anderson around 1990, in a book called The Adaptive Character of Thought.

The core claim is simple to state: the mind is adaptive, meaning it has been shaped by evolution and by learning to do a good job in the environment it actually faces.

So if you want to understand why the mind behaves a certain way, you should first understand the problem the environment sets, and then work out what the best behaviour would be.

Anderson laid this out as a series of steps, which are worth walking through slowly because they are the heart of the whole approach.

First, you state precisely what the mind is trying to achieve, that is, its goal.

Second, you build a careful, formal description of the environment, meaning the structure of the world the mind is adapted to, including which events are common and which are rare.

Third, you make only the smallest necessary assumptions about the mind's internal limits, such as limits on speed or memory, so that the environment does most of the explaining.

Fourth, you work out mathematically what the best possible behaviour would be, given the goal, the environment, and those minimal limits.

Fifth, you compare that ideal behaviour against what real people actually do in experiments.

Sixth, if the prediction is wrong, you go back and revise your description of the goal or the environment, and try again.

The word "optimal" appears a lot in this area, and it simply means the best possible given the circumstances, not perfect in some absolute sense.

A helpful way to see the role of the environment is an example about memory that Anderson made famous.

Your memory seems to make some things easy to recall and other things hard, and at first this can look like a flaw.

But Anderson pointed out that the things you have encountered recently, or encountered often, are exactly the things you are statistically most likely to need again soon.

So a memory system that makes recent and frequent items easiest to retrieve is not being lazy; it is betting sensibly on the future based on the pattern of the past.

The environment, in this example, is the statistics of when information tends to be needed, and the mind's behaviour turns out to match those statistics remarkably well.

This is the signature of rational analysis: a puzzling quirk of the mind becomes sensible once you look at the shape of the world the mind is solving for.

It is worth being honest about a limitation that critics have raised.

Because the method lets you revise your description of the environment when a prediction fails, a determined theorist can sometimes make almost any behaviour look "rational" after the fact, which weakens the claim.

The best practitioners guard against this by fixing the environment description in advance using independent data about the world, rather than tuning it to fit the very behaviour they are trying to explain.


53.1.2 Rational models of memory, categorisation, and inference

Anderson did not leave rational analysis as an abstract slogan; he applied it in detail to several specific mental abilities, and this sub-section walks through them.

The first is memory, which we have just met.

The rational model of memory treats remembering as a prediction problem: at each moment the mind estimates the probability that a given piece of information will be needed, and it prioritises retrieval accordingly.

This single idea reproduces several well-known laws of memory, such as the fact that items seen more recently and more frequently are recalled better, because those really are the items most likely to be relevant, given how information tends to recur in everyday life.

The second application is categorisation, which is the mental act of sorting things into kinds, such as deciding that a new animal is a dog.

The rational model of categorisation treats this as guessing which hidden category best explains the thing in front of you, and using that guess to predict the thing's other, unseen properties.

Rather than storing one fixed definition of "dog," the model builds up clusters from experience and asks which cluster a new item most probably belongs to, which nicely handles the fact that real categories have fuzzy, graded membership.

The third application is causal inference, which is working out what causes what, for example learning that a certain plant makes you ill.

The rational model treats this as estimating, from your history of observations, how strongly one thing raises or lowers the probability of another.

Across all three cases the pattern is identical: take a mental ability, describe the statistical problem the world poses, and show that human behaviour looks like a good statistical solution to that problem.

The lasting influence of this work is that it made "what is the mind optimally solving for" a respectable and productive question, and it fed directly into the broader Bayesian programme that the rest of this chapter describes.


53.2 The Bayesian programme

The Bayesian programme is the larger research movement that grew up around the idea that the mind is, at heart, an engine for reasoning under uncertainty.

Its name comes from Bayes' theorem, a rule from probability theory, and this section explains what that rule is and how it has been used to model thinking.


53.2.1 Bayes as a computational-level theory of induction

To understand this sub-section we first need the word "induction."

Induction means reasoning from limited evidence to a general conclusion, such as seeing a few white swans and forming a belief about swans in general.

Induction is hard because the evidence never fully pins down the answer, so you can only ever hold beliefs with some degree of confidence, never certainty.

This is exactly the kind of problem probability theory was built for, and Bayes' theorem is the specific rule for updating beliefs in the light of evidence.

Named after the Reverend Thomas Bayes, an eighteenth-century English clergyman and mathematician, the theorem tells you how to combine two things.

The first thing is your "prior," which is how strongly you believed each possibility before seeing the new evidence.

The second thing is the "likelihood," which is how well each possibility predicts the evidence you actually observed.

Multiply the prior by the likelihood, tidy up the numbers so they add to one, and you get the "posterior," which is your updated belief after seeing the evidence.

In plain words: sensible belief is a blend of what you expected beforehand and how surprising the new data would be under each explanation.

Now the phrase "computational-level theory" deserves unpacking, because it is doing careful work.

It refers to a distinction made by the vision scientist David Marr, who said you can describe a mental ability at three levels.

The computational level asks what problem is being solved and what the ideal solution is; the algorithmic level asks what steps and representations are used; and the implementation level asks how the brain physically carries it out.

To call Bayes a computational-level theory is to say it describes the problem of induction and its ideal solution, without yet claiming that neurons literally carry out Bayes' theorem step by step.

This is an important and honest caveat, because it means a Bayesian model can be a good description of what the mind achieves even if the brain reaches that achievement by some other, approximate route.


53.2.2 Hierarchical Bayesian models and learning to learn

A hierarchical Bayesian model is a Bayesian model with more than one level of belief stacked on top of each other, and this stacking turns out to explain something deep about human learning.

The word "hierarchical" here just means layered, with general beliefs sitting above more specific ones.

Picture a child learning words for kinds of things.

At the bottom level, the child learns specific facts, such as what a particular ball looks like.

At a higher level, the child can learn a general lesson about categories themselves, for example that objects of the same kind tend to share their shape more than their colour or size.

A hierarchical Bayesian model captures both levels at once, and the higher-level lesson then guides all future lower-level learning.

This gives rise to a striking and well-documented effect called "learning to learn," sometimes called forming an overhypothesis.

Learning to learn means that once you have grasped a general regularity, you can master each new specific case from far less evidence than before.

The child who has learned that "kinds go by shape" can learn a brand new word from a single example, because the higher-level knowledge tells her which features matter.

Researchers such as Joshua Tenenbaum, Charles Kemp, and their colleagues showed that hierarchical Bayesian models reproduce this pattern, and they even predict a surprising detail.

The detail is that the broad, abstract lesson can be learned before all the specific details are filled in, which matches the finding that young children show category biases before they have learned all their categories.

This mattered because a long-standing objection to statistical accounts of the mind was that children learn too fast, from too little data, to be mere statistics-gatherers.

Hierarchical models answer that objection by showing how abstract knowledge, itself learned statistically, can make later learning fast and data-thrifty.


53.2.3 Structured probabilistic knowledge: grammars, graphs, and programs

This sub-section makes a point that is easy to miss but very important: being Bayesian does not force you to think of knowledge as a flat list of probabilities.

The probabilities can be laid over rich, structured representations, and choosing the right structure is often where the real explanatory power lies.

The word "structure" here means the shape or organisation of the knowledge, the way its parts connect.

Three kinds of structure come up again and again in this literature.

The first is a graph, which in this technical sense means a set of nodes connected by links, used to show which things influence which others.

A causal graph, for instance, can represent your belief that clouds cause rain, with an arrow from cloud to rain, and probability theory then tells you how to reason over that graph.

The second is a grammar, which is a set of rules for building complex structures out of simpler parts, borrowed from the study of language.

A probabilistic grammar can capture the idea that thoughts, sentences, or even melodies are built by combining pieces according to rules, with probabilities attached to the choices.

The third and most general is a program, meaning a small piece of a step-by-step procedure that generates data.

In this view a concept can be represented as a little probabilistic program that, when run, produces examples of the concept, and learning the concept means inferring the program.

The unifying insight, argued by researchers including Tenenbaum, Kemp, Thomas Griffiths, and Noah Goodman, is that human knowledge is both structured and probabilistic at the same time.

Structure captures the compositional, rule-like richness of thought, and probability captures our ability to cope with uncertainty and to learn from noisy, incomplete evidence.

The claim that these two ingredients belong together, rather than being rival visions of the mind, is one of the defining ideas of modern computational cognitive science.


53.3 The domains of Bayesian cognition

Having laid out the machinery, this section shows it at work in three concrete areas of thinking, so that the abstract ideas become tangible.

The pattern in each case is the same: take an everyday human ability, and show that people behave as if they were doing careful probabilistic reasoning.


53.3.1 Concept learning and the size principle

Concept learning means figuring out the meaning of a category, such as what counts as a "dog" or a "prime number," from examples.

A famous puzzle is that a few examples usually leave the answer wildly ambiguous, yet people converge on sensible meanings anyway.

Suppose someone points at a few numbers, say 16, 8, 2, and 64, and calls them all "blickets."

The examples fit many rules: powers of two, even numbers, numbers under a hundred, and so on, so how does a learner pick?

Tenenbaum's Bayesian model of concept learning, from the late 1990s, offered an elegant answer built on something called the size principle.

The size principle says that, all else equal, a narrower, more specific hypothesis should be preferred over a broader one when both fit the examples equally well.

The reasoning is that if the true category were the broad one, say "all even numbers," it would be a strange coincidence for every example you were shown to also happen to be a tidy power of two.

The narrow hypothesis "powers of two" predicts the actual examples much more strongly, so it earns a higher likelihood, and Bayes' theorem then favours it.

Crucially, this preference for the narrow hypothesis grows exponentially stronger with each additional example, because each new example that fits the narrow rule makes the broad rule's "coincidence" even more unlikely.

This is a lovely result because it explains, in exact numbers, the human intuition that a run of suspiciously specific examples points to a specific rule.

It also shows how a Bayesian learner can generalise sensibly from just a handful of positive examples, without ever being told what does not count as a blicket.


53.3.2 Intuitive physics as probabilistic simulation

Intuitive physics means the rough, automatic sense we all have of how physical objects will behave, such as knowing a leaning tower of blocks is about to topple.

You did not compute any equations to feel that; the understanding was fast, effortless, and approximate.

A leading account, developed by Peter Battaglia, Jessica Hamrick, Kevin Smith, Tomer Ullman, Tenenbaum and colleagues, proposes that the mind contains an "intuitive physics engine."

The comparison is to the physics engines inside video games, which are pieces of software that simulate how objects move, fall, and collide well enough to look right, without being perfectly accurate.

The proposal is that your mind runs a similar internal simulation: it imagines how a scene will unfold and reads off the likely outcome.

The probabilistic part is essential and clever.

Because you are never quite certain of the exact positions, weights, and speeds of things, the mind is thought to run the simulation several times with slightly different guesses about those details.

If most of the imagined runs end with the tower falling, you feel confident it will fall; if the runs disagree, you feel unsure.

This single idea accounts for a wide range of findings, including how people judge stability, how they predict where objects will land, and how their confidence tracks the genuine ambiguity of a scene.

It is a strong example of the Bayesian programme, because it treats a fast, intuitive human skill as approximate probabilistic reasoning over an internal model of the world.

It is worth noting that this remains an active research area, and some recent work argues that people also fall back on simpler shortcuts when full simulation would be too costly, which connects to the resource-rational ideas of the next chapter.


53.3.3 Intuitive psychology as inverse planning

Intuitive psychology, often called theory of mind, means our everyday ability to make sense of other people in terms of their beliefs and goals.

When you see someone hurry past the bus stop toward a shop, you effortlessly infer they wanted something from the shop more than they wanted the bus.

The Bayesian account of this ability, developed especially by Chris Baker, Rebecca Saxe, and Tenenbaum, is called inverse planning, and the name captures the idea neatly.

Planning, in this technical sense, means working forward from a goal to the actions that would achieve it: given that I want coffee, I walk to the cafe.

Inverse planning runs that logic backward: given that I saw you walk to the cafe, I infer that you probably wanted coffee.

More precisely, the model assumes that people are roughly rational agents who choose actions that tend to achieve their goals, and then it uses Bayes' theorem to work out which goals and beliefs best explain the actions you observed.

The framework rests on the tools of decision-making under uncertainty, in which an agent with goals picks actions to reach them, and the observer inverts that process to recover the hidden goals.

This account is attractive because it explains not just single guesses but the whole graded pattern of our social inferences, including how we revise our guess about someone's goal as their path unfolds.

Recent work has begun to join intuitive psychology and intuitive physics together, so that an observer reasons about what someone wants while also reasoning about the physical world that person is acting in, which is closer to how real social understanding works.


53.4 Bayes at the neural level

So far Bayes has been a description of what the mind achieves, at Marr's computational level.

This section turns to the harder question of how a brain made of neurons could actually carry out anything like probabilistic reasoning.

Two main proposals compete, and they make different bets about what the noisiness of the brain is for.


53.4.1 Probabilistic population codes

To understand this we need the idea of a population code.

A population code means representing something not with a single cell but with the combined pattern of activity across a whole group, or population, of neurons.

For example, the direction of a moving object might be encoded by which cells in a group fire most strongly and how strongly, rather than by any one cell alone.

A probabilistic population code, developed by Wei Ji Ma, Jeff Beck, Peter Latham, Alexandre Pouget and colleagues around 2006, adds a crucial twist.

The twist is that the population does not just signal a single best guess; it automatically represents a whole probability distribution, that is, a spread of how likely each possible value is.

The clever part is that the natural variability of neurons, the fact that they fire a slightly different number of spikes each time, is not treated as a nuisance to be averaged away.

Instead, that variability is exactly what carries the information about uncertainty: broadly speaking, a stronger and crisper burst of population activity signals a more confident, narrower estimate, and a weaker one signals more doubt.

A further attractive feature is that, under this scheme, combining two sources of evidence in the statistically correct way turns out to correspond to simply adding the two populations' activity together, which is something neurons can plausibly do.

So probabilistic population codes offer a concrete story in which representing and combining uncertainty falls naturally out of ordinary neural machinery.


53.4.2 Sampling against parametric representations of uncertainty

This sub-section lays out the main rival to the population-code story, and the debate between them.

The two proposals differ in what a moment of neural activity is taken to represent.

The population-code view just described is often called parametric, meaning the neural activity at any instant encodes the full probability distribution all at once, spelled out in its shape.

The sampling view, developed by researchers including Jozsef Fiser, Pietro Berkes, Gergo Orban, and Mate Lengyel, proposes something quite different.

On the sampling view, the brain represents a probability distribution not by holding it whole at every instant, but by drawing examples from it one after another over time.

An analogy helps: if you want to describe the range of heights in a city, you could either write down the full curve of how common each height is, which is the parametric way, or you could just call out a series of individual people's heights, which is the sampling way, letting the pattern emerge over the sequence.

On this account the moment-to-moment fluctuation of neural activity is not noise around a fixed answer; it is the brain trying out different possibilities, each fluctuation a fresh sample from its beliefs.

Each view has appeal.

The parametric view explains how the brain can combine and act on uncertainty instantly, while the sampling view explains why neural activity is so variable and why our own judgments seem to fluctuate as if we were drawing from a distribution.

The honest current state of the science is that this is unsettled, and interestingly some recent analyses suggest the two views may not be as opposed as they first seemed, since certain sampling schemes can be read as producing a kind of population code.

For a beginner, the key point to carry away is that there is a genuine, live scientific question here, and researchers have not yet agreed on how, or even whether, the brain literally implements probabilistic reasoning.


53.5 The process-model question

This final section confronts a gap that runs through the whole chapter.

The gap is between saying what the ideal answer is, at the computational level, and saying how a real, limited mind actually reaches an answer in real time, which is the level of process.


53.5.1 Rational process models and sampling algorithms in the mind

A process model is a theory of the actual steps a mind takes, moment by moment, as opposed to just the ideal outcome it approximates.

This matters because exact Bayesian reasoning is usually far too hard to compute in full; the number of possibilities to weigh can be astronomically large.

So if the mind is even roughly Bayesian, it cannot be doing the exact calculation; it must be using some shortcut that lands close enough.

A leading idea is that the mind uses sampling algorithms, which are methods that approximate a probability distribution by drawing a manageable number of examples from it rather than considering every possibility.

Statisticians and computer scientists rely on exactly these methods, under names such as Monte Carlo methods, precisely because they make otherwise impossible probability calculations practical.

The proposal, developed by Griffiths, Tenenbaum, Ed Vul, Goodman and others, is that the mind does something similar, and that this explains features of human thought that look irrational at first.

For instance, our guesses are noticeably variable, we give somewhat different answers to the same question on different occasions, and sampling predicts exactly this kind of scatter.

There is even a striking analysis by Vul, Goodman, Griffiths, and Tenenbaum showing that, when thinking is costly, it can be sensible to base a decision on just one or a very few samples rather than many.

This reframes what looks like sloppiness as a reasonable trade-off between accuracy and effort, and it ties the Bayesian programme directly to the resource-rational ideas of the next chapter.

So rational process models try to keep the successes of the Bayesian computational-level story while facing up to the fact that real minds must approximate, and they propose sampling as the bridge.


53.5.2 The probabilistic language of thought

The probabilistic language of thought is an ambitious attempt to bring together the two big themes we have seen: rich, structured, program-like knowledge, and probabilistic reasoning under uncertainty.

The older phrase "language of thought," from the philosopher Jerry Fodor, is the idea that thinking happens in an internal, language-like system with words and grammar of its own, so that thoughts are built from parts according to rules, much as sentences are.

The probabilistic version, developed by Goodman, Tenenbaum, and colleagues, says that this internal language is one for writing little probabilistic programs.

A probabilistic program, recall, is a short procedure that generates data with some randomness built in, so that running it produces not one fixed output but a range of possible outputs with different likelihoods.

On this view a concept is a program that can generate examples of itself, a belief about the world is a program that generates possible observations, and reasoning is running and inverting these programs.

To make this concrete and testable, researchers built an actual computer programming language for it, called Church, named in honour of the logician Alonzo Church.

Church and its successors let scientists write down a candidate mental model as real code, run it, and compare its behaviour against what people do, which turns philosophical proposals into precise, checkable predictions.

The appeal of the probabilistic language of thought is that it promises the best of both worlds at last: the compositional, unlimited creativity of structured symbolic thought, and the graceful handling of uncertainty that probability provides.

Whether the human mind really works this way is far from settled, and the framework is demanding to test, but it stands as one of the most complete visions on offer for how a single system could be both structured and probabilistic.


CHAPTER 54. BOUNDED, RESOURCE-RATIONAL, AND ECOLOGICAL RATIONALITY (FRAMEWORK)

The previous chapter asked what an ideal mind would do.

This chapter asks a more down-to-earth question: what should a mind do when it is not ideal, when its time, memory, and computing power are all sharply limited?

That question turns out to change the picture in deep ways, because once you take limits seriously, behaviour that looked foolish can start to look wise.

This chapter introduces three closely related traditions that each take limits as their starting point: bounded rationality, resource-rational analysis, and ecological rationality.

They share a hopeful conviction, that human thinking is much smarter than the long catalogue of human "biases" would suggest, once you judge it by the right standard.


54.1 Bounded rationality

Bounded rationality is the founding idea of this whole family: that real minds are rational within bounds, doing the best they can with the limited resources they have.

It was the great insight of Herbert Simon, an American scientist so wide-ranging that he won both a Nobel Prize in economics and the top award in artificial intelligence.


54.1.1 Satisficing and aspiration levels

Simon coined the word "satisficing," a blend of "satisfy" and "suffice," and it names one of the most useful ideas in the study of decision-making.

Satisficing means choosing the first option that is good enough, rather than searching on and on for the very best option.

The contrast is with "optimising," which means finding the single best possible choice, something that often requires examining every alternative.

Simon argued that optimising is usually impossible in real life, because there are too many options, too little time, and too little information to consider them all.

So instead of maximising, people set what Simon called an "aspiration level," which is a threshold of acceptability, a bar for how good is good enough.

You then search through options one at a time and stop as soon as something clears the bar.

Think of looking for somewhere to eat in an unfamiliar town: you do not survey every restaurant and rank them; you walk until you find one that looks decent enough, and you go in.

The aspiration level is not fixed forever; it adjusts to experience.

If good options keep turning up easily, you raise your bar, and if everything is disappointing, you lower it, so the standard itself adapts to the environment.

Simon's point was not that people are lazy or stupid, but that satisficing is a genuinely intelligent response to a world too complex to fully compute.

This reframing, that stopping when you have enough can be the smart move, is the seed from which the rest of the chapter grows.


54.1.2 The scissors of mind and environment

Simon offered a memorable image for how thinking works, and it is worth learning because it recurs throughout this field.

He said that rational behaviour is shaped "by a scissors whose two blades are the structure of task environments and the computational capabilities of the actor."

The point of the scissors image is that a single blade cuts nothing.

To understand why someone behaves as they do, you cannot look only at the mind, and you cannot look only at the world; you have to see how the two meet, just as cutting needs both blades pressing together.

The first blade is the mind's limits: how much it can remember, how fast it can compute, how much it can attend to.

The second blade is the structure of the environment: which situations arise often, how regular or predictable the world is, what information is freely available.

A behaviour that seems irrational when you stare only at the mind can turn out to be an excellent fit once you see the shape of the world it evolved and learned to handle.

This is a profound methodological lesson, and it directly connects Simon's bounded rationality to Anderson's rational analysis from the previous chapter, since both insist that you cannot understand the mind without understanding its world.

The scissors image is the shared foundation that the two remaining traditions in this chapter build upon, each emphasising one blade or the way the blades are matched.


54.2 Resource-rational analysis

Resource-rational analysis is a modern, mathematically precise upgrade of Simon's bounded rationality.

Its guiding idea is to treat the mind's limits not as an excuse for failure but as a formal part of the problem to be solved.


54.2.1 The optimal use of limited computation

The central proposal, developed especially by Tom Griffiths, Falk Lieder, and their colleagues in the 2010s, can be stated in one sentence.

Resource-rational analysis says the mind makes the best possible use of its limited computational resources, so it optimises subject to the cost of thinking.

Notice the careful shift from the previous chapter.

Classical rational analysis asked, what is the best answer, and it ignored how hard that answer is to compute.

Resource-rational analysis asks, what is the best answer you can afford, given that thinking itself takes time and effort that are worth something.

Formally, this means the mind is imagined to weigh two things against each other: the quality of the decision it would reach, and the computational cost of the thinking needed to reach it.

The right amount to think is the amount where a little more thinking would no longer be worth its cost.

This is a powerful reframing because it turns human limits from a problem into part of the solution.

A person who thinks quickly and roughly rather than slowly and exactly is not failing to be rational; they may be being rational about the price of their own thinking.

The approach has been used to re-derive many well-known mental shortcuts as the answers you should give if you correctly account for the cost of computation, which is the theme of the sub-sections that follow.


54.2.2 Rational metareasoning and the value of computation

This sub-section introduces the machinery that lets resource-rational analysis actually work: reasoning about your own reasoning.

The technical term is "metareasoning," where the prefix meta means about itself, so metareasoning means thinking about how to think.

The idea is that a smart but limited agent should not just think about the world; it should also make good decisions about how much thinking to do and which thoughts to have.

To make this precise, researchers use a quantity called the "value of computation."

The value of computation is the expected benefit you would gain from performing a particular mental operation, such as considering one more option or imagining one more outcome, minus the cost of doing it.

If a further step of thinking is likely to improve your decision by more than it costs, it is worth taking; if not, you should stop and act.

Rational metareasoning, then, is the policy of always choosing the mental operation with the highest value of computation, and stopping when no operation is worth its cost.

This gives a principled answer to a question that plagues any limited thinker: when should I stop deliberating and just decide?

Lieder and Griffiths used this framework to model how people select among different problem-solving strategies, treating the choice of strategy as itself a rational decision about how to spend limited mental effort.

The beauty of the approach is that it explains the flexible, situation-dependent way people switch between careful thought and quick shortcuts, without having to call either one irrational.


54.2.3 Heuristics as resource-rational strategies

A heuristic is a mental shortcut, a simple rule of thumb that gives a good-enough answer quickly instead of a perfect answer slowly.

For decades, many heuristics were viewed mainly as sources of error, the origins of the famous "biases" catalogued in the study of judgment.

Resource-rational analysis offers a strikingly different reading: many heuristics are exactly the strategies a limited mind should use, because they buy most of the benefit of full reasoning at a fraction of the cost.

A clear example is the anchoring effect, the well-documented tendency for people's numerical estimates to be pulled toward whatever number they happened to consider first.

This has long been listed as a bias, an irrational contamination of judgment.

But Lieder, Griffiths and colleagues showed that if you start from an initial guess and then adjust it by a series of small mental steps, each step being costly, then stopping the adjustment early, and therefore staying somewhat anchored, is precisely what you should do to balance accuracy against effort.

On this reading the anchoring bias is not a flaw in the machinery; it is the fingerprint of a mind spending its limited thinking wisely.

The general lesson is that before you call a mental shortcut irrational, you should ask what the ideal strategy would be for a thinker who has to pay for every computation, because the shortcut may turn out to be that ideal strategy.
