Productivity is the fact that you can understand and produce an effectively unlimited number of new thoughts you have never met before.

No one had ever considered the sentence a purple giraffe is reading Tuesday to the moon before you read it just now, yet you grasped it instantly, and this endless novelty from finite means cries out for explanation.

Systematicity is the fact that the ability to think certain thoughts comes bundled with the ability to think related ones, in a non-accidental pattern.

Anyone who can think John loves Mary can also think Mary loves John; you never meet a mind that can think the first but is constitutionally unable to think the second, and this reliable bundling looks like no coincidence.

Compositionality is the underlying explanation the language-of-thought camp offers for both: it is the principle that the meaning of a complex thought is determined by the meanings of its parts and the way they are put together.

Because John, loves, and Mary are reusable parts with stable meanings, and because there are rules for combining them, you automatically get both the endless novelty of productivity and the reliable bundling of systematicity, all from a small stock of symbols and a grammar for arranging them.

The argument, then, is an inference to the best explanation: the easiest way to explain why thought is productive, systematic, and compositional is to suppose that thoughts really do have parts and structure, that is, that there really is a language of thought.

This is a genuinely powerful argument, and it sets the challenge that the rival camp, connectionism, has spent decades trying to answer, which is the subject of the next section.


58.2 The classical and connectionist debate

This section stages the central confrontation of the chapter.

On one side stands the classical view just described, that the mind is a symbol-manipulating system with a language-like structure.

On the other stands connectionism, the view that the mind is a neural network of simple interconnected units whose knowledge lives in the strengths of their connections rather than in stored symbols.

The section follows the argument through its famous opening challenge, the replies it provoked, and its surprising return in the age of modern artificial intelligence.


58.2.1 The systematicity challenge

This sub-section states the objection that has organised the whole debate since the late 1980s.

In 1988 Jerry Fodor and Zenon Pylyshyn published a long and forceful article, Connectionism and Cognitive Architecture: A Critical Analysis, which threw down a challenge that connectionists have been answering ever since.

Their argument, boiled down, was this: thought is systematic, as the previous section explained, and the classical view explains that systematicity naturally, because a symbol structure literally contains reusable parts that can be recombined.

A connectionist network, they charged, has no such built-in parts; it is a soup of activation across units, and nothing in its basic design guarantees that a network able to represent John loves Mary must also be able to represent Mary loves John.

Therefore, they concluded, insofar as connectionist networks do manage to be systematic, they must be doing so by secretly implementing a classical symbol system underneath, in which case connectionism is not a rival theory of the mind's architecture but merely a story about how the brain's hardware might run the real, symbolic software.

The force of the challenge is that it does not deny neural networks can be built or can learn; it denies that they explain the structured character of thought without smuggling in the very symbols they claimed to replace.

This put the burden squarely on connectionists to show either that their networks can be genuinely systematic on their own terms, or that human thought is less rigidly systematic than Fodor and Pylyshyn assumed, and both replies were duly attempted.


58.2.2 The connectionist replies and tensor-product binding

This sub-section covers the most important technical answer to the challenge.

The central difficulty for a neural network is called the binding problem for representation: how can a network keep track of which role each thing plays, so that John-as-lover and Mary-as-loved do not smear together into a mere set containing John and Mary with no who-did-what-to-whom?

The most influential answer came from Paul Smolensky, who proposed a mathematical technique called tensor-product binding in work through the late 1980s and early 1990s.

The idea, in plain terms, is to represent each element of a thought as a pattern of activity for its content - a pattern for John, a pattern for Mary - and to separately represent each structural slot as another pattern - a pattern for the lover role, a pattern for the loved role.

Binding a filler to a role is then done by a specific mathematical combination, the tensor product, which fuses the John pattern with the lover-role pattern into a single composite pattern that keeps the two locked together, so the network can tell John-as-lover from John-as-loved.

By adding up such role-filler bindings, a network can encode a whole structured thought as one big activity pattern, and crucially it can later pull the pieces back out, which shows a network can carry genuine structure without a classical list of symbols.

Smolensky offered this as proof that connectionism could answer the systematicity challenge on its own ground, honouring structure while remaining a network rather than a symbol processor.

Fodor and his collaborator Brian McLaughlin replied in 1990 that the trick did not fully work, arguing that tensor-product representations have their constituents only in a weak sense - the parts can be extracted by computation but are not literally present and causally active in the way classical symbols are - so the deep explanatory advantage of the classical view survived.

The exchange never reached a knock-out on either side, and it left the field with a sophisticated toolkit for building structure into networks and a lingering philosophical disagreement about whether that structure is the real thing or a clever imitation.


58.2.3 The modern reprise: systematic generalisation in neural networks

This sub-section brings the decades-old debate right up to the present, because it has been reborn inside modern artificial intelligence.

The old philosophical question turned into a concrete engineering test the moment powerful neural networks began doing impressive things, because one could now simply measure whether they generalise systematically.

Systematic generalisation means handling new combinations of familiar parts: if a system has learned the word jump and has learned to do things twice, it should be able to jump twice the first time it is asked, without special training on that exact combination.

In 2018 the researchers Brenden Lake and Marco Baroni built a clean test of this, a task called SCAN in which a network learns to turn simple commands into sequences of actions, and they arranged it so the test demanded new combinations of words the network had only seen separately.

Their result was a sharp rediscovery of Fodor and Pylyshyn's point: standard sequence-learning networks did nearly perfectly when the test items resembled the training items, but failed badly when success required recombining known parts in genuinely new ways, which is exactly the systematicity that classical symbols deliver for free.

This shows the forty-year-old debate was not idle philosophy; the same crack reopened in the most advanced learning systems of the day.

The story does not end in defeat for networks, however.

In 2023 Brenden Lake and Marco Baroni reported in the journal Nature that a network trained with a technique called meta-learning - roughly, training the network on a stream of little learning problems so that it learns how to recombine parts in general, rather than memorising any one mapping - could reach human-level systematic generalisation on these tasks.

The careful lesson for a beginner is balanced: systematic, compositional generalisation does not come automatically to neural networks and remains a real weakness of many of them, yet it is not proven impossible either, and it appears to be something a network can be taught to do rather than something it must have wired in from the start.

That balance is why the classical-versus-connectionist question is best regarded not as won by either side but as reshaped, with modern work trying to get the structure-respecting strengths of symbols and the learning strengths of networks in one system, which is a central ambition for projects like konnectome.


58.3 The hard problems of representation

This section confronts two deep difficulties that any theory of internal representation must eventually face, whichever side of the previous debate it favours.

The first is how a symbol inside a head, or a pattern inside a network, comes to be about anything in the world at all.

The second is how a mind manages to focus on what matters and ignore the endless things that do not, in a world where almost anything could in principle be relevant.

Both problems are famous for being easy to state and stubbornly hard to solve.


58.3.1 The symbol grounding problem restated

This sub-section revisits, in the setting of this chapter, a problem introduced earlier in the outline, because it strikes right at the language-of-thought view.

The symbol grounding problem, named and sharpened by the cognitive scientist Stevan Harnad in a 1990 paper, asks how the symbols inside a mind or a computer come to have meaning rather than being empty tokens.

Harnad's vivid way of posing it was to imagine trying to learn a first language purely from a dictionary written in that same unknown language: every word is defined only by other words you also do not know, so you spin forever among meaningless symbols and never touch anything real.

A pure symbol system, like the classical language of thought or a traditional artificial-intelligence program, seems to face just this predicament, because its symbols are defined only by their relations to other symbols and rules, with no anchor to the world outside the system.

Harnad's proposed cure was grounding through the senses and the body: at least some symbols must be tied directly to the system's own perception and action - the symbol for red hooked to the actual detection of red things, the symbol for grasp hooked to actual grasping - so that meaning can climb up from that sensory footing rather than floating free.

This connects the whole debate of this chapter back to the embodied and enactive ideas of Chapter 56, because grounding is essentially the demand that symbols be rooted in a body's real dealings with a real world.

The problem has taken on fresh urgency with today's large language models, which learn from vast amounts of text and can be seen as a modern version of the dictionary-go-round, learning words only from other words, and researchers now actively debate how much such systems really understand and whether adding images, sound, and action - so-called multimodal grounding - genuinely solves the problem or only softens it, a question that is very much open.


58.3.2 The frame problem and the problem of relevance

This sub-section explains a difficulty that many regard as the single hardest obstacle for building a general mind.

The frame problem began as a narrow technical puzzle in artificial intelligence, first named by John McCarthy and Patrick Hayes in 1969, about how a reasoning program should keep track of what stays the same when an action happens.

If a robot moves a cup, it should update the cup's location but somehow know, without checking every fact it holds, that moving the cup did not change the colour of the walls, the day of the week, or the price of tea, and stating all the things that do not change turns out to be maddeningly hard.

Philosophers, above all Jerry Fodor and Daniel Dennett, broadened this into a far deeper worry usually called the problem of relevance.

The problem of relevance is this: in any real situation, an unbounded number of facts might conceivably bear on what to do, and there is no obvious way for a mind to zero in on the few that actually matter without somehow already reviewing the countless ones that do not.

When you plan a trip you effortlessly ignore that you own an umbrella of a certain colour and that Rome was founded long ago, yet in some odd circumstance either fact could be the crucial one, so relevance cannot simply be fixed in advance by a rule.

Fodor argued this makes central cognition - the open-ended, bring-anything-to-bear part of thinking, as opposed to walled-off perception - especially resistant to explanation, and he expressed his pessimism in a wry law that the more global and free-ranging a cognitive process is, the less anyone understands it.

The reason this cuts against the classical symbol picture is that a system of symbols and rules seems to have no efficient way to survey its whole store of knowledge for relevance without grinding to a halt, whereas humans do it in an instant and usually without effort.

A fair statement for a beginner is that the frame and relevance problems remain genuinely unsolved in the general case; they are a large part of why common sense has proven so much harder to build than narrow expertise, and they set a real bar that any candidate architecture of mind, konnectome included, has to face honestly.


58.4 Modularity

This section addresses the final structural question of the chapter, whether the mind is one thing or many.

Modularity is the idea that the mind is made up of separate, specialised subsystems - modules - each dedicated to a particular job, rather than being one flexible general-purpose processor.

The section contrasts a limited version of this idea with a far more sweeping one, and then returns to the relevance problem to explain why the disagreement matters.


58.4.1 Fodorian and massive modularity

This sub-section lays out the two main versions of the modularity idea and who argued for each.

The influential starting point is Jerry Fodor's 1983 book The Modularity of Mind, which proposed what is now called Fodorian modularity.

Fodor argued that the input systems of the mind - perception and language, the parts that take in sensory signals and decode speech - are modules, and he gave a list of properties that make something a module.

The key properties are that a module is domain-specific, meaning it handles only one narrow kind of information such as vision or grammar; that it is mandatory, meaning it runs automatically whether you want it to or not; that it is fast; and above all that it is informationally encapsulated, meaning it does its work using only its own limited store of information and cannot consult everything else the mind knows.

The classic evidence for encapsulation is a visual illusion that persists even after you learn it is an illusion: the two lines in the Muller-Lyer figure keep looking unequal in length no matter how firmly you know they are equal, because your visual module cannot be talked out of its output by your beliefs.

Crucially, Fodor held that only the input systems are modular, and that central cognition - reasoning, believing, deciding - is precisely not modular but open and unencapsulated, which is why, on his view, it falls prey to the relevance problem and resists scientific understanding.

The rival and much bolder view, called massive modularity, was developed by evolutionary psychologists such as Leda Cosmides and John Tooby and defended philosophically by Peter Carruthers in his 2006 book The Architecture of the Mind.

Massive modularity claims that the whole mind, all the way up through reasoning and decision, is composed of many special-purpose modules, each shaped by evolution to solve a specific recurring problem faced by our ancestors, such as detecting cheaters in social exchange, choosing mates, or avoiding contamination.

On this view there is no single general-purpose thinker at the centre; what feels like general intelligence is the combined output of a large committee of specialised devices, and the appeal of the theory is that it explains how a mind could be built up by natural selection acting on one problem at a time.

The two views frame a real spectrum, from a mostly general mind with a few modular senses to a mind that is modular through and through, and where the truth lies is still debated.


58.4.2 The problem of central, isotropic cognition

This closing sub-section explains the sticking point that keeps the modularity debate alive, and it ties the whole chapter together.

The word isotropic is borrowed from physics, where it means the same in every direction, and Fodor used it to describe a troubling feature of central thinking: in principle, any piece of knowledge you have can be brought to bear on any problem, so information flows in from every direction with no fixed walls.

Central cognition is also what Fodor called Quinean, after the philosopher Willard Van Orman Quine, meaning that whether you should believe something can depend on your entire web of beliefs at once, the way a scientist judging a new theory may have to weigh it against everything else science holds.

These two features - isotropic and Quinean - are exactly what makes central cognition powerful and flexible, and exactly what makes the relevance problem of the previous section so severe, because a system open to everything has no easy way to avoid considering everything.

Fodor's pointed conclusion was that modularity works as an account of the mind's edges, the input systems, precisely because those systems are walled off and limited, but that the same trick cannot be extended to the open, isotropic centre, and that is why he thought the hardest part of the mind was also the least understood.

This is where the massive-modularity camp pushes back hardest, insisting that even the centre is really a collection of specialised modules and that the appearance of open, anything-goes reasoning is a kind of illusion produced by many narrow devices working together, though critics doubt a pile of specialists can ever capture the genuine flexibility of human thought.

The reason a beginner should care, and the reason this makes a fitting close to the chapter, is that the whole matter bears directly on how one would build a mind: a designer who believes in massive modularity will assemble many special-purpose components, while a designer who believes central cognition is genuinely general and isotropic will search for one flexible reasoning engine and must then confront the still-unsolved relevance problem head-on.

That unresolved choice - many specialised machines or one general one, and how either could tame relevance - is one of the central open questions this outline carries forward into its later treatment of complete cognitive architectures, and it is one of the deepest questions facing any project, konnectome among them, that hopes to build a mind rather than merely a clever tool.

PART FOURTEEN. COGNITIVE ARCHITECTURES: UNIFIED THEORIES OF MIND

================================================================================

CHAPTER 59. WHAT A COGNITIVE ARCHITECTURE IS (ARCHITECTURE)

This chapter introduces one of the biggest ideas in the science of the mind: the notion of a cognitive architecture.

A cognitive architecture is a proposed blueprint of the fixed machinery of thinking, the part of the mind that stays the same no matter what task you happen to be doing.

The idea matters because most research studies one small ability at a time, like memory for a list of words or the speed of noticing a light, while a cognitive architecture tries to say how all of those abilities fit together inside a single working mind.

In this chapter we will build up the concept slowly, meet the argument that the mind needs one unified theory rather than a hundred separate ones, list the jobs any mind has to do, and then survey the main families of architectures that researchers have built.


59.1 The concept

This section explains what people mean by the word architecture when they are talking about the mind, and why that word was borrowed from building design and computer engineering.

The short version is that an architecture is the stable framework, and knowledge is the changing content that gets poured into it.


59.1.1 The fixed architecture against the variable knowledge that runs on it

The central idea here is a split between two things: a fixed part that does not change from moment to moment, and a variable part that does.

Think of a modern computer.

The hardware and the operating system are fixed for the whole time you own the machine.

The documents, photos, and programs you load onto it change all the time.

A cognitive architecture is meant to be like the fixed part: the built-in structure and processes of the mind that stay constant across every task, every day, and every topic.

The variable part is your knowledge, meaning the specific facts, skills, and memories you happen to have picked up.

Here technical jargon is worth pausing on: by knowledge, architecture researchers mean any content the mind holds and uses, from a fact like Paris is in France to a skill like how to tie a shoelace.

The claim is that the same fixed machinery lets one person become a chef and another become a violinist, because the machinery is identical but the knowledge loaded onto it differs.

An everyday way to picture it is a kitchen.

The stove, oven, sink, and counters are the fixed architecture.

The ingredients and recipes are the variable knowledge.

You can cook thousands of different meals without ever changing the kitchen, and that is exactly the sort of stability an architecture is supposed to have.

Researchers care about this split because if you can pin down the fixed part, you have found something deep and general about how minds work, rather than just a fact about one particular skill.


59.1.2 The distinction from a single-task model

This sub-section contrasts an architecture with something narrower called a single-task model.

A single-task model is a small theory or computer program built to explain just one behaviour, such as how quickly people read a word, or how they decide whether two shapes are the same.

Single-task models are extremely common in psychology, and they are useful, because focusing on one thing lets you be precise about it.

The weakness is that a mind is not a stack of unrelated gadgets.

The same person who reads words also remembers faces, plans a route home, and feels frustrated in traffic, and all of that happens inside one head using overlapping machinery.

A cognitive architecture is deliberately the opposite of a single-task model: it is meant to run many different tasks using one shared set of parts, so that reading, remembering, and planning all draw on the same memory and the same decision process.

An analogy is the difference between a single kitchen gadget and a whole kitchen.

An egg slicer does exactly one job.

A kitchen can produce breakfast, a birthday cake, and a soup, because its parts combine flexibly.

The test of an architecture, then, is breadth: can this one framework, without being rebuilt, take on a task its designers did not have in mind when they made it.

That breadth is hard to achieve, which is why architectures are ambitious and why relatively few of them exist compared with the huge number of single-task models.


59.1.3 Where an architecture sits among Marr's levels

To place architectures precisely, it helps to use a famous three-way distinction from the vision scientist David Marr, published in his 1982 book Vision.

Marr argued that any information-processing system, including the brain, can and should be described at three separate levels of analysis, and that confusing the levels causes muddled thinking.

The first level is the computational level, which asks what problem is being solved and why: for vision, the goal of recovering the shapes of objects from patterns of light.

The second level is the algorithmic level, which asks what procedure and what representations are used to solve that problem: the specific step-by-step recipe and the form the information takes.

Here representation is jargon meaning a way of standing in for information, such as a list of numbers, a picture, or a symbol.

The third level is the implementation level, which asks how the procedure is physically carried out: in the brain, that means neurons and their connections; in a computer, transistors.

A cognitive architecture lives mainly at Marr's middle level, the algorithmic one, because it specifies the representations the mind uses and the processes that operate on them.

Some architectures reach downward toward the implementation level by trying to match brain regions or by using simulated neurons, and some reach upward by taking seriously what problems the mind evolved to solve.

The useful takeaway for a beginner is that an architecture is not mainly a theory of neurons and not mainly a theory of life goals; it is a theory of the mental machinery in between, the format of thoughts and the operations that shuffle them around.


59.2 Unified theories of cognition

This section introduces the dream that motivated the whole field: the idea that psychology should aim for one grand theory that ties everything together.

The person most associated with this dream is Allen Newell, an American scientist who helped found both artificial intelligence and cognitive psychology.


59.2.1 Newell's argument that cognition needs one theory, not many

In 1990 Allen Newell published a book called Unified Theories of Cognition, based on lectures he had given, and in it he made a pointed complaint about his own field.

His complaint was that psychology had become a heap of small, disconnected findings, each explained by its own little model, with nothing to hold them together.

Newell argued that this was a scientific dead end, because you can always invent a fresh mini-theory for each new experiment, and doing so never forces your ideas to be consistent with each other.

His proposal was that researchers should try to build a single unified theory of cognition, one framework required to account for memory, perception, language, problem solving, and the rest all at once.

The discipline of a unified theory is that every piece has to work with every other piece, so a choice you make to explain memory constrains what you are allowed to say about attention.

Newell did not claim to have finished such a theory; he offered his own architecture, called Soar, as a candidate and an example of the effort, not as the final answer.

It is fair to note that not everyone agreed then or agrees now.

Many psychologists still find focused single-task models more productive, and some doubt that one theory can or should cover everything.

But Newell's challenge reshaped the field, and the very existence of cognitive architectures is largely his legacy.


59.2.2 The functional criteria a mind must satisfy

Newell did not just say build one theory; he tried to say what such a theory would have to explain, by listing the functions a real mind must perform.

The word functional here means defined by what it does rather than what it is made of, so a functional criterion is a job the mind must accomplish, regardless of whether neurons or silicon do it.

Newell offered lists of requirements that a human cognitive architecture would have to satisfy in order to count as genuinely mind-like.

These included things like behaving flexibly as a function of the environment, showing adaptive and goal-directed behaviour, operating in real time, using vast amounts of knowledge, using natural language, and learning from experience.

The point of such a list is to raise the bar: a toy model that does one clever trick but cannot learn, cannot use language, and cannot act in real time has not really explained a mind.

By writing the requirements down, Newell turned a vague ambition into a checklist that any proposed architecture could be measured against.

This checklist idea is important because it gives the field a shared standard, so that different research groups building different architectures can at least ask the same questions about each one.


59.2.3 The Newell test as a multi-criterion evaluation

The checklist idea was later sharpened into something now called the Newell Test, in an influential 2003 article by John Anderson and Christian Lebiere in the journal Behavioral and Brain Sciences.

Anderson and Lebiere took Newell's overlapping lists and distilled them into twelve criteria for judging a theory of cognition.

Their twelve were, in plain words: behaving flexibly, adapting behaviour to reach goals, operating in real time, holding up under real-world complexity, using a vast store of knowledge, integrating diverse knowledge, using natural language, learning from the environment, showing development from infancy to adulthood, arising through evolution, and being realizable in the brain, together with dynamic responsiveness to changing situations.

The word multi-criterion simply means judged by many standards at once rather than a single score.

Their key argument was that no theory should be praised or dismissed on one dimension alone; instead each theory should be graded on every criterion, and its pattern of strengths and weaknesses laid bare.

To demonstrate, they graded two rivals: classical connectionism, meaning neural-network style models, and their own architecture ACT-R.

They concluded that connectionism scored well on learning and development but poorly on handling symbols and structured knowledge, while ACT-R scored well precisely because it combined a symbolic level with a sub-symbolic one.

Whether or not you accept their verdicts, the deeper lesson is the method: honest evaluation means showing where your favourite theory is weak, not just where it shines.


59.3 The functional requirements of any mind

This section walks through the jobs a mind has to do, grouped into a few clusters, so that a beginner can see the full scope of what an architecture must deliver.

Think of it as a job description for a mind, written before we look at any particular candidate for the post.


59.3.1 Memory, learning, perception, and action

At the most basic level, a mind must take in information, hold onto information, improve with experience, and do something in the world.

Perception is the intake: turning raw signals from the eyes, ears, skin, and other senses into usable information about what is out there.

Memory is the holding: keeping information available over time, from a few seconds of holding a phone number in mind up to a lifetime of remembering your childhood home.

Architects usually distinguish a short-term or working memory, which holds a small amount of information you are actively using right now, from long-term memory, which stores knowledge more or less permanently.

Learning is the improving: changing the mind's knowledge or skills as a result of experience, so that next time you do better or faster.

Action is the output: moving muscles, speaking, or otherwise affecting the environment based on what you have perceived and decided.

Every architecture in this book must provide some account of all four, because a system that perceives but never remembers, or remembers but never acts, is plainly not a mind.

An everyday illustration ties them together: you hear a kettle whistle (perception), recall that this means the water is boiling (memory), get quicker at responding to that sound over the years (learning), and reach out to switch it off (action).


59.3.2 Decision, goal management, and attention under bounded resources

Beyond the basics, a mind must choose what to do, keep track of what it is trying to achieve, and focus its limited capacity wisely.

Decision means selecting one option out of several, such as which route to take or which word to say next.

Goal management means holding and organizing the things you are trying to accomplish, including breaking a big goal like cook dinner into smaller sub-goals like boil the pasta and heat the sauce.

Attention means directing limited processing capacity toward some information and away from the rest, because a mind cannot fully process everything at once.

The crucial phrase is bounded resources, which is jargon for the plain fact that a real mind has limits: limited time, limited memory, limited attention, and limited energy.

This idea is often called bounded rationality, a term from the economist and cognitive scientist Herbert Simon, meaning that people make reasonable decisions within their limits rather than perfect decisions with unlimited thinking.

An architecture that assumed infinite memory or instant, cost-free thinking would be unrealistic, so a good architecture must show how a limited system still manages to act sensibly.

For example, when you walk into a crowded party looking for a friend, you cannot inspect every face at once; attention lets you scan a few at a time, and goal management keeps you searching until you succeed or give up.


59.3.3 Metacognition, motivation, and emotion

The most advanced requirements concern a mind thinking about itself, wanting things, and feeling things.

Metacognition means cognition about cognition, that is, the mind monitoring and controlling its own thinking, such as noticing that you do not understand a sentence and choosing to reread it.

Motivation means the forces that energize and direct behaviour, the reasons a system does anything at all, from hunger to curiosity to the wish to finish a job.

Emotion means states like fear, joy, or frustration that colour thinking, shape priorities, and prepare the body and mind to respond.

For a long time these were treated as outside the core of cognition, sometimes dismissed as messy extras, but most researchers now agree that a complete theory of mind must include them.

The reason is that motivation decides which goals get pursued, emotion rapidly flags what matters and adjusts behaviour, and metacognition lets the system correct and manage itself.

It is honest to say this cluster is where architectures are weakest and where researchers most disagree, because feelings and self-awareness are genuinely hard to pin down and measure.

Some architectures, which we will meet later, make motivation and emotion central, while others leave them mostly untouched, and there is no settled consensus yet on the right approach.


59.4 The taxonomy of architectures

A taxonomy is a way of sorting things into groups, the way biologists sort living things into families.

This section gives the standard sorting of cognitive architectures into a few broad families, so you have a map before we tour individual examples.


59.4.1 The symbolic, the emergent, and the hybrid

The most common taxonomy splits architectures into three families based on how they represent and process information: symbolic, emergent, and hybrid.

Symbolic architectures represent knowledge using discrete symbols and explicit rules, much like sentences and if-then instructions, so that a thought is built out of nameable parts you could in principle read off.

An everyday image is a filing cabinet full of written rules and labelled cards; thinking is manipulating those cards according to the rules.

Emergent architectures, also called connectionist or neural, represent knowledge in the pattern of activity and connection strengths across many simple units loosely inspired by neurons, so that a thought is a spread of activity rather than a single symbol.

Here emergent means that intelligent behaviour arises from the interaction of many small, unintelligent parts, none of which contains the whole idea by itself, the way a wave emerges from many water molecules.

Hybrid architectures deliberately combine both styles, using symbols and rules for some jobs and neural-style distributed processing for others, on the bet that the mind itself uses both.

Each family has real strengths and real weaknesses: symbolic systems handle structured reasoning and language cleanly but can be brittle and hard to make learn; emergent systems learn gracefully and tolerate noise but struggle with precise rules and structured symbols; hybrids try to get the best of both, at the cost of greater complexity.

There is no universal agreement on which family is correct, and the three-way split is a useful map rather than a proven fact about the brain.


59.4.2 The forty-year survey and the landscape of the field

To see the whole landscape at once, it helps to look at a large survey published by Iuliia Kotseruba and John Tsotsos, which reviewed roughly forty years of cognitive-architecture research.

Their paper, whose final version appeared in 2020 in the journal Artificial Intelligence Review, examined a curated set of 84 architectures, of which they counted 49 as still actively developed at the time.

They noted that the true number of architectures ever proposed runs into the hundreds, so even a big survey covers only part of a sprawling field.

They organized the field using the same symbolic, emergent, and hybrid families described above, and they compared architectures on core abilities such as perception, attention, action selection, memory, learning, and reasoning.

They also surveyed practical uses, reviewing hundreds of real projects in which architectures had been applied to things like robotics, human-computer interaction, and games.

Two honest lessons come out of such a survey.

First, the field is large, lively, and fragmented, with many architectures pursuing different bets rather than converging on one winner.

Second, most architectures remain research tools rather than finished theories of the mind, and no single architecture yet meets all of Newell's criteria, so the grand unified theory Newell called for is still a work in progress.


CHAPTER 60. SYMBOLIC AND PRODUCTION-SYSTEM ARCHITECTURES (ARCHITECTURE)

This chapter looks closely at the symbolic family, and especially at a workhorse design within it called a production system.

A production system is jargon for a style of program built out of many if-then rules, where each rule is called a production, and thinking proceeds by repeatedly finding a rule whose if part matches the current situation and carrying out its then part.

The two most developed and most studied cognitive architectures in the world, Soar and ACT-R, are both production systems, and most of this chapter is devoted to explaining how they work in plain terms.

We will then meet three further production-system architectures, each of which made its own distinctive bet about what matters most in a mind.


60.1 Soar

Soar is one of the two flagship cognitive architectures, first developed in the 1980s by Allen Newell, John Laird, and Paul Rosenbloom, and still actively maintained today, mainly under John Laird.

The guiding idea of Soar is that all intelligent activity can be cast as searching for a way to reach a goal, and that a small set of uniform mechanisms can carry out that search across every kind of task.


60.1.1 Problem spaces and the decision cycle

Soar frames every task as movement through a problem space, which is jargon for the set of all situations you could be in plus the actions that move you between them.

A simple example is a maze: the problem space is every spot you could stand and every step you could take, and solving the maze means finding a path through that space from start to goal.

In Soar, the current situation is called a state, and the actions that change one state into another are called operators.

Soar runs continuously through a repeating loop called the decision cycle, which you can think of as the heartbeat of the system.

Modern descriptions break each decision cycle into phases: taking in new input from the senses, proposing which operators are relevant right now, comparing and selecting one operator, applying it to change the state, and sending any output to the muscles or effectors.

The comparisons in the selection phase are made using preferences, which are bits of knowledge saying things like this operator is better than that one, and Soar gathers all such preferences before committing to a choice.

The important beginner takeaway is that Soar never chooses blindly; on every cycle it lets all of its relevant knowledge speak, then picks the operator that its knowledge most supports.


60.1.2 Impasses and automatic subgoaling

Sometimes Soar's knowledge is not enough to make a clean choice, and this is where one of its most elegant ideas comes in.

When the available preferences do not point to a single best operator, whether because none is proposed, several are tied, or the choice is contradictory, Soar reaches what it calls an impasse.

An impasse is simply a moment of being stuck, the mental equivalent of pausing because you do not know what to do next.

Instead of crashing or guessing, Soar responds by automatically creating a new sub-goal whose whole purpose is to resolve the impasse, a process called automatic subgoaling.

In plain terms, when Soar cannot decide what to do, it sets itself a smaller problem, namely figure out what to do, and it attacks that smaller problem with exactly the same decision cycle and problem-space search it uses for everything else.

This is powerful because it gives Soar a uniform account of many advanced abilities: planning, reasoning about its own choices, and breaking hard problems into easier ones all fall out of the same impasse-and-subgoal machinery.

An everyday parallel: if you are cooking and suddenly cannot decide which pan to use, you stop and pose a little side question, which pan is right for this, solve that, and then continue with the main recipe.

Soar makes that stop-and-solve-a-side-problem move a built-in, automatic feature of the whole system.


60.1.3 Chunking, reinforcement learning, and the memory systems

Soar would be slow if it had to reason its way through the same impasse every time, so it learns, and its original and most famous learning mechanism is called chunking.

Chunking works like this: when Soar resolves an impasse in a sub-goal, it records a new rule that captures the lesson learned, linking the situation that caused the impasse to the answer that resolved it.

The next time a similar situation arises, that new rule fires immediately and there is no impasse at all, so effortful problem solving gradually turns into automatic, fast responding.

This mirrors human experience: a beginner driver thinks hard about every gear change, while an expert just does it, because practice has compiled the deliberate steps into automatic skill.

Newer versions of Soar add reinforcement learning, which is jargon for learning from rewards and punishments by adjusting the value attached to choices based on how well they turned out.

Chunking and reinforcement learning complement each other: chunking creates new rules to handle situations, and reinforcement learning gradually tunes the preferences among competing operators so that the more rewarding ones win out over time.

Modern Soar also contains several distinct long-term memories, each mirroring a kind of human memory.

There is procedural memory, holding the if-then rules for how to do things; semantic memory, holding general facts about the world; and episodic memory, holding records of specific past experiences, like a diary of what happened and when.

All of these feed the same central decision cycle, so the takeaway is that Soar is not one trick but a coordinated set of memories and learning mechanisms wrapped around a single, uniform way of making decisions.


60.2 ACT-R

ACT-R is the other flagship cognitive architecture, developed over several decades chiefly by John Anderson at Carnegie Mellon University.

The name stands for Adaptive Control of Thought - Rational, and its guiding idea is that the mind is finely tuned by experience to the statistics of the environment, so that its behaviour is rational given what it has encountered.

Where Soar emphasizes uniform search, ACT-R emphasizes a modular design closely tied to the brain and a careful account of the timing and probability of behaviour.


60.2.1 The modules, the buffers, and their mapping to the brain

ACT-R pictures the mind as a set of separate modules, each specialized for a different job and each thought to correspond to particular regions of the brain.

There are perceptual modules, such as a visual module for seeing and an aural module for hearing, and motor modules, such as a manual module for hand movements and a vocal module for speech.

There are two central memory modules: a declarative module holding facts and a procedural module holding rules, which we will detail shortly.

There are also modules for tracking the current problem state and control state, which keep track of what the system is working on.

Crucially, the modules do not talk to each other directly; each communicates through a small holding area called a buffer that can contain only one item at a time.

This one-item-at-a-time limit is ACT-R's way of building in the narrowness of human thought, the fact that we can only focus on so little at once, and it is a major source of the architecture's realism.

A central procedural system watches the contents of all the buffers and coordinates the whole system by firing rules based on what it sees there.

A distinctive feature of ACT-R is that its modules are mapped onto specific brain areas: for instance the declarative module is associated with regions around the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, the procedural module with the basal ganglia deep in the brain, and the visual and manual modules with the corresponding sensory and motor areas.

This brain mapping lets researchers make and test predictions against brain-imaging data, giving ACT-R an unusually direct bridge from a psychological theory down toward the biology.


60.2.2 Declarative chunks and procedural rules

ACT-R divides long-term knowledge into two kinds, matching a distinction psychologists draw between knowing that and knowing how.

Declarative knowledge is knowing that, the facts and memories you could in principle state out loud, and ACT-R stores each such fact as a small record-like structure called a chunk.

A chunk might encode a fact like four plus three equals seven, or a memory like the meeting was on Tuesday, bundling together a few related pieces of information into one unit.

Beware that ACT-R uses the word chunk for a stored fact, which is different from Soar's use of chunking for learning a new rule; the shared word is a historical accident, and the two ideas are not the same.

Procedural knowledge is knowing how, the skills for doing things, and ACT-R stores these as production rules, each an if-then statement that inspects the buffers and, if its conditions match, takes an action such as retrieving a fact or moving a hand.

Only one production rule fires at a time, and firing one takes a fixed small amount of simulated time, about a twentieth of a second, which is part of how ACT-R predicts how long tasks take.

So in ACT-R, thinking is a chain of single rule firings, each of which reads the current mental state from the buffers and updates it, gradually retrieving facts and issuing actions until the goal is met.

This clean split between factual chunks and procedural rules makes ACT-R models both readable and testable, because a modeller can point to exactly which facts and which skills are being used.


60.2.3 The subsymbolic layer: activation, utility, and the learning equations

Above we described ACT-R's symbolic level, the discrete chunks and rules; but ACT-R also has a subsymbolic level, and this is what gives it much of its power and precision.

Subsymbolic means below the level of named symbols: instead of a fact simply being present or absent, each chunk and each rule carries continuous numerical quantities that govern how it behaves.

For declarative chunks, the key quantity is activation, a number reflecting how likely and how useful that fact is right now, computed from how often and how recently it has been used plus how well it fits the current context.

Activation has concrete, testable consequences: a chunk with higher activation is retrieved faster and more reliably, while a chunk with low activation is slow to come to mind or may fail to be retrieved at all, which is ACT-R's account of forgetting.

This directly models everyday memory: a fact you use daily springs to mind instantly, while one you have not thought about in years is slow to surface or simply will not come, exactly as low activation predicts.

For procedural rules, the key quantity is utility, a number summarizing how rewarding it has been to use that rule in the past, so that when several rules could fire, the one with the highest utility tends to win.

Both quantities change through learning equations, which are mathematical formulas that update activation and utility with experience: activation rises with practice and decays with disuse, and utility is adjusted toward the rewards that actually followed each choice, a form of reinforcement learning.

The reason this matters is that the equations let ACT-R produce precise numbers, predicted reaction times in fractions of a second and predicted error rates as percentages, which can be checked directly against how real people perform.

That combination of a readable symbolic story on top and exact quantitative predictions underneath is the heart of why ACT-R has been so widely used across psychology.


60.3 The other production-system architectures

Soar and ACT-R are the giants, but they are not the only production-system architectures, and this section introduces three others, each of which pushed hard on a particular question.

Meeting them shows that the symbolic family is a spread of different bets, not a single design.


60.3.1 EPIC and the parallel peripheral processors

EPIC, which stands for Executive-Process Interactive Control, was developed in the 1990s by David Kieras and David Meyer to answer one main question: how do people do two things at once.

Its distinctive bet is on parallelism in the peripheral systems, meaning the sensory and motor machinery that surrounds central thought.

The word peripheral here means the outer processors that handle perception and movement, as opposed to the central processor that handles reasoning, by analogy with a computer's peripherals like its keyboard and printer.

EPIC surrounds a central production-rule processor with several perceptual and motor processors, for vision, hearing, hands, and speech, and crucially it lets all of these run at the same time rather than one after another.

Even its central cognitive processor is unusual in that it can fire many production rules in parallel on each cycle, rather than the strictly one-at-a-time firing of ACT-R.

Because so much runs in parallel, EPIC predicts that the true bottleneck in doing two tasks at once is often not raw thinking capacity but the physical limits of the peripherals, for example that you have only one pair of eyes and two hands, plus the strategies people use to schedule those shared resources.

EPIC has been especially influential in human-computer interaction, where it is used to predict how long skilled users take to operate an interface and where the real slow points lie.

The lasting lesson from EPIC is that a great deal of the structure of human multitasking comes from the body and the senses, not only from a central thinking engine.


60.3.2 PRODIGY and the integration of planning with learning

PRODIGY was a research architecture developed from the mid-1980s at Carnegie Mellon University, associated with Jaime Carbonell, Manuela Veloso, and colleagues, and its central concern was planning.

Planning is jargon for working out a sequence of actions in advance that will get you from a starting situation to a goal, like plotting all the moves to solve a puzzle before making the first one.

PRODIGY's core planning method was means-ends analysis, an old and intuitive strategy that repeatedly asks what is the difference between where I am and where I want to be, and then picks an action that reduces that difference.

The distinctive bet of PRODIGY was to weld planning tightly together with learning, so that the system did not just make plans but got better at making them over time.

At each point where the planner had to make a choice, it could learn search-control rules, which are rules that guide future choices so the planner does not repeat the same wasted effort.

Importantly, PRODIGY learned from failures as well as successes: when a chosen path led to a dead end, it analyzed why and formed a rule to avoid that mistake in similar situations later.

It supported several learning methods at once, all sharing the common purpose of making planning faster and smarter with experience.

The lasting lesson from PRODIGY is that planning and learning are natural partners, because a planner that remembers what worked and what failed steadily turns slow deliberation into quick, informed choices.


60.3.3 ICARUS and the architecture for physical agents

ICARUS is a cognitive architecture developed chiefly by Pat Langley and Dongkyu Choi, and its guiding concern is agents that live and act in the physical world, whether real robots or simulated bodies.

An agent is jargon for any system that perceives its surroundings and acts on them to pursue goals, and a physical agent is one whose actions move a body through an environment rather than just shuffling abstract symbols.

ICARUS's distinctive bet is that perception and action should be first-class parts of the architecture, tightly bound to its knowledge, rather than added on at the edges.

It organizes knowledge into two matching kinds: concepts, which describe situations the agent can recognize in the world, such as an object being on top of another, and skills, which describe the actions the agent can take to achieve goals.

Both concepts and skills are arranged in hierarchies, meaning big ones are built from smaller ones, so a complex skill like clear the table is composed of simpler skills like pick up and put down.

On every cycle ICARUS perceives the current scene, recognizes which concepts are true of it, and then selects and executes skills to move toward its goals, blending moment-to-moment reactive behaviour with longer-range problem solving when needed.

This tight loop between recognizing the world and acting in it is what makes ICARUS well suited to embodied tasks, where an agent must continually keep its thoughts in step with a changing physical situation.

The lasting lesson from ICARUS is that for a mind attached to a body, perception, concepts, and skills have to be woven together from the ground up, because such an agent cannot afford to treat thinking and acting as separate stages.


CHAPTER 61. CONNECTIONIST AND EMERGENT ARCHITECTURES (ARCHITECTURE)

This chapter turns to the second great family, the emergent or connectionist architectures, which take their inspiration from the brain rather than from the logic of rules.

Connectionist is jargon for an approach that models the mind as a network of many simple, neuron-like units that pass signals along weighted connections, so that knowledge lives in the pattern of connection strengths rather than in explicit written rules.

The big promise of this family is that intelligence can emerge from the cooperation of many simple parts, and that such systems learn naturally from experience and cope gracefully with noise and damage.

We will start with the founding tradition, then examine three influential examples that range from brain-detailed models to systems that recover the power of symbols using vectors of numbers.


61.1 The parallel-distributed-processing tradition

This section introduces the intellectual movement that revived neural-network thinking in psychology in the 1980s, known as parallel distributed processing.

Its ideas underpin everything else in this chapter and much of modern artificial intelligence too.


61.1.1 The founding principles

Parallel distributed processing, usually shortened to PDP, was launched into the mainstream by a two-volume book of that name published in 1986 by David Rumelhart, James McClelland, and a group of collaborators known as the PDP Research Group.

The name captures two founding principles.

Parallel means that many simple processing units work at the same time, side by side, rather than one step after another as in a conventional program.

Distributed means that any single piece of knowledge is spread across the pattern of activity over many units, and each unit takes part in representing many different pieces of knowledge, so there is no single spot where one idea is stored.

The units are loosely modelled on neurons: each receives numerical signals from others, adds them up, and passes on a signal of its own, and the connections between units carry weights, which are numbers that set how strongly one unit influences another.

Knowledge in such a network is nothing but the whole set of connection weights, and learning is the gradual adjustment of those weights, most famously by a procedure called backpropagation that nudges each weight to reduce the network's errors.

Distributed representation brings real advantages: the network degrades gracefully, meaning it still works reasonably if some units are damaged, and it generalizes naturally, treating similar inputs similarly because they produce overlapping patterns of activity.

These properties feel brain-like, since real brains also keep working after minor damage and naturally see the resemblance between similar things, which is a large part of why the PDP approach was so influential.


61.1.2 Emergence as an explanatory strategy

The deepest idea in this tradition is emergence, and it represents a genuinely different way of explaining behaviour.

Emergence means that a complex, orderly behaviour arises from the interaction of many simple parts following simple local rules, without any part containing or directing the overall behaviour.

A natural example is a flock of birds: each bird only follows a few simple rules about its neighbours, yet the flock as a whole sweeps and turns in graceful coordinated shapes that no single bird planned.

Applied to the mind, the emergentist strategy says we should not write down the rule of grammar or the rule of categorization directly; instead we should build a network of simple units and let the rule-like behaviour emerge from learning.

This contrasts sharply with the symbolic approach of the previous chapter, where rules are stated explicitly and stored as such.

A celebrated example is the past tense of English verbs: rather than programming in the rule add -ed, PDP researchers trained a network on many examples, and the network came to produce regular and irregular past tenses, and even to make the sort of overgeneralization errors children make, such as saying goed, all without any explicit rule.

The pay-off of emergence as an explanatory strategy is that it can capture the soft, graded, exception-riddled character of much human behaviour, which rigid rules often handle badly.

The honest counterpoint, which symbolic researchers press, is that some human abilities, especially structured reasoning and language, look genuinely rule-like and systematic, and it remains debated how fully emergence alone can account for them, a debate that has run since the 1980s and is not settled.


61.2 Leabra

Leabra is a connectionist architecture developed by Randall O'Reilly and colleagues that aims for strong biological realism, meaning it tries to respect what is actually known about how real neurons and brain circuits behave.

Its name is an acronym for Local, Error-driven and Associative, Biologically realistic Algorithm, which already advertises its central bet: that a single network can combine several learning principles in a brain-plausible way.


61.2.1 The combination of error-driven and Hebbian learning

Leabra's signature idea is that the brain uses two complementary kinds of learning at once, and that a realistic model should include both.

The first kind is Hebbian learning, named after the psychologist Donald Hebb, and often summarized as neurons that fire together wire together, meaning that when two units are active at the same time the connection between them strengthens.

Hebbian learning is good at soaking up the statistical structure of the world, noticing which things tend to occur together, but on its own it is undirected and does not aim at any particular outcome.

The second kind is error-driven learning, in which connection weights are adjusted specifically to reduce the difference between what the network produced and what it should have produced, so learning is steered toward correct answers.

Error-driven learning is powerful and goal-directed but, in its pure textbook form, is often criticized as biologically unrealistic.

Leabra's contribution is to blend the two, so that every weight change is a mix of a Hebbian component that captures co-occurrence and an error-driven component that pushes toward correct performance, using a biologically motivated version of error-driven learning that avoids the least realistic assumptions.

Leabra also builds in other brain-like features, notably inhibitory competition among units, which keeps only a small fraction of units active at once, producing what are called sparse representations that resemble the selective firing seen in real cortex.

The takeaway is that Leabra tries to be both a working learning system and a faithful model of cortical biology, rather than sacrificing one goal for the other.


61.2.2 The prefrontal and basal-ganglia model of working memory and control

Leabra's most influential application is a detailed model of how the brain holds information in mind and controls its own thinking, built around two brain structures.

The prefrontal cortex is the front part of the brain, just behind the forehead, long associated with working memory and planning; working memory is the ability to keep information active and available for a short time while you use it.

The basal ganglia are a cluster of structures deep in the brain, known to be involved in selecting actions and in learning from rewards.

O'Reilly and Michael Frank built a model, published in 2006 and often called PBWM, for Prefrontal cortex, Basal ganglia, Working Memory, that explains how these two structures cooperate to manage working memory.

The core insight is a gating mechanism: the prefrontal cortex can hold information stably over time, and the basal ganglia act like a gate that decides when to let new information in and when to protect what is already being held.

An everyday analogy is a doorway with a guard: the prefrontal cortex is a room where you keep the things you are currently thinking about, and the basal ganglia are the guard who decides which new items to admit and when to keep the door shut so current contents are not disturbed.

Crucially, the model learns when to open and close this gate through reinforcement learning driven by reward signals, believed in the brain to be carried by the chemical dopamine, so the system discovers on its own the right moments to update its working memory.

This matters because controlled, flexible behaviour, the ability to hold a goal in mind, ignore distractions, and update when appropriate, is one of the hardest things for any model to capture, and the prefrontal and basal-ganglia account gives a concrete, biologically grounded story of how it could work.


61.3 The neural engineering framework and Spaun

This section covers an approach that tries to have it both ways: to build models out of realistic spiking neurons while still performing the structured, symbol-like tasks that connectionist models often struggle with.

It was developed principally by Chris Eliasmith and colleagues at the University of Waterloo, and it culminated in a famous large-scale brain model called Spaun.


61.3.1 The three principles of representation, transformation, and dynamics

The foundation is the Neural Engineering Framework, usually shortened to NEF, a set of mathematical methods for building networks of simulated neurons that carry out desired computations.

Spiking neurons is jargon for model neurons that communicate with brief electrical pulses called spikes, just as real neurons do, rather than with the smooth numerical signals of simpler network models, which makes NEF models unusually close to real brain activity.

The NEF rests on three principles.

The first is representation: a group of neurons can stand for a mathematical vector, which is just an ordered list of numbers, through the combined pattern of their spiking, so that populations of cells encode quantities like a position or a colour.

The second is transformation: the connections between two groups of neurons can be set so that the receiving group computes some function of what the sending group represents, for example adding two quantities or comparing them, so that computation is built right into the wiring.

The third is dynamics: by wiring a group of neurons back onto itself with recurrent connections, the represented values can change over time in controlled ways, which lets the network hold information, build up quantities, and generate movements that unfold in time.

Together these three principles amount to a recipe: decide what quantities your neurons should represent, decide what computations should transform them, and decide how they should evolve over time, and the NEF tells you how to set the connections to achieve it.

The importance of the NEF is that it turns building a spiking brain model from guesswork into something like engineering, which is exactly what its name promises.


61.3.2 The semantic pointer architecture

On top of the NEF sits the Semantic Pointer Architecture, usually shortened to SPA, which is Eliasmith's proposal for how such neural machinery can support full-blown cognition.

The key concept is the semantic pointer, and the phrase is worth unpacking slowly.

A pointer, borrowed from computer science, is a small item that stands in for a larger body of information and can be used to fetch it, rather like a library call number that points to a whole book.

Semantic means related to meaning, so a semantic pointer is a compact vector that both stands in for a rich concept, so it can be shuffled around cheaply like a symbol, and still carries a compressed trace of the concept's meaning, so it is not an arbitrary tag.

This gives SPA the best of both worlds: semantic pointers can be combined and manipulated with the structured operations symbols allow, yet they are patterns of neural activity built and processed by the NEF, keeping the model biologically grounded.

To combine semantic pointers into structured thoughts, SPA uses mathematical operations on the vectors that can bind items together, for instance tying the role subject to the filler dog, and later pull them apart again, which lets the system represent structured propositions rather than isolated concepts.

The importance of SPA is that it offers a concrete answer to a long-standing challenge: how a brain made of neurons could nonetheless carry out the systematic, structured, symbol-like reasoning that human thought clearly involves.


61.3.3 Spaun as a large-scale functioning brain model

Spaun, which stands for Semantic Pointer Architecture Unified Network, is the showpiece that put all of these ideas together, unveiled in 2012 by Eliasmith and colleagues and reported in the journal Science.

Spaun is a simulated brain built from about 2.5 million spiking neurons, wired up according to the NEF and the SPA and organized into components loosely corresponding to real brain areas, including a single eye for input and a simulated arm for drawing its answers.

What made Spaun striking is that this one fixed model, without being rewired between tasks, could perform eight different tasks, including copying handwritten digits, recognizing and continuing number patterns, remembering lists, doing simple arithmetic, and answering questions, switching between them based on instructions given through its eye.

That breadth is exactly the unified, multi-task behaviour that cognitive architectures aim for, achieved here entirely with simulated spiking neurons producing physical actions through a modelled arm.

Spaun also reproduced human-like details, such as remembering the beginning and end of a list better than the middle, and its neurons behaved in ways comparable to recordings from real brains, giving it a rare double grounding in both behaviour and biology.

It is fair to keep the achievement in proportion: Spaun is far smaller and far less capable than a real brain, which has tens of billions of neurons, it is slow to simulate, and it handles only a fixed set of tasks, so it is a landmark demonstration rather than a finished model of the mind.

Even so, Spaun stands as one of the most complete demonstrations that a single, biologically grounded neural model can perceive, remember, reason, and act, and it remains a reference point for the ambition of building a working brain.


61.4 Vector-symbolic architectures and hyperdimensional computing

This final section covers a family of methods that pursue the same goal as the semantic pointer idea, structured symbol-like reasoning in a distributed, brain-friendly form, but as a general mathematical toolkit in its own right.

These go by two names, vector symbolic architectures and hyperdimensional computing, and they are now often discussed together as one field.


61.4.1 High-dimensional vectors and the algebra of binding and bundling

The starting point is to represent every concept as a very long list of numbers, a high-dimensional vector, often with thousands of elements, which is where the word hyperdimensional comes from.

A striking mathematical fact makes this work: in spaces of very high dimension, two randomly chosen vectors are almost always nearly unrelated to each other, so you can hand out a distinct random vector to each concept and be confident they will not accidentally clash.

On these vectors the approach defines a small algebra, meaning a handful of operations you can perform to combine and manipulate them, and two operations are central.

Bundling, also called superposition, combines several vectors into one, typically by adding them element by element, and it produces a result that is similar to each of its ingredients, so bundling is how you represent a set or a collection, the vector equivalent of a bag holding several items.

Binding combines two vectors into a new one that is dissimilar to both, and it is how you tie two things together into a pair, for example linking a role like colour to a filler like red, so binding is the vector equivalent of gluing two items into a labelled unit.

Binding comes with an inverse, an unbinding operation that lets you recover one member of a bound pair if you know the other, which is what makes the structures useful rather than one-way scrambles.

With just these operations, and one more that reorders a vector's elements to mark sequence, you can build up structured records, lists, trees, and simple sentences, all as single vectors of the same fixed length, which can then be compared for similarity by a simple numerical measure.

The beginner takeaway is that this is a way of doing the structured, symbol-like work of thought using nothing but big vectors of numbers and a few tidy operations on them.


61.4.2 The family of models and their binding operators

Vector symbolic architectures are not a single model but a family, and the members differ mainly in what kind of vectors they use and, above all, in how they define the binding operation.

The term vector symbolic architecture was coined by the psychologist Ross Gayler, while the closely related term hyperdimensional computing was introduced by the computer scientist and neuroscientist Pentti Kanerva, and today the two labels name overlapping views of the same family.

One influential member is Holographic Reduced Representations, developed by Tony Plate in the 1990s, which uses vectors of ordinary numbers and binds them with a mathematical operation called circular convolution, a way of blending two lists into one of the same length.

Another member, often called the Multiply-Add-Permute scheme associated with Gayler, uses vectors whose entries are just plus one or minus one and binds them by simply multiplying the two vectors element by element, which is fast and easy to compute.

Kanerva's Binary Spatter Codes use vectors of zeros and ones and bind them with the exclusive-or operation, a basic logical operation that returns one when two inputs differ, again giving a cheap and hardware-friendly binding.

The reason there are several schemes is that each strikes a different balance among ease of computation, how cleanly items can be recovered, and how well the method suits particular hardware, so no single member is best for every purpose.

For a beginner the pattern to notice is that all these models share the same overall plan, concepts as high-dimensional vectors combined by binding and bundling, and differ mainly in the arithmetic details of how binding is carried out.


61.4.3 The solution to variable binding and its robustness

The deepest reason to care about this family is that it offers a clean answer to a classic difficulty for brain-style models known as the variable binding problem.

The variable binding problem is the challenge of representing which value goes with which slot, for instance keeping straight that in the cat chased the dog it was the cat doing the chasing and the dog being chased, and not the other way around, without the two roles getting confused.

Simple neural networks that just blend everything into one activity pattern have long struggled with this, because they tend to lose track of what is attached to what, an issue raised forcefully by critics of connectionism in the late 1980s.

Vector symbolic architectures solve it directly with the binding operation: you bind the role chaser to the filler cat and the role chased to the filler dog, add the two bound pairs together into one vector, and later use unbinding to ask who was the chaser and correctly recover cat.

This gives a distributed, neuron-friendly system genuine structured representation, the ability to hold and query who-did-what-to-whom, which was exactly the capacity symbolic critics said connectionist models lacked.

A further attraction is robustness, meaning the representations tolerate error and noise well: because information is spread across thousands of vector elements, corrupting or losing some of them degrades the answer only gradually rather than destroying it, much as a smudged photograph is still recognizable.

This graceful tolerance, together with the fact that the operations are simple and highly parallel, has made hyperdimensional computing attractive not only as a theory of how brains might bind variables but also as a practical, energy-efficient style of computing for real hardware.

The honest summary is that vector symbolic architectures provide one of the most promising bridges between the two great families of this book, keeping the learning and robustness of the emergent approach while recovering the structured, symbol-like power of the symbolic approach.

CHAPTER 62. HYBRID ARCHITECTURES (ARCHITECTURE)

This chapter is about a family of blueprints for a whole thinking machine that deliberately refuse to pick a single method.

A cognitive architecture is a proposed design for the fixed machinery of a mind, the permanent parts that stay the same no matter what the mind happens to be thinking about.

A hybrid architecture is one that mixes two very different styles of building that machinery, and it does so on purpose because each style is good at something the other is bad at.

The first style is symbolic, which means it stores knowledge as clear-cut symbols and rules, rather like sentences and if-then statements you could read on paper.

The second style is connectionist, which means it stores knowledge as patterns of activity spread across many simple units wired together, rather like the way a brain spreads a memory across many neurons.

Symbolic systems are excellent at careful step-by-step reasoning but poor at learning fuzzy patterns from raw experience, while connectionist systems are excellent at learning fuzzy patterns but poor at exact reasoning, so a hybrid tries to get the best of both.

This chapter walks through the best known hybrids one at a time, and for each one it explains, in plain terms, what the designer was trying to solve and how the pieces fit together.


62.1 CLARION

This section introduces CLARION, a hybrid architecture built around a single big idea, which is that a mind has two layers of knowledge, one you can put into words and one you cannot, and that the two layers constantly teach each other.

CLARION was created by the research group of Ron Sun, a cognitive scientist, and its name is an acronym for Connectionist Learning with Adaptive Rule Induction On-line.


62.1.1 The explicit and implicit levels

The central claim of CLARION is that human knowledge comes in two kinds at once, and that any honest model of the mind has to represent both.

Explicit knowledge is knowledge you can state out loud, inspect, and reason about deliberately, such as the rule "if the light is red, then stop".

Implicit knowledge is knowledge you have but cannot easily put into words, such as the feel of riding a bicycle or the hunch that a chess move is strong.

CLARION gives each of these its own home inside every part of the system, so it has what its designers call a dual representational structure.

The explicit level is stored in a symbolic form, meaning as tidy rules and clearly labelled items that the system can point at and manipulate.

The implicit level is stored in a connectionist form, meaning as the weights of a small neural network, which is a web of simple units whose connection strengths encode the knowledge in a smeared-out, hard-to-read way.

A helpful everyday picture is the experienced driver who reacts correctly to a sudden hazard before they could possibly explain in words what they just did, and who only afterward puts the reaction into a spoken rule.

The distinctive bet of CLARION is that these two levels are not the same knowledge written twice, but genuinely different, and that intelligent behaviour comes from their interaction rather than from either one alone.

Because the model keeps both levels for every task, it can reproduce a wide range of laboratory findings in which people plainly know how to do something before they can describe how they do it.


62.1.2 The action-centred, non-action-centred, motivational, and metacognitive subsystems

CLARION is not a single undivided blob, but a set of four cooperating subsystems, each responsible for a different job, and each one carrying the two-level implicit-and-explicit structure inside it.
